This is the annotated edition of System Design: the Northstar demo of the Forma company app platform (Two apps in one platform build, Northstar's outbound investigation and Spend Review, as one team's reduced deployment of the platform designed in `tasks/forma-generative-app-platform-v2/`; the demo recorded for YC.): the full design document, unchanged, with a teaching layer over it. Written for a developer with two years' experience who has worked through the platform's annotated edition, is reading a second design document, and will build this demo next.

Method: what this section of any design document is forWhy: why this design chose what it choseTry it: a question to answer before reading onG1, D4, TH3: identifiers link to their definition, hover to read itterms are defined on hover and in the glossary

72 design notes, 17 method notes, 237 terms, 16 exercises, 324 flashcards, 145 identifiers defined, 68 links to read more.

A design document is an argument, not a manual. It says: here is a problem, here is what done looks like, here is the shape I chose, here is why the other shapes lose, here is what could go wrong and what I will do about it. Read it the way a reviewer does, with questions, not the way you read a novel, from the first page to the last.

Read it in three passes. First the summary, the goals and the pictures in the architecture overview (a context and a container diagram on most documents): twenty minutes, and you should be able to say in two sentences what the system is and what it gives up. Second the key-decisions table and the alternatives: now you know why it has this shape and not another. Third, the section that matters to you: the data flows if you will build it, the threat model if you will attack it, the operations section if you will run it.

Keep three questions beside you as you read. What breaks if this is wrong? Every number, every decision and every assumption in a good document says. Who enforces this? A claim with no component behind it is a wish. Where is the cost? Everything added for speed, safety or scale also adds complexity, money, a surface to attack and something to monitor; a document that lists only benefits is hiding the bill.

Identifiers are the document's way of pointing at itself. G is a goal, R a functional requirement, N a quality requirement, with its number or the reason it has none, A an assumption, SR a security requirement, D a decision, F a flow on a data-flow diagram, and Q, in some records, an open question. The threat model adds families of its own: invariants, threats, mitigations, trust levels, entry points, assets, threat actors, attack goals and accepted risks, and the risk register and the scenarios may have theirs. Their letters differ from one document to the next, so read each family's prefix from the table that introduces it. The data-flow diagrams name their elements P (a process), DS (a data store), EE (an external entity) and B (a trust boundary). In this edition every identifier the text defines is a link with its definition on hover, and a diagram element shows its label on hover.

The brief's asks, and where the record answers them

The controlling definition is the App Platform definition, which PRODUCT-BRIEF.md restates for the demo and the record cites as §16 (the six acts), §18 (the completeness test) and §19; SCENARIOS.md turns it into the fixtures S01 to S07, and BUILD-HANDOFF.md lists the eight legitimate reductions, each with the seam the platform must keep.

Ask in the brief Where the record answers it What to learn from it
§16 act 1, enter the company workspace: click and /security resolve to one space, only permitted items show, an unknown command creates nothing R1, 5 (act 1), 7.1 (act 1), 6.1, D4, D9 Start with the platform, not the app; the first evidence is an absence, nothing created and no model called, which only an audit row can show.
§16 act 2, bring evidence and describe the job: a CSV by drop and an XLSX by keyboard Upload, interpretations confirmed, revisions pinned, nothing published R2, A6, 6.4, 7.1 (act 2), TH10 An import is untrusted input until a person confirms its meaning; real caps make the refusal on camera a test rather than a prop.
§16 act 3, form and transform a useful app: six linked views labeled retrieved, adapted or generated, a meaningful change as a patch with preview, diff and undo R3, 5 (act 3), 6.4, 6.5, 7.1 (act 3), D5, D8, TH11, TH12 A meaningful change is a calculation that changes, the whole-window denominator, shown as a semantic diff; a restyle would not count.
§16 act 4, publish and run: the reviewer approves the exact draft, the author's own publish is refused, live work with receipts survives a reload R4, R5, 5 (act 4), 6.2, 7.1 (act 4), N2 The refusal is as much evidence as the approval, and a restart filmed and timed turns the design's weakest point into a measurement.
§16 act 5, share the work and reuse the tool: the same case reopened by a colleague, new work with its own identity, revocation R6, G3, 5 (act 5), 7.1 (act 5), 6.3 Sharing gives a second person the same identity under a new grant, reuse gives a new identity with new bindings; keep the two apart and both can be tested.
§16 act 6, create a different app: a queue, a detail view and a decision form through the same path, a duplicate-safe retry, a stale-edit conflict, the return to Security R7, G2, G4, 7.2, 8, 9, N9, D3 A second app proves the platform only if nothing changed between the two: one build digest, a silent deploy log and the platform's own command code.
§18: at least two apps with different purposes exercise one creation, publication, access and saved-work model, with no developer changing platform code G1, G2, N9, D3, 7.2, 13.3 Generality is observable only as an absence: no branch on a tenant's name and no deploy between the apps.
§18: a second user completes supported work independently G3, R6, 7.1 (act 5) Independence is a separate work id with empty findings beside the first user's untouched totals.
§18: saved work reopens with its context intact R5, R7, N2, 6.1, 7.2 (step 7) Context that survives a reload and a restart lives on the server; the browser only drops late answers.
§18: revoked permission prevents further access R6, SR6, 7.1 (act 5), 7.2 (a revocation racing a paused command), TH9 Revocation is an epoch checked on every request and at delivery, so queued work is denied too; a download already made cannot be recalled.
§18: a changed source or calculation produces an understandable state R3, R6, 6.2, 9 Every change makes a new identity, a revision or a digest, so old approvals and old work cannot silently follow it.
§18: a published app stays usable when a new draft or generation attempt fails R4, N4, 6.4, 7.1 (act 4), 11.4 Keep the model off the published app's path; its outage then ends a take but never breaks published work.
§18: a reused app binds to the new user's permitted data G3, R6, 7.1 (act 5) Reuse copies the app, never the evidence: new bindings and new totals.
§18: organization boundaries hold G5, R8, SR2, D2, TH4, 7.2 (step 8) Isolation is proved by an adversary you script and pair with the owner's success, every take.
§19: a synthetic demo is not evidence of adoption 3.2, A10, N8, 13.2 Say what the evidence cannot prove: a synthetic recording shows mechanisms, not customers.
S01 platform home and meaningful creation: one id for click and slash, permitted items only, labeled creation, both import paths and the keyboard path R1, R2, R3, N12, 5 (acts 1 and 3), 7.1 Accessibility is an acceptance path, not a finish: the keyboard path imports and navigates like the mouse.
S02 Northstar arithmetic and source interpretation: the half-open window, 1,140,000 bytes, 240,000 matched and 900,000 unmatched, the whole-window rate, late epochs dropped R2, R5, N6, 6.5, 7.1 (acts 2 and 4) Pin meaning in the fixture: integers recomputed on the server, a half-open window and a whole-window denominator leave no room for a plausible wrong number.
S03 transform, preview and publication: a patch with a semantic diff, undo as a revision, a stale patch refused, approval of the exact draft, self-publication refused R3, R4, 6.2, 7.1 (acts 3 and 4) Approve a digest, not a draft number, so that any later change voids the approval.
S04 same work, new work and version adoption R6, G3, 7.1 (act 5), 9 Two identities, one for continuing and one for starting, each with its own grants and its own revocation.
S05 a second app with writable records R7, G4, 6.3, 7.2, 8, 9 One transaction holding outcome, version, epoch and audit gives idempotency and visible conflicts together; the order of the checks is the design.
S06 failure and adversarial cases N4, N7, R8, 10.4, C, 11.4 Each hostile stimulus becomes a test that captures the server's denial and the absence of effect, never a model's refusal.
S07 evidence packet for a working demo R9, G6, D7, 6.7, SR4, 13.3 The packet, not the video, is the evidence: pins, digests, receipts and outcomes as received, every simulated step labeled, the manifest anchored.
Reduction: two synthetic organizations and manually provisioned accounts 6.8, 6.1, 6.7, D6 Shrink the number of tenants, never the tenancy: real membership replaces the script through the same adapter without touching authority.
Reduction: one operated deployment with small stores 6.8, 6.6, D1, D10, 11.1 Collapse deployments, not boundaries: database roles keep the write grants when the network hops go, and the organization id in every key lets the stores split later.
Reduction: small CSV and XLSX fixtures 6.8, 6.4, A6 Lower the limits and keep the pipeline: the same bounded parser, its caps raised when measured.
Reduction: two apps and a small trusted component library 6.8, 6.5, D5 A library change is a release made before the build digest is taken, never a change during the recording.
Reduction: one configured model, or synthetic composition fixtures in an early spike 6.8, 6.4, D8, TH12 A stand-in for the model must be labeled where it is made, in the admission report, so it can never pass as generation.
Reduction: manual policy and retention administration 6.8, 6.2, 6.7, D6, RK4 Administration by script still goes through the platform's own administration API and its audit, and a check before every take keeps the script honest.
Reduction: no simultaneous coediting 6.8, 6.3, 3.2 Expected versions and visible conflicts prove the property co-editing would need, no silent overwrite, at a fraction of the cost.
Reduction: no live connector or external action 6.8, 6.3, 7.2 (step 6) Keep internal records and external effects apart: a "reviewed" decision pays nobody.

How this document was made

The record was written in phases, each with a checkpoint. Intake read the brief and turned every unanswered question into a numbered assumption. Targets wrote the context, the goals and the requirements with derived numbers. Shape drew the context and container pictures and sketched the API and the alternatives. Detail wrote the component cards, the data flows and the data model. Attack built the threat model from the data-flow diagrams and fed the mitigations back into the design as security requirements. Run wrote the operations section. Honest wrote the drawbacks, the alternatives, the risks and the open questions. Finish wrote the summary last, moved reference material to the appendix and sent the document through a gate: a script that checks the mechanical rules, a fresh reviewer who had never seen it, a security reviewer where the mode or the brief calls for one, a check of every product claim against the vendor's own documentation, for a document that describes existing code a check of every code claim against the repositories at their pinned commits, a cross-check of the finished document against the research it was built from, and a scored comparison against an exemplar of the same size. Refine derived the reader's edition and the presenter notes, which a fresh reader then checked, and Receive put the submission in front of a reader playing its recipient, each unless the head waived it, and the cross-check's edition slice ran after Receive. Teach produced this edition, and a junior reader and the cross-check's teaching slice then checked it. A later version revises the one before rather than starting again, names what it supersedes, and goes back through the same gate.

The order matters more than it looks. Writing the problem before the solution keeps the problem honest. Drawing the pictures before the component detail keeps the detail attached to a shape. Attacking the design after the flows exist, and before operations, means the mitigations are real components with failure modes, not a paragraph of good intentions. Writing the summary last means it summarises what was built, not what was planned.

System Design: the Northstar demo of the Forma company app platform

Two apps in one platform build, Northstar's outbound investigation and Spend Review, as one team's reduced deployment of the platform designed in `tasks/forma-generative-app-platform-v2/`; the demo recorded for YC.
AuthorVictor Villacis
Date2026-10-22
StatusProposed
RevisesDesign B v5 (task/forma-mvp/v5, the earlier demo record) in direction: the demo inside the platform, now two apps on the typed app definition instead of the insurance demo on markup modules; none of v5's scenes, fixtures or modules carries over
ReviewersA fresh reviewer and the security reviewer at phase 7 (L2); recorded in STATUS.md
ApproversVictor Villacis (the head)
Review by2026-11-05
Read firstinput/brief.md; PRODUCT-BRIEF.md (the controlling definition, the six acts); SCENARIOS.md; BUILD-HANDOFF.md; the platform record tasks/forma-generative-app-platform-v2/design.md and its reading note

How to read this record. "§N" is section N of the controlling definition, the App Platform definition in input/context/, which PRODUCT-BRIEF.md in this folder restates for the demo, SCENARIOS.md turns into the fixtures S01 to S07 and BUILD-HANDOFF.md into eight reductions with their seams; this record's own sections are cited as plain numbers. "The platform record" is tasks/forma-generative-app-platform-v2/design.md, the design this demo reduces; it revises design A (task/forma-platform/v4, the security-first platform on markup modules), as this record revises design B (task/forma-mvp/v5, design A's insurance demo). Identifier families: K1 to K5 are the head's kickoff rulings of 2026-10-22, recorded in both tasks' intake.md: K1 the typed app definition rendered by first-party components, K2 standard mode at L2, K3 the stack tickets assumed done, K4 fAuth first, its build checked viable and its sign-in moment ruled in on 2026-10-22 as a quiet real moment with no passkey button, K5 Parquet and DuckDB for sources with PostgreSQL for records. C01 to C16 are the shared contracts (SHARED-CONTRACTS.md, lock edition prep-2026-10-22.1). A bare D, G, A, R, N, F, SA, AG, TH, M, AR, RK or SR number is this record's, and TL, SI, AS and TA continue the platform's numbering; the platform's are always prefixed "platform", and platform D15, hosting on AWS in one region, is the one platform decision this record reduces rather than binds (D10). A1 to A10 come from the intake, A11 to A14 from the K rulings and the fAuth check (review/fauth-viability.md). EXP-002 is S05's fixture expense, 45,000 cents; ik-1 and ik-2 are the packet's names for the idempotency keys of its two record commands, ik-3 the stale edit's. The 28,100 B budget is Forma's gzip ceiling for one route's Forma payload (BUILD-819), the figure the canvas route is measured against. Status tags: [built] exists at a named pin; [proposed] is this design; [reduced: the platform's X] replaces the platform's X here, with the seam in section 12; a tag may name the part it covers, as in [built: the rendering]. Terms, in the platform's sense: a space is a company-defined area of apps inside an organization, Security and Finance here; the canvas is the surface on which an app's views are arranged, rendered by one browser island; the composer is the assistant that turns an intent into a proposed definition or patch, through a job the worker runs; the control plane admits definitions and alone writes publications and policy, and its admission report says what it checked and refused; the data service runs typed queries and record commands; a receipt is the server's record of exactly which sources, revisions, parameters and policy produced a number; a case is saved work, one id pinned to the publication it was started on with its bindings, records and notes, moved to a newer publication only by explicit adoption; an expected version is the record version a command was based on, so a stale command conflicts; an epoch is a counter that a change of filter, membership or policy advances, so a late result can be told from a current one; the canary is the second synthetic organization whose scripted suite replays every call with Northstar's identifiers and must be denied; the packet is the evidence bundle delivered with the recording (S07); the platform key is fAuth's credential for creating tenants, held only by the operator's script.

1. Summary

Method

For. The reviewer asks: what did you build, what did you give up, and what is hard to undo? Three to five sentences answer it; one of them says what the design optimises for and at whose expense; one names the scope; one names the one-way doors, the decisions that are expensive to reverse.

Look for. The sentence of the form "optimises for X at the expense of Y". If you cannot find Y, the author has not chosen yet. Typical one-way doors: how stored data is laid out, public contracts, the identity or isolation model. A service split can go either way, which is why the decisions table labels each door, and some doors are costly to reverse because reversing them needs someone else's action. Everything else can be changed on a Tuesday.

Pitfall. Writing the summary first. It then describes the plan rather than the design, and it drifts as the sections below change. It is written last and read first.

Why

Before you start: whose identifier is it? The reading note above the summary sorts every identifier into two kinds. A bare one, such as D5, G6, TH15 or SR2, belongs to this record: it is defined here, and it is what you will build. One after the word "platform", as in "platform D5", "the platform's A4" or "Platform SR1, SR2", belongs to the platform record and is only cited; the demo inherits it unchanged. So does every number in a table column whose heading names the platform: "The platform's" in 5.3, "Seam, the platform's" in 6.8. This edition leaves the parent's identifiers unlinked, so a link always leads to a definition in this record. The two numberings are independent, so one number can mean two things: D5 here is the component library the demo ships with, platform D5 is the record command; D1 here is one process, platform D1 is the typed app definition. Four families continue the platform's numbers instead of restarting, TL, SI, AS and TA, so TL9 is the first trust level this record adds and TA11 the first threat actor; TL0 to TL8 and TA1 to TA10, cited bare, are the platform's. The notes on 10.2 and 10.3 say what each of the platform's is. The rest of the reading note points at documents beside this one: K1 to K5 the head's rulings, C01 to C16 the shared contracts, S01 to S07 the fixtures in SCENARIOS.md, and §16, §18 and §19 sections of the controlling definition.

A dependent record. This record writes only what differs from the platform record and cites the rest, so that each fact has one home and the two documents cannot drift apart. It keeps without restating the platform's contracts, its decisions platform D1 to D14, its component cards, its flows and its data model, and writes in full what is new: one process instead of four deployments, the eight reductions, the operator's three tools (the provisioning script and the evidence recorder, which run on the operator's machine, and the reset, the binary's one demo-only part, 6.7), the evidence packet, and the threat rows whose control is the demo's own. The price is that some mechanisms are explained only in the platform record, which is why each borrowed sentence names its platform section. Pitfall. Reading "the demo" as a smaller, separate program. It is the platform's own code run as one process on one host, plus one demo-only route behind a flag; "keeps the platform's code" in the summary is literal, and it is what lets the demo grow into the platform (G7).

Notice what the summary does with its weakest point. One host with no standby is the design's largest cost, and the summary states it plainly: "a restart that is a scene". The design does not hide the restart; it films it and times it against a 30-second limit (N2, in 4.2), so the cost becomes a measurement a partner can weigh instead of the first question a partner asks.

The Northstar demo is the platform record's design as one process on one host, recorded in six acts: Maya forms an investigation app over imported evidence, Sarah publishes it, Jordan reuses her work, and Maya forms Spend Review, a different app, by the same path, no deploy between (section 5). A recording of two fixed dashboards would prove none of it (section 2), so the design keeps the platform's code, reduces its deployment eight ways with named seams (6.8), adds three operator tools, the reset under a rehearsal flag (6.7), and signs in through fAuth as a registered client (D9). It optimises for generality and isolation, one build digest across six acts and nothing of Northstar reaching the canary, at the expense of scale, availability, generation latency and cost: one host, no standby, a restart that is a scene. It covers the six acts, the spike, the rehearsal procedure and the packet; a pilot on real data, a production SLO and the passkey button are out (3.2). One-way doors: the organization id in every key (D2), the platform's definition and command code (D3), the integrity rule once the packet is submitted (D7); the rest of 5.3 reverses.

Try it

The summary names three one-way doors: the organization id in every key (D2), the platform's definition and command code (D3), and the integrity rule once the packet is submitted (D7). Before reading 5.3, write for each what reversing it a month after the recording would require, and whose action it would need. Then say why the hand-added client row (D9), awkward as it is, is not on the list.

Answer

D2 needs our own action, but on everything stored: the organization id is in every key in every store from the first row, so reversing it means a migration of all stored data and every reference to it, and the isolation the recording showed would then describe keys the system no longer has ("keys cannot be retrofitted on camera", 12.2). D3 needs our own action too: a second implementation of the definition, admission and command code, after which every contract reopens and act 6 would have proved an implementation that no longer runs (12.2). D7 needs someone else's: the packet is with YC, so relabeling a step would take the recipient's action, not ours ("a packet cannot be relabeled after YC has it", 12.2). Two doors are one-way because of what a reversal would touch, the third because the reversal is out of our hands. D9 is one row and one redirect URI in fAuth's database: replacing it, with the refresh-cookie bridge or a future client API (13.2's POST /manage/oauth-clients), is our action on one adapter's input and touches nothing the platform stores, which is why 5.3 marks it two-way (1, 5.3, 12.2).

All exercises

2. Context and problem statement

Method

For. The reviewer asks: do you understand the problem, independent of your solution? This section is facts and constraints only, told so that if the design were rejected tomorrow, the section would still be useful to whoever tries next.

Look for. The problem as a mechanism: what breaks, at which step, at what number. "The dashboard is slow" is an adjective; "a filter over a million rows scans the table and returns in nine seconds" is a mechanism. The constraints, sorted: technical (the platform, languages and products already chosen), organisational (team, budget, deadline), conventions (the standards and ways of working the design must follow). The scale regime: a startup's and an established product's answers differ on nearly every later page.

Pitfall. Smuggling the solution in. "The problem is that we do not have a queue" is a solution wearing a problem's clothes. The problem is what happens without one.

Why

Why the problem is told as three shortcuts. Nothing is built yet, so there is no broken system to describe; the failure this section describes is a recording that looks right and proves nothing. Each shortcut is the cheapest way to make one act look done, and each names what it leaves untested: the denominator lives in code, the decision lives in the browser, one session plays three people. That is the "problem as a mechanism" rule applied to a demo: what fails, at which step, and why a video cannot show it. The design answers all three the same way, with evidence kept outside the video: the packet (S07).

What a reduction is, and what it is not. The constraints end with four things that are not reductions: a login dropdown, work kept only in browser memory, faked commits and a hardcoded act 6. The test that separates them: a reduction makes something smaller (fewer organizations, smaller files, a script instead of a page) and keeps the platform's interface for it, the seam through which the platform's mechanism will later replace it; each of the four replaces a mechanism with its appearance, so there is no interface to grow back into. Apply the same test to any shortcut you are tempted by while building.

Read "What exists" as your starting line. Three things are [built] at pins you can check out: Forma 3.0.0, fAuth and the composition fixture. Everything else in this record is [proposed], still to be written. Keep the fixture's 27,674 of 28,100 B in mind, 28,100 B being the most compressed Forma code one route, one page, may load; the D5 note explains what the 426 B left can and cannot pay for.

This record designs the platform's demo: two apps formed, published and reused on one reduced build, recorded for YC against its request A Cloud for Small Software, which asks that small software be as easy to share with colleagues as a Google Doc (§20). The platform forms governed apps over imported data: a model proposes a typed definition, a reviewer publishes it, every number carries a receipt. Market framing and the prototypes' limits: platform section 2.

What the demo must establish. The controlling definition has six acts (§16): enter the workspace, bring data, form and transform an app, publish and run it, share and reuse it, build a different app. The last "must show a meaningful difference in purpose and behavior, not merely two fixed dashboards behind different colors" (§16). The completeness test (§18) asks that "at least two apps with different purposes or interactions" exercise one creation, publication, access and saved-work model, that a second user works independently, saved work reopens with its context, revocation holds, and a published app survives a failing draft. S01 to S07 (SCENARIOS.md) are those clauses as fixtures.

What exists. The platform record (tasks/forma-generative-app-platform-v2/design.md) at its phase 7 gate commit 0de0308: contracts C01 to C16 at lock edition prep-2026-10-22.1, decisions D1 to D15, binding except D15, which D10 reduces. The native composition fixture (platform review 4.3), which compiled a canvas of four component kinds on Forma 3.0.0 2006423b with data at first paint, at 27,674 B of the route's 28,100 B gzip budget. fAuth, Forma's own identity service (getforma-dev/gatewasm), at b750ca53: 44 smoke tests pass, the northstar tenant is provisioned (review/fauth-viability.md).

What a recording of two fixed dashboards would fail to prove. The fixtures are S02's five connection events, 1,140,000 bytes in a ten-minute window, and S05's expense EXP-002, whose decision moves from needs_context to reviewed. Take the shortest path to pixels:

  1. A developer writes a handler that sums S02's bytes and divides by ten minutes. The number is right, but the denominator lives in code; act 3's "meaningful change" is a commit the recording cannot attribute. Act 6 fails §18 outright: Spend Review is a second handler.
  2. The decision form on EXP-002 keeps needs_context in browser state. S05's 64,000-cent table and 45,000-cent queue display correctly; a reload loses the decision, a retried submit makes two, and nothing holds an expected version (platform R8).
  3. One session plays Maya, Sarah and Jordan. No publish is refused, no shared work reopens under another principal, no canary organization is denied; §18's isolation and reuse clauses go untested.

Each shortcut is invisible in a video; the record, not the recording, carries the evidence (S07).

Constraints. Technical: one process on one host (platform D11); synthetic data; the typed app definition (K1; platform D1); the native composition fixture as the spike's first step; the eight reductions of BUILD-HANDOFF.md, each naming the platform seam that replaces it (section 6's table); Forma's compiler limits unchanged (platform section 2). Organisational: the spike precedes any rehearsed scene; one founder builds and operates; fAuth's sign-in moment is ruled in, quiet (K4). Conventions: Northstar is fictional; simulated behavior is labeled and "excluded from working-capability acceptance" (PRODUCT-BRIEF.md); a login dropdown, work only in browser memory, faked commits or a hardcoded act 6 are not reductions.

Scale regime. A rehearsal, not a service: two organizations, five accounts including the operator, at most four concurrent sessions, about 0.8 actions/s sustained (A4). The platform's envelope is its section 4.

Try it

Write a fourth shortcut in section 2's form, for act 5, share and reuse: the fastest way to make Jordan's reopening of Maya's case look right on screen, other than section 2's third, which already has one session play everyone. Then name what it leaves untested, by the goal or requirement it fails, and the observation in the packet that would expose it.

Answer

One version: give Jordan a copy of Maya's case under a new id; the screen shows the same findings. A copy is a different work id, so G3's "reopens Maya's case by its work id at its pinned publication with its records" fails, and so does R6's same id, records and pin. It also outlives revocation, because revoking Jordan's grant on Maya's case does not touch his copy, so R6's "revocation denies later results" cannot be shown, and a concurrent edit cannot conflict because the two cases share no record (G3's visible conflict). The packet would expose it twice. Act 5's "both work ids" must be Maya's own id, reopened under Jordan's session, and his new one for ops-runner-04; with the copy, the case Jordan opens carries an id Maya never had. And no denial follows the revocation (5 act 5's "Captured"; 7.1 act 5; S04). Any answer is right that names a mechanism replaced by its appearance and the identity or denial that the evidence would then lack (2).

All exercises

3. Goals, non-goals, and assumptions

Method

For. The reviewer asks: what does done look like, and what did you choose not to do? Goals are checkable; non-goals are things that could reasonably have been goals and were declined, with the reason; assumptions are the questions the brief left open, each with what changes if it is wrong.

Look for. A "done when" clause on every goal. A non-goal that someone might argue for; "the system must not crash" is not a non-goal, it is a platitude. The assumptions list is the author's honesty about what they did not know: every one of them is a question a reviewer can answer and change the design with.

Pitfall. Goals that cannot fail. "Secure" and "scalable" are not goals; "a payment is applied at most once, however often the client retries" is, because a test can break it.

3.1 Goals

Why

A goal that can fail. Each "done when" names a fixture value or an observable absence: G3's 210,000 bytes beside Maya's untouched 1,140,000, G4's version 1 and then version 2, G2's runtime with no branch on Northstar, Security or Finance. Each goal is therefore a test that can come out red, which is what separates a goal from a hope. G2 is the hardest kind to prove, because generality shows only as an absence: a search of the runtime that finds none of those names, and a deploy log with nothing in it between the two apps.

G7 is about the demo's afterlife. The other goals are about the recording; G7 asks that every container map onto a platform container, so that the demo is the platform's first deployment rather than a prototype to throw away. It is the goal behind every "seam" you will meet from here on.

The design goals are six acts on one build (one image digest, no deploy between acts), generality (one typed definition path, no branch on a name), governed persistence (records in one transaction under expected versions and idempotency keys), isolation (the organization id in every key, row-level security, two data keys), integrity (every scene names its mechanism, the packet carries the evidence) and a path to the platform (every reduction names its seam), checked on the running demo.

Why

Three labels, and why a label is not an apology. A step is seeded when its state was put in place rather than produced on camera (the reset restoring a captured state between takes, a take being one recording of an act or of the whole run; or a fixture proposal standing in for the model's, as in the spike, the measurement run before any scene), simulated when the script provokes or fakes a behavior (act 6's response dropped at the browser to force a retry), and manual when a person does by hand what the product would do. A labeled step may appear on screen, but it is excluded from acceptance: it never counts as evidence that a capability works. 13.3's "What is simulated?" is the full list of the demo's labeled steps, by label. Labels are what let the demo show a hard case honestly, a lost response on camera, without pretending the network failed by chance. Pitfall. Treating labels as bookkeeping to finish later. Once YC holds the packet nothing can be relabeled (D7), so an unlabeled seeded step voids the claim it touches.

  • G1 Six acts, one build. Done when acts 1 to 6 (§16) run end to end on one build digest on which S01 to S07 pass and the seven completeness clauses (§18) are ticked.
  • G2 Two apps, one authoring path. Done when act 6 creates Spend Review through act 3's interface with no commit or deploy between, and the runtime has no branch on Northstar, Security or Finance (platform G1, R14; S07).
  • G3 Work continues and reuses. Done when Jordan reopens Maya's case by its work id at its pinned publication with its records, a concurrent edit conflicts visibly, and his work for ops-runner-04 totals 210,000 bytes under its own id while Maya's 1,140,000 stand (S04).
  • G4 Records persist, retry safely, conflict visibly. Done when EXP-002's decision survives refresh and restart, an ik-1 retry yields one revision and one audit event, a stale version conflicts, and ik-2 makes version 2 (S05; platform G4, D5).
  • G5 Isolation shown with the canary. Done when the canary organization replays every call and link with Northstar's identifiers and gets nothing, not even metadata; a Security-only principal cannot read Finance; revocation stops derived and queued results (S01, S06; platform G5).
  • G6 Nothing simulated passes as working. Done when every scene names its mechanism, every seeded, simulated or manual step is labeled and excluded from S07's acceptance measures, and the packet holds pins, digests, receipts, record outcomes and the rehearsal log (S07).
  • G7 The demo grows into the platform. Done when each reduction names its seam (section 12) and every container maps onto a platform container under D1 to D14 (platform C16).

Success: six acts on one build, Spend Review made without a developer, every section 4 target met. Failure (intake item 35): two fixed dashboards, a per-example platform change, lost work, unsafe reuse, a security tool posing as the platform.

3.2 Non-goals

Why

Each non-goal is something a viewer might ask for. A partner could expect a passkey sign-in, a live co-editing cursor, or the MCP scene the earlier demo had, and each line says why the recording does without it. The passkey button would spend act 1 on the identity service's feature instead of the platform's. Live co-editing is one of the demo's reductions (6.3, 6.8), and the property that matters, that no edit is silently lost, is shown in act 6 more cheaply: every edit carries the version it was based on, its expected version, so a stale edit is refused as a visible conflict instead of overwriting. Notice "Platform 3.2's non-goals hold here": a demo cannot be larger than its platform, so it inherits every refusal and adds only its own.

Platform 3.2's non-goals hold here. The demo adds:

  • Customer data or a pilot. Synthetic rows prove mechanisms, not adoption (§19).
  • A production SLO. One host and one operator cannot promise one (platform N2); we measure.
  • fAuth's passkey button. Server-ready, unwired at b750ca53; ruled out (K4): sign-in is ten quiet seconds.
  • An MCP scene and a public page. Design B v5 had both; K1 needs neither, §18 defers both.
  • Coediting. Act 6 shows a conflict, not a cursor; expected versions are the seam.

3.3 Assumptions

Why

Read each "If wrong" as a map of what moves. The useful clauses are the narrow ones: A12's "only act 1 changes" says a sign-in problem stays inside the first act, and A9's "G7's seams are exercised" says a second host would test the very interfaces the reductions keep. A clause that said "redesign" would tell a reviewer nothing. A11 states the whole dependency on the platform in one line: if a platform decision moves, this record follows it.

One Chrome profile an actor (A13). A profile keeps its own history, passwords, settings and accounts apart from the other profiles on the machine (Chrome profiles), so Maya, Sarah and Jordan can each hold a real, separate session on the one recording machine. It is the direct answer to section 2's third shortcut, one session playing three people.

Envelopes, not forecasts (provenance: the reading note).

Why

Why caps far above the fixtures. The fixtures are a six-row CSV and a two-row XLSX, with Jordan's two-row CSV in act 5, so a cap set just above them would refuse almost any real file and say nothing about the parser. A6 sets limits between the fixtures and the platform's own, so that the one refusal act 2 captures (S06) comes from the bounded parser's real limits rather than from a cap tuned to the fixture. The limits are a reduction with a seam: the same pipeline, raised when measured (6.4).

  • A1 Audience. A YC partner watching, an engineer reading. If wrong: the editions.
  • A2 Roles. Maya builds, Sarah reviews, Jordan reuses, under explicit grants. If wrong: grants move, authority holds.
  • A3 One operator provisions, resets and restores. If wrong: section 11 names more.
  • A4 Scale and rate. Two organizations, five accounts, four sessions, 0.8 actions/s sustained, four-action bursts. If wrong: remeasure.
  • A5 Read-heavy, writes measured in rehearsal. If wrong: load-test commits.
  • A6 Input caps. CSV 10 MiB, 100,000 rows; XLSX 5 MiB compressed, 50 MiB expanded, 10,000 rows × 32 columns per sheet: a tenth of the platform's A4 for CSV and half for XLSX, a reduction (6.4) still far above the fixtures, so the oversize refusal is real. If wrong: raise when measured.
  • A7 Fan-out. Six linked views per filter. If wrong: bound query concurrency.
  • A8 No SLA for a synthetic demo. If wrong: a pilot sets one.
  • A9 One process, one host. If wrong: G7's seams are exercised.
  • A10 Synthetic data only. If wrong: redo data classes and threats.
  • A11 Platform D1 to D14 hold at the lock. If one moves: this record follows.
  • A12 Sign-in. fAuth opens act 1 (K4); the platform's minimal login behind the same adapter is the fallback. If wrong: only act 1 changes.
  • A13 Recording. Chrome, one profile an actor; sign-in is the platform's PKCE authorization-code flow as a registered fAuth client (platform SR2), one hand-added oauth_clients row. If wrong: the same-site refresh-cookie bridge, same adapter.
  • A14 Spike first. The spike (section 5) passes before any rehearsal. If wrong: the recording waits.
Try it

It is the morning of a rehearsal and sign-in is broken, in one of three ways: (a) fAuth's service is down; (b) the provisioning script inserted the client row with a typo in its redirect URI; (c) the head learns that fAuth at the pin cannot hold a registered client at all. From section 3 alone, name the assumption each case breaks, if any, and what you would do. Then derive what the assumptions only imply: for (a), what must already be true of the design for A12's "only act 1 changes" to hold; for (c), which goal A13's fallback strains, and why. Check (a) against 6.9 and 11.1, and (b) against SR3 and 11.4, when you reach them.

Answer

(a) breaks the first half of A12, fAuth opening act 1: wait for fAuth, or switch before the take to A12's fallback, the platform's minimal login behind the same adapter; either way only act 1's scene changes. For "only act 1 changes" to hold, a session must not need fAuth once it exists: the platform keeps its own sessions and checks fAuth's tokens without calling fAuth. It does: sessions are PostgreSQL rows that live 12 h, tokens are verified offline against the cached key set, and the fallback is switched before a take, never during it (5.1, 6.1, 6.9, 11.1; 11.4's fAuth row: act 1 waits, later acts continue). (b) breaks no assumption: A13 holds, since fAuth can hold the row, and the row is simply wrong, so nothing in the design moves. Correct the row by hand and prove sign-in before the camera rolls; the record's check is the dry sign-in, which stops a take until it passes (SR3, 6.1; 11.4's row for the provisioning script's output), and D9 being a two-way door is why a hand fix is enough. (c) breaks A13: its fallback is the same-site refresh-cookie bridge behind the same adapter, so act 1's mechanism changes and D9 would be revisited. The goal it strains is G7: the bridge is a session contract the platform never ships, so either the demo signs in in a way the platform does not, or the platform carries it for one demo, and 12.2 rejects it for that reason (12.2's table, 12.3). The three mornings look alike, "sign-in is broken", and the assumptions separate them: one has a fallback, one is an error to correct, one moves a decision (3.3, 5.3, 12.2).

All exercises

4. Requirements

Method

For. The reviewer asks: what exactly must the system do, in numbers, and what will prove it? Users on two axes (people or programs; consumers or enterprises), functional requirements R-n with MUST, SHOULD, MAY, quality requirements N-n each with a number and the derivation behind it, or the reason it is not required, and the security requirements SR-n that section 10 emits.

Look for. Where each number came from. A rate per user, times users, times a peak factor, gives a rate per second; that chain should be visible. Percentiles rather than averages: "p99 under 2 s" means one request in a hundred may be slower, and says so. The requirement, or requirements, the design deliberately lowers; every design lowers at least one, and the honest ones say which. A short fault model: which failures are tolerated by redundancy, which by isolation, and which, usually a data leak, must be prevented rather than survived.

Pitfall. Requirements as wishes. "The system should be fast" asks nothing. "Search returns its first page in under 300 ms at p99, measured at the client" can be tested, missed and argued about.

Why

The canary is a stakeholder. The table gives a row to a hostile principal, the canary, whose concern is that every replay is denied and audited. Writing the attacker's experience as a requirement turns isolation into something a test checks on every take, rather than a property you hope holds. Notice who is absent: a customer, because the data is synthetic and a pilot is a non-goal (3.2).

Stakeholder Concern Section
The head two apps, one path, nothing hidden 5, 12, 13
The YC partner is the second app real; what is simulated 5, 7, 13
The engineer which contract each piece implements 5, 6, 9
Maya, Sarah, Jordan an app from evidence; the reviewed draft ships; reuse copies nothing 6, 7
The operator provisioning, reset, restore, budget 11
The canary every replay denied and audited 10

4.1 Functional

Why

How to read an R line. Each line says what must hold, then three kinds of citation in brackets: the act and fixture where the recording shows it (act 6, S05), the platform requirements it inherits (platform R8), and the shared contracts (C07). MUST and MAY carry their RFC 2119 meanings: a MUST that fails is a defect, a MAY is permission. The paragraph above the list already holds the rule section 5 builds on: "a take has one actor at a time".

Five manual enterprise accounts: Maya builds in Security and, by grant, Finance; Sarah reviews; Jordan reads shared work and writes his own; the operator provisions, restores and files the packet, reading only synthetic data; the canary, in the second organization, gets nothing. Rate (A4): 0.8 actions/s over four sessions, 4.8 query operations/s over six linked views, a burst of 24; a take has one actor at a time (5.2). Northstar reads; Spend Review writes about twenty records a rehearsal.

Why

One policy per organization. R7, below, has Sarah approve Spend Review "under the organization's one policy". Security and Finance are spaces, areas of apps inside one organization, and publication policy belongs to the organization, not to a space or an app (platform R9). So Spend Review inherits Northstar's independent review, and Sarah's approval is ten seconds of act 6. Pitfall. Reading a space as a wall between tenants. The wall between companies is the organization, and the canary is another one; inside one organization, grants decide who reaches which space, which is why "a security-only principal cannot read Finance" is tested on its own (7.2).

Why

Why a denial needs its owner's success. A 404 alone cannot tell "refused" from "no such thing". Pairing each replay with the owner's 200 on the same identifier in the same take is what turns the canary's 404 into evidence of a refusal: the identifier was real and live when the canary was turned away. The canary gets 404 rather than 403 so that a refusal never confirms that the thing exists; HTTP allows exactly this, a 404 from a server "not willing to disclose" that a resource exists (RFC 9110).

  • R1 Home. Maya MUST sign in through the adapter and reach Security by click or /security, one id; home and recents show permitted items only; a command matching nothing creates nothing and calls no model (act 1, S01; platform R1, R15; C03).
  • R2 Import. Maya MUST import the six-row events CSV by drop and the two-row inventory XLSX by keyboard Upload into inspected source cards, units, window and match rules confirmed, revision pinned, nothing published (act 2, S02; platform R3; C05).
  • R3 Composition and change. Maya MUST get six linked views over one declared asset, window and filter, each labeled retrieved, adapted or generated; the transfer-rate measure (whole-window denominator) and an observation form MUST arrive as patches with preview, semantic diff and undo; a stale patch conflicts; previews write apart; partial output never executes (act 3, S01, S03; platform R4, R5, R7; C04, C08, C13).
  • R4 Publication. Sarah MUST approve the exact draft under Northstar's independent-review policy; Maya's self-publish is refused; a later change invalidates the approval (a test); a failing draft never disables the published version (act 4, S03; platform R9, R13; C09).
  • R5 Saved work. Maya MUST start live work from the published version, see each number with a receipt and save her observation; a reload restores work and view state; a prior-epoch response is discarded; the assistant MAY set a declared filter, marked and undoable (act 4, S02, S04; platform R2, R6, R12; C02, C06, C12).
  • R6 Share and new work. After separate grants the case MUST reopen for Jordan with its id, records and pin; a bare link reveals nothing; revocation denies later results, delayed ones included; his ops-runner-04 work, on evidence he imports, has its own id and empty findings; cases stay pinned until explicit adoption (act 5, S04; platform R2, R10, R11; C02, C10, C11).
  • R7 Spend Review and return. Through the same path Maya MUST form a queue at amount_cents >= 20,000, a detail view and a decision form, Sarah approving it under the organization's one policy (platform R9); EXP-002 under ik-1 at version 0 commits version 1 with one audit event; ik-1 retried returns that outcome; a stale version conflicts; reviewed under ik-2 commits version 2; no payment occurs. Back in Security, case and view state return, a late Finance response fills no Security card, a security-only principal cannot read Finance (act 6, S05; platform R1, R8, R14; C03, C07, C11, C13).
  • R8 The canary. Every call replayed with Northstar's identifiers MUST be denied before data or metadata and audited, each denial paired with its owner's 200 that take (S06, S07; platform R15, R16; C01).
  • R9 Evidence. The packet MUST hold the pins, both definitions and digests, fixtures, receipts, record outcomes and a rehearsal log with S07's times, sample sizes and conditions; simulated behavior is labeled and excluded from acceptance (S07; C16; §16).
  • R10 Reductions. Each of the eight reductions MUST name its seam, the platform mechanism replacing it (6.8; platform R14; C16).
  • R11 The spike first. Before any scene, BUILD-HANDOFF's path MUST pass on the real library and route: definition, query, receipt, command, outcome, reopen, the duplicate submission, the version conflict, the route's payload against 28,100 B (platform 5, A14; C16).

4.2 Quality requirements (non-functional)

Why

Measured, not promised. N3 copies the platform's latency targets, but on one host with no standby the demo cannot promise them, so it reports them with their sample sizes. A percentile is a statement about many samples: "p99 1 s" says one interaction in a hundred may take longer, so a p99 means little until there are hundreds of samples (SRE book on objectives).

Read the ranking with the faults paragraph. N9 ranks first because it is the claim the recording is judged on (§18): two apps on one unchanged build. Each rank carries its reason in one clause, and N7's, "not traded", means no gain anywhere else justifies a leak. The faults paragraph makes the same split by kind of failure: a lost host is survived by snapshot and restore, while a cross-organization leak is "prevented, not tolerated", because nothing restores data once another company has read it.

Load is the envelope, no skew; ten rehearsals, each one whole-run take filmed at most twice. A 30-minute rehearsal, one actor at a time at one action per 5 s, holds about 360 interactions: about 200 six-view refreshes (1,200 operations), 40 navigations, 20 commits, the rest edits and uploads.

Why

N2 counts restarts, not uptime. N2, below, has no availability percentage to promise, since there is no SLA, so it is written from the recording's side: a restart may happen, and it must cost one redone step, never a lost act. It reports the maximum over twenty restarts rather than a percentile, because twenty samples are too few for a percentile and because one slow restart is one lost scene. Its last clause, zero platform-caused retakes in the last three rehearsals, reads as the readiness test.

  • N1 Scalability. Not required beyond the envelope; scale is the platform's N1 through R10's seams; A6's caps enforced (S06).
  • N2 Availability. No SLA (A8), no lost scene: after a process restart saved work reopens within 30 s (one restart a whole-run take, the maximum over twenty), so one step is redone, not an act; platform-caused retakes in the last three rehearsals: zero.
  • N3 Latency at the client, the platform's targets measured, not promised: navigation p50 250 ms, p99 1 s; six-view refresh p50 500 ms, p99 2 s; commit p50 300 ms, p99 1 s; revocation within 5 s; sample sizes in 11.3; jobs show state within 1 s.
  • N4 Fault tolerance. Safety: no fault serves Northstar's data to the canary, widens authority, duplicates a record or shows an unreceipted number. Liveness: a committed record survives a restart; a provider outage leaves navigation, queries and forms working, generation failing visibly within 1 s; a restore is timed and reported (S06).
  • N5 Consistency. The platform's N5 holds: linearizable record commands, compare-and-set publication and adoption, read-your-write, revocation within 5 s (C07, C09, C10).
  • N6 Accuracy. The fixtures recompute server-side in integers, 1,140,000 bytes, 900,000 unmatched, 114,000 a minute, 210,000 and 21,000 for Jordan, 64,000 cents and the 45,000-cent queue; every shown number equals its receipt (S02, S04, S05; platform N6).
  • N7 Security. R8's replay and every S06 row run as tests, denial and absence of effect captured.
  • N8 Privacy. Synthetic data only (A10); the composer's real-data disclosure stays off; every provider request is inspected (C12).
  • N9 Maintainability. Zero commits and deploys between acts 3 and 6: one build digest, both definition digests under it, no organization, space or app name in the runtime's control flow (S07; platform N9; C13).
  • N10 Cost. Unknown yet; the requirement is the meter, tokens a call and hosting a rehearsal, reported with the recording.
  • N11 Sustainability. Not required separately; N10's meter bounds it.
  • N12 Accessibility. S01's keyboard path and an automated WCAG 2.2 AA check on every state of the demo's components (platform N12).

Duplicate retry (N5): after a lost response the island re-submits EXP-002 under ik-1; the stored outcome returns; one revision, one audit event (S05). Provider outage (N4): the provider fails in act 3; the published app, queries and form answer within N3, the composer fails within 1 s; a drill confirms. The second app (N9): Maya forms Spend Review from primitives Northstar never used, same build; revision and deploy logs show no change (S07).

Ranked: N9, N7, N6, N5, N2. N9 is the claim the recording is judged on (§18); N7 is not traded; N6 and N5 make a decision worth keeping; N2 keeps the recording honest. Acknowledge now, deliver later: imports, generation, export. Complete before answering: commands, publication, adoption, saves. Lowered on purpose: scale, availability, generation latency, cost.

Faults: hardware, one host, met by snapshot and restore; software, a renderer or parser bug, by bounded parsing, a published version outliving a failing draft and the canary per build; human error, by confirmed interpretations, diffs, review and undo; a cross-organization leak or model-widened authority is prevented, not tolerated. Data classes (10.6): synthetic rows Confidential; credentials, sessions and keys Restricted and real; the recording Internal.

Why

Why both ends of every take. The run at the start of a take replays against the restored state and the build about to be filmed, so a failure stops the take before the camera rolls; the run at the end replays the identifiers the take itself created, new work ids, a new record and idempotency keys, which did not exist at the start (11.1, steps 4 and 6). "Behind M29's allowlist" places the suite, like the whole host during rehearsals, behind a list of the only addresses allowed to connect: the recording machine and the operator's.

Why

What anchoring the manifest digest buys. The packet outlives the video: a partner may read it weeks later, and nothing in a folder of files stops someone editing it. So after each take the recorder computes a digest of the packet's manifest, the list of what the packet holds (a digest is a short hash that changes if any byte of its input changes), and writes it as an audit event. The audit trail is a hash chain whose latest link is copied to storage under Object Lock, which in compliance mode no user, the root user included, can overwrite or delete before its retention date (S3 Object Lock), so the recorded digest cannot be quietly changed later. Anyone can recompute it from the packet and compare: an edited packet no longer matches. The rest of SR4, a scan for headers, cookies, tokens and keys, keeps the packet from carrying a credential to every recipient.

  • SR1 The reset MUST exist only under flag and role, restore digest-matched states, keep audit (M1 to M4, M15, M16). Tests: 404 per build; a tampered state 412.
  • SR2 The canary suite MUST run per build and at both ends of every take, every replay 404 against an identifier its owner resolved with 200 in that take, behind M29's allowlist (M7, M8, M25, M26, M29). Test: no non-404, none without its 200.
  • SR3 Sign-in MUST use the registered client, one redirect URI, dry-run per take (M5, M6). Test: a wrong URI.
  • SR4 Packet and recording MUST hold no header, cookie, token or key; the packet's manifest digest anchored before delivery (M11, M12, M30, M31). Check: pattern scan; the anchor.
  • SR5 Operator keys MUST stay in the keychain, then die; operator actions and build digest audited (M9, M10, M13, M14, M27, M28). Check: the packet.
  • SR6 Revocation and reset MUST reach every tab within 5 s; the sandbox dies first; injection and unknown operations fail whole (M17 to M24). Test: S06's rows.
  • Platform SR1, SR2, SR4 to SR7 and SR10 to SR13 hold; platform SR3's service token is replaced by the typed principal (10.5), platform SR8's signed release by one image digest and the per-build test (11.1); platform SR9's second person accepted away (AR1).
Try it

4.2's basis is ten rehearsals, each one whole-run take filmed at most twice, and a 30-minute rehearsal holds about 360 interactions: about 200 six-view refreshes (1,200 operations), 40 navigations, 20 commits, and edits and uploads for the rest. Rebuild the 360 and the 1,200, and work out how many edits and uploads remain. Then, before reading 11.3, decide over how many rehearsals you would pool navigations and commits to report a p99, and count the samples that would lie above the p99 in each case, compared with the 200 refreshes of one whole-run take.

Answer

30 minutes is 1,800 s; one action every 5 s is 360 interactions; 200 refreshes times six views is 1,200 query operations; 360 − 200 − 40 − 20 = 100 edits and uploads. A p99 leaves one sample in a hundred above it, so one whole-run take's 200 refreshes leave 2 above it, enough to say something, while its 40 navigations or 20 commits leave less than one, so their "p99" would just be the slowest sample. Pooling ten rehearsals, one whole run each, gives 400 navigations, 4 above the p99, and 200 commits, 2 above, which is what 11.3 does; the refresh needs no pooling because one take of the whole run already holds 200 (4.2, N3, 11.3). The counts are per whole run: a take of one act holds only that act's share of them.

All exercises

5. Architecture overview

Method

For. The reviewer asks: can I hold the whole system in my head after this section, and do I know which decisions matter? One worked scenario told as if the system exists, the system context picture, the container picture as a zoom of it, a fit check that lands the numbers on the boxes that carry them, and the key-decisions table.

Look for. The context picture first: the system as one box, every kind of user and every outside system it talks to. Then the containers: the deployable pieces and the stores, with arrows that say what crosses and how. The "like X, unlike X" sentence that places the system next to one you know. The decisions table: each row says whether the door is one-way or two-way, which goal it serves, and where the alternatives are argued.

Pitfall. Pictures without arrows that mean anything. An unlabelled line between two boxes tells the reader nothing; a line that says "HTTPS, OAuth bearer token, order events as JSON" tells the reader three things to check.

Why

Read each act's "Captured" line first. Each act gives its mechanism, its fixture values and what the recording keeps. The "Captured" list is the act's acceptance test and the mechanism is how the build produces it; a builder who starts from the captured evidence builds what proves the claim rather than what merely looks right. The six lists together are most of the packet (S07).

The spike is the first thing you build. "Prototyped" names what is already measured, the four-kind canvas, and says that nothing of the demo's own is. The spike (D8, R11) is the first real work: one complete path from definition to reopen, with the duplicate submission and the version conflict, on the real library and route. It runs before any scene because its numbers can change decisions (5.3).

The demo is the platform record's design as one process on one host, an ECS task by default (D10): two synthetic organizations, two apps, a script for administration. It optimises for N9, one build digest across the acts, and N7, nothing of Northstar reaching the canary, at the expense of scale, availability, generation latency and cost (section 4). The [built] pins are Forma 3.0.0 2006423b, fAuth b750ca53 and the composition fixture.

The six acts: mechanism, fixture values, what the recording captures.

  1. Enter the workspace (S01). Maya signs in at fAuth [built] (D4) and lands on the company home; click and /security resolve to one id; an unknown command creates nothing and calls no model (platform C03).
  2. Bring evidence (S02). She drops the six-row events CSV and the two-row inventory XLSX; the sandboxed parser writes revision 1 as Parquet under Northstar's key; she confirms bytes, UTC, exact entry first (platform C05).
  3. Form and transform (S01, S03). The worker alone calls the provider for a typed AppDefinition [proposed], the labeled fixture in the spike (platform D8); the control plane admits it; six linked views render, labeled retrieved, adapted or generated [built: the rendering]. She patches the transfer-rate measure, 114,000 bytes a minute over ten minutes, and the observation form; a stale patch is 412 (platform D9). Captured: the admission report, the semantic diff.
  4. Publish and run (S03, S02). Maya's own publish is refused; Sarah approves the digest; the control plane writes publication 1 (platform D2). Live work: five events, 1,140,000 bytes, 240,000 matched and the 900,000 unmatched all to 198.51.100.7, each with a receipt (platform C06); a restart reopens the case within 30 s (N2). Captured: the refusal, six receipts, the restart time.
  5. Share and reuse (S04). After separate grants Jordan reopens the case by its id; a bare link is 404; for ops-runner-04 he imports his own two-row CSV and starts new work, 210,000 bytes, 30,000 unmatched, 21,000 a minute; Maya revokes his grant from the share control (C11), and his next refresh within 5 s is denied, a queued result included (platform C10, C11). Captured: both work ids, the 404, the late denial.
  6. A different app (S05). In Finance, by the same path on the same build, Maya forms the 64,000-cent table, the queue at amount_cents >= 20,000 holding EXP-002 at 45,000 cents, and the decision form; Sarah approves it under the organization's one policy (platform R9); needs_context under ik-1 at version 0 commits version 1; the ik-1 retry returns that outcome; a second expected-0 edit is 409; reviewed under ik-2 is version 2 (platform D5, C07). Security's case returns; a late Finance response is dropped. Captured: an unchanged deploy log, both digests, two audit events.

Then the canary's replays (S06) and the packet (S07; R9).

Like a staged product demo it is rehearsed, synthetic and thirty minutes long; unlike one, every number has a receipt the record reproduces, and the second app is made on camera through act 3's interface, not loaded.

Prototyped: the platform review's composition fixture, a four-kind canvas on Forma 3.0.0 at 27,674 of 28,100 B gzip (platform 5); nothing of the demo's own. The spike (D8; R11) runs first on the real library and route: BUILD-HANDOFF.md's path from definition to reopen, with the duplicate submission and the version conflict; 5.2 lists its measurements.

5.1 System context

Why

What the context picture argues. A context diagram usually shows the users and the services a system calls; this one also draws an adversary as a user. The canary's arrow carries the proof on its label, 404 before any data and audited, and the canary enters through the same door as Maya (B10 is "a second B1 crossing"), so its replays test the real path rather than a special one. Why the two outside systems see opposite halves. fAuth knows who signs in and never sees data; the model provider sees schemas and synthetic rows and never learns who asked (N8), so a compromise of either yields only half the picture.

The demo as one box, [proposed] except fAuth [built at b750ca53]: Northstar's people and the operator at their entry points, the canary apart, the two systems called.

What matters: the canary's arrow is the isolation proof, every call made with Northstar's identifiers from another organization's session answered 404 before any data (G5), 404 rather than 403 by the platform's rule that existence must not leak (platform 9); and the externals see opposite halves: fAuth who signs in, never data, its EdDSA tokens verified offline against its key set; the provider schemas and synthetic rows, never who asked (N8). Boundary B1 is Northstar's people and the operator in Chrome (A13); B10 is the canary's browser, a second B1 crossing from another organization. Simplified: sign-in is a redirection drawn as the demo's call; the operator's script runs from the operator's machine with fAuth's platform key (7.3); the provider is absent while the spike uses the labeled fixture.

5.2 Containers

Why

Five database roles in one process, and why that is not one shared credential. The four platform roles, workspace, control, data and worker, run as modules of one binary, but each opens its own connection pool as its own PostgreSQL role, a database identity with its own grants (permissions to insert into or update particular tables). So a bug in a page handler cannot insert a publication: PostgreSQL refuses the workspace role, whatever the code forgot. The trap this avoids is 12.2's option B, every module through one credential, where any bug can write anything. What the design does not buy is protection from hostile code: the process runs as one cloud identity, its task role, which may connect as all five roles, so an exploit inside the process can open any pool. The walls stop mistakes, not an attacker already inside (AR2). The fifth role, reset, exists only for the rehearsal reset (6.7).

The burst one action causes. The averages, 0.8 actions and 4.8 query operations a second, are not what sets latency here. One filter change fans out to six queries at once, one per linked view, and the data service runs only two of one organization's queries at a time and queues the rest, so a refresh arrives in waves. That is why "one actor at a time" is part of the design rather than a stage direction: the rehearsal script, not the code, keeps the burst at six (11.1, 11.2).

A restart that is not a task replacement. A load balancer probes its target every 10 s and takes it out of service after a run of failed checks, three here (target group health checks). Without a supervisor, a crashed binary would end its container and ECS would replace the task: pull the image, start it, register it, pass a health check, a sequence nobody has timed against 30 s. The supervisor, a small process inside the container whose only job is to restart the binary, brings it back in place before the third failed check, so the restart costs only the process start, its pools, one key-set fetch and the browser's reload. One full task replacement is still timed, apart, because that number decides which host the demo runs on (13.2).

A zoom into diagram 01's demo box: the host's edge, the four roles in one process, the parser's WebAssembly sandbox, the two stores, the outside services; each role keeps its database role, so the platform's write grants survive; one task role connects as all five, so the separation holds against logic bugs, not against code in the process (D1; platform D11; AR2).

Two paths, one authorization point (platform 5.2). Interactive, down the right: the browser workspace [built: the rendering] adopts pages the workspace server renders and calls the JSON API; the workspace server is the one authorization point and the only caller of the control plane and the data service, in process here, HTTP there (D1). Background, from the left: the worker claims jobs from PostgreSQL under role worker, writes their state back, runs the parser as a WebAssembly module with no system interface, writes Parquet to object storage and alone calls the provider. Only role control writes publications and policy; only role data reads Parquet and commits records. The load balancer ending TLS is P1 [reduced: the platform's edge, no CDN, no WAF]. Left out: the operator's script, on the same API; key management, one data key an organization (platform D3).

The fit check lands section 4's numbers on this process. Load (A4). Four sessions at one action per 5 s are 0.8 actions/s, 4.8 query operations/s over six linked views, a burst of 24. The island fans six queries at once (platform 6.5) and the data service admits two of an organization's at once (platform 5.2); the rehearsal script has one actor act at a time (11.1), so a take's burst is six operations, 2 running and 4 waiting, three waves and 0.3 s at the platform fit check's 100 ms an operation, inside N3's 2 s. The envelope's burst of 24 would queue 22, past the 20 that return 429 (platform 6.3): four simultaneous actors are not a take. Twenty commits a rehearsal are one transaction each on an instance without a standby [reduced: the platform's Multi-AZ; backup and timed restore the seam], so N3's p50 300 ms is the round trip plus two session reads. Latency (N3). Navigation p50 250 ms is a session read, an epoch read and one render of typed props; revocation within 5 s is the epoch checked on every request plus the canvas refresh, at most 5 s apart (platform 6.5). Restart (N2). The 30 s is the process start, its pool, one key-set fetch and the island's reload; one restart a whole-run take, twenty, the maximum reported. An ECS task replacement is unmeasured against 30 s, so a supervisor restarts the binary in place inside the load balancer's grace of three failed checks 10 s apart; one full replacement is timed apart (11.2). Availability (A8). No SLA; the hard chain is the process, PostgreSQL and object storage; fAuth and the provider are soft (12-hour sessions; generation fails visibly, R13). Storage is kilobytes; retention per the platform's A6. The spike measures the real route, the commit against N3, the route's bytes against 28,100 B with the renderer library imported, the restart maximum, one bounded XLSX refusal, and the server's render rate and memory per render on the task (platform 5).

Try it

Rebuild a take's burst from 5.2's rules: how many query operations one filter change puts at the data service, how many run and how many wait, how many waves, and how long at 100 ms a warm operation. Then redo it for a version of Spend Review with eight linked views during a scene where two actors act at once: the operations, the waves, the time, any 429s, and the warm operation time at which N3's 2 s would stop holding.

Answer

One actor, six linked views: six operations; the data service admits two of an organization's at once, so 2 run and 4 wait, three waves, 0.3 s at 100 ms, inside N3's 2 s (5.2); the waves are why 6.3 puts the ceiling at a warm operation of about 650 ms, three waves inside 2 s. Two actors, eight views: 16 operations in one organization, 2 running and 14 waiting; 429s begin only past 20 waiting (5.2; platform 6.3), so none is refused; eight waves of two, 0.8 s at 100 ms, still inside 2 s; and N3's 2 s stops holding at a warm operation of about 2 s ÷ 8 = 250 ms. The envelope's burst of 24 is different in kind: 22 waiting is two past the 20, those two are the 429s, and that is why four simultaneous actors are not a take (5.2, 6.3, 11.2).

All exercises
Try it

5.2 has the supervisor restart the binary "inside the load balancer's grace of three failed checks 10 s apart". (a) From those two numbers, how soon after a crash can the third failed check come? (b) Predict what the take sees if the binary takes 40 s to come back. (c) Act 4's restart drill falls between acts 3 and 6, where N9 allows no deploy. From N9's own wording, decide what a change must alter to count as a deploy, and so whether the drill is one; then design the check that would tell a restart from a deploy in the evidence, and compare it with 6.7 and TH14 when you reach them.

Answer

(a) Checks come every 10 s, so the first failure lands up to 10 s after the crash and the third 20 s after the first: between about 20 and 30 s after the crash the target is taken out of service (5.2; the load balancer's failure threshold). (b) At 40 s the target has been taken out of service, so the load balancer stops sending it requests and Maya's reload fails until the binary is back and the checks pass again (11.4's first row: the target re-registers on the next check); the case reopens later than N2's 30 s, and a miss of N2 ends the take (11.1, step 5), so act 4 is retaken from s3, and the acts after it with it (8). One more consequence is an inference the record implies without stating it: 5.2 puts the restart inside the grace so that it triggers "no task replacement", so a restart past the grace may bring the task replacement as well, the sequence nobody has timed against 30 s (RK8). (c) N9 asks for one build digest for both apps and no deploy between acts 3 and 6, so what it forbids is a change of the image that runs. A restart, in place or even as a new task, runs the same image digest, so it is not a deploy, as 6.7 says outright: "a task start on the same image digest, act 4's restart drill, is not a deploy". The check follows from that definition: read the task's image digest at the take's start and end, and the deploy log between them. A restart leaves both unchanged; a deploy changes the digest or writes to the log, and either fails acceptance. That is TH14's M28, run by the evidence recorder (6.7, N9, TH14).

All exercises

5.3 Key decisions

Why

Why only three doors are one-way. The test is what reversing a decision would take. D2: rewriting every key in every store, because the organization id is in all of them from the first row. D3: re-proving every contract, because a fork would make act 6 prove a different implementation. D7: someone else's action, because once YC holds the packet nobody here can relabel it. Every other row is a reduction or a choice the platform's own mechanism can replace later. The one-way and two-way door language comes from Amazon's 2015 shareholder letter.

The last column names the platform decision each binds to, so the demo grows into it without a rewrite (G7; platform C16); alternatives are in 12.2.

Why

Why "a kind is a release". D5's row below fixes the component library. A component kind (a summary, a table, a timeline, a form) is renderer code compiled into the build, so adding one during the recording would be a deploy between acts, which N9 forbids; every kind both apps use is registered before the build digest, the hash of the exact image that is filmed, is taken. The row also names two operators, registered calculations an app definition may call: the CIDR lookup, which matches an address to an inventory network, and the integer currency operators, which keep money in whole cents. What 426 B of headroom means. The route has two budgets: Forma's own code, at most 28,100 B compressed, of which the fixture's four kinds used 27,674 B, and the route's 365 KiB of JavaScript, against which each kind's own code counts (6.5). Only the first is scarce, and a new kind spends it only by importing a Forma module the four did not, createResource or the HTML runtime; so what a kind costs is not its own size but what it pulls in from the framework. That is why the spike imports all nine before any scene (R11), and why the way out, FORMA-232's application budget or a kind cut, is a two-way door.

Why

Why a script and not administration pages. Pages only the operator uses would be built and tested before any pilot asks for them (12.2's table), while a script that calls the platform's own administration API exercises exactly the interface a later page will call: the seam. The cost is "kept true by hand": nothing stops the script being wrong, so the pre-take assertion compares the live memberships and policies with the script's manifest before every take (6.7, 11.1).

Why

Why measure before rehearsing. Each of the spike's numbers can change a decision: the route's bytes decide whether a kind is cut (D5), the commit's latency tests N3's commit target (p50 300 ms, p99 1 s), the restart maximum tests N2's 30 s. Found on camera, any of them would waste takes (12.2's table). The cost is that the first rehearsal waits. Pitfall. Treating the spike as a throwaway prototype. It runs the real path on the real library and route (R11), so what it measures is the code that will be filmed.

Why

A public client: why the row holds no secret. In the authorization-code flow the browser comes back from fAuth with a one-time code, which the platform exchanges for a token (RFC 6749, section 4.1). A confidential client would prove itself at that exchange with a client secret; this one is public and uses PKCE instead: at the start of each sign-in the platform makes a random code verifier and sends fAuth only its hash, and at the exchange it sends the verifier, which fAuth hashes and compares (RFC 7636). A code stolen on its way back is useless without the verifier. The registration row then needs no secret, only the client's identity and its one redirect URI, the single address a code may be sent to, so there is nothing in it to store, rotate or leak into the packet. It is added by hand because fAuth at the pin has no API for clients (AR4).

Why

The one decision that reduces rather than binds. The platform runs on AWS in one region (platform D15). The demo keeps the region and the core services, ECS, RDS, S3, KMS and a load balancer, but runs one task instead of four services spread over two zones, with no standby, no content network and no firewall (11.1). Notice the cost column, "money, metered": this is the only decision whose cost arrives every month whether or not anyone rehearses (11.2), which is why its cheaper alternative, a host that costs nothing, gets its own argument in 12.2.
