6. Component design

Method

For. The reviewer asks: does each piece have one job, a clear interface, known dependencies and a known ceiling? Each container that holds a hard choice gets a card: responsibility in one sentence, why it is a separate box, its contract, its dependencies, its extension points, a worked example, what can go wrong, and the ceiling: "stops working at N because M".

Look for. The ceiling line on every card. A component with no stated ceiling has not been thought through; everything stops working somewhere. The dependency table, in section 6 or the appendix it points to: which dependencies are hard (the component is down when they are) and which are soft (it degrades). The sentence that says what the component deliberately does not do.

Pitfall. Describing what the code does instead of what the box is for. A card that lists methods is a class diagram; a card that says "its one job is to decide whether a payment may be applied, and it refuses everything else" is a design.

Why

Every card must justify its box again. In the platform each card is a separate deployment, a box because a network separates it. Here all four share one process, so each card answers "Why still a boundary" afresh, and the answer is always what one role's credential can do that the others' cannot: write a publication, read Parquet and commit a record, reach the provider. Read each card for that line and for "In a rehearsal", the demo's version of the platform cards' "What can go wrong": the failure that costs a take, not an incident. Notice that the cards name no extension point of their own, because the platform's hold unchanged (the section's first line). To practise Lesson 4's form, "to add Y you add Z without editing W", use 6.8's seams instead: 6.1's is already written that way, real membership replacing the script "without touching authority".

The platform record's section 6 is the parent: its cards, write paths and extension points hold unchanged. Element ids are the platform's; the demo adds P9 the provisioning script and P10 the evidence recorder, which run on the operator's machine against the API the binary ships (section 9; diagram 04), and P11 the reset job behind the rehearsal flag, a setting the platform's deployment never sets, the binary's only demo-only component. No level-3 diagram; platform diagram 03 applies.

6.1 Workspace server (P2, role workspace)

Why

Why a token without tenant_id mints nothing. The claim is optional in fAuth's tokens, and the platform takes the organization from that claim alone, so a token without it has no organization to give a session. Refusing is what failing closed means here: there is no default organization a token could fall into.

A restart is a reload, not a sign-in. Sessions are rows in PostgreSQL (DS4), not memory in the process, so a restart signs nobody out. That is what makes N2's 30 s possible at all: otherwise every restart would send three actors back through fAuth's page.

Responsibility. Platform 6.1, the one authorization point; fAuth behind the session adapter, the minimal login its fallback (D4). Why still a boundary. Role workspace cannot insert a publication or a record (platform 6.1), so a page handler's logic bug has the platform's reach (code in the process has every role's, AR2); the collapse swaps HTTP for an in-process call. Reduction. Two synthetic organizations and accounts by script [reduced: the platform's membership]; the seam is the adapter minting a session from tenant_id and sub (platform D6), so real membership replaces the script without touching authority.

Example. Maya's callback (tenant_id northstar, sub maya) mints session S1 at membership epoch 7, a PostgreSQL row (DS4): a restart is a reload, not a sign-in (N2); a token without tenant_id, optional in fAuth's claims, mints nothing. Revoking Jordan in act 5 sets epoch 9; his refresh within 5 s is denied, a queued result of his at delivery (C10, C11).

In a rehearsal. A missing client row or a wrong redirect URI (A13) stalls act 1 at fAuth's error; the pre-take assertion includes a dry sign-in. Ceiling. Four sessions are idle; the platform's limit is per view, about 300 KiB of typed props, and the six-row table is kilobytes. Cost: none added.

6.2 Control plane (P3, role control)

Why

What the demo changes, and the failure only a script can cause. The approval is the platform's, unchanged: Sarah approves a content digest, a hash of the exact admitted definition, so any change after her approval makes a new digest that the approval no longer matches. The card's example is that case, R4's test that "a later change invalidates the approval"; in the recording the denominator is patched in act 3, before anyone approves (7.1). What the demo changes is who sets policy: a script, through the platform's administration API (the administration group). A wrong value there crashes nothing; it changes what a take can show, which is why the pre-take assertion reads each organization's policy row against the manifest before every take.

Responsibility. Platform 6.2, admission and publication under the organization's policy. Why still a boundary. The only credential writing a publication, a policy or a governance audit row; the role handling model output shares its process and still cannot (12.2's test). Reduction. Policy and retention by script through the administration group (6.7) [reduced: the platform's administration pages]; the seam is the versioned policy table and its audit. Write path. The platform's SERIALIZABLE transaction, unchanged.

Example. Draft sha256:2f9c… admitted; Maya's own approve is 403 naming the rule; Sarah's makes publication 1; the denominator patch makes a41e… and the approval no longer matches (S03).

In a rehearsal. The script sets a wrong policy kind, owner publication, and act 4 loses its refusal; the pre-take assertion reads each organization's one policy row (per organization, platform R9, shared by Security and Finance) against the manifest. Ceiling. Two publications a rehearsal against admission's 24 views and 8 operations a view.

6.3 Data service (P4, role data)

Why

The server simulates nothing. S05's lost response is made by the rehearsal script, which drops the response at the browser; the server receives a real second request and answers it with its real logic. With the fake on the client's side, the server's behavior on camera is the behavior that ships. Why the reset deletes outcomes. An outcome is the stored answer to a command's idempotency key, returned to any retry for 24 hours (section 9). If the reset left them, the next take's ik-1 would come back with the previous take's answer, a dead take answering a live one (TH13).

Responsibility. Platform 6.3, every number with a receipt, every record in one transaction. Why still a boundary. The only credential that reads Parquet or writes records. Reduction. No coediting [reduced: the platform's shared work under expected versions]; the seam is the record command, which carries the expected version and returns an authorized recovery view on 409 (platform D5): act 6 shows a conflict, not a cursor. No connector or external action also bites here (platform D12; 6.8). Write path. Platform 6.3's, read committed with explicit locks, unchanged.

Example. EXP-002 under ik-1 expecting version 0 commits version 1 with one audit event; ik-1 again returns that outcome before any version check; a second edit expecting 0 is 409; reviewed under ik-2 is version 2; 64,000 cents unchanged (S05).

In a rehearsal. S05's lost response is the rehearsal script dropping it at the client and forcing the re-submission (7.2), a labeled step (G6); the server simulates nothing. Stored outcomes and the result cache would answer ik-1 with the last take's state, so the reset (6.7) deletes and flushes them, leaving a take's first refresh cold for N3's measurement. Ceiling. Two operations at once an organization (5.2) run a take's six-query burst in three waves, so N3's 2 s stops holding at a warm operation over about 650 ms; the spike measures it. Cost: the DuckDB engine in the trusted base, as on the platform.

6.4 Workers and the parser sandbox (P5, P6, P7, role worker)

Why

The heading's P numbers are the platform's. Diagram elements keep the platform's ids (7), so P5 is the composer worker, P6 the import parser in its sandbox and P7 the index builder, which embeds each published app's description, examples and field names into one index file an organization, rebuilt on publication (platform 6.4, platform 7). The card names P7's work only as "indexing", and 7's "P2 to P5 and P7 share the one process" puts it in the binary with the rest. Why act 6 navigates by alias. P7's index, the one retrieval searches, can lag a publication by 60 s (platform A17), while an alias resolves to the app's stable id without the index (platform 6.1), so the scene cannot catch the index mid-rebuild.

Responsibility. Platform 6.4, parsing, generation, indexing and explanation as jobs with visible state. Why still a boundary. Role worker alone has egress to the provider; P6 stays a WebAssembly module with no system interface, so no socket and no credentials endpoint (B6). Reductions. Small fixtures [reduced: the platform's input limits]: A6's caps, a tenth of the platform's A4 for CSV and half for XLSX, far above the fixtures, one oversize refusal captured (S06); the seam is the same pipeline, limits raised when measured. One model, or the labeled fixture in the spike [reduced: the platform's provider adapter]; the seam is platform D8's provider interface; the fixture's proposal never counts as generated (G6).

Example. The six-row CSV and the two-row XLSX each parse in under a second into revision 1 under Northstar's key; Maya's intent returns, in one of two attempts, six views admission accepts.

In a rehearsal. The provider down in act 3 is provider_unavailable within 1 s (R13; a 1 s connect and 60 s request timeout) and a retake, never a continuation on the fixture; N4's drill is its own scene. Retrieval may lack Spend Review for 60 s after publication (platform A17), so act 6 navigates by alias. Ceiling. Eight slots against two jobs at once; two 60 s attempts are two minutes of a five-minute act. Cost: the provider's tokens, metered (N10).

Try it

Act 2 must capture one oversize refusal (S06). The platform record's example of a bomb is a 9 MiB XLSX that inflates past 100 MiB (platform 7.1). Explain why a 9 MiB file could never test the demo's expansion cap. Then, before reading 7.1's act 2, predict what a 4 MiB file that inflates past 50 MiB tests instead: which of A6's limits fires, and where; what stops and what survives; what the job and the recording show. Finally say what the module's 2 GiB memory cap is for, if a limit fires long before it.

Answer

A6 caps an XLSX at 5 MiB compressed and 50 MiB expanded, and a file's compressed size is known before anything opens it, so a 9 MiB file is turned away at the size check and never expands: it tests the byte cap, not the expansion cap (appendix C confirms it in TH10's M19: "the byte caps refuse before parsing"). In the platform, whose compressed cap is 10 MiB (platform A4), the same file does reach the parser, which is why it is the platform's example. The 4 MiB file passes the byte cap, so the parser starts inflating it inside its WebAssembly sandbox and meets the 50 MiB expanded cap: the parse stops there and the file is refused, the job carries the reason, the import fails visibly, the refusal is captured, and the process and the take carry on (7.1 act 2; 11.4's parser row). The 2 GiB memory cap never fires in this case: it is the backstop. If a parse ever got past the expanded cap, the runtime would still stop the module at 2 GiB, and the task's 8 GiB is sized so that 2 GiB fits beside everything else the process holds, so even then the module, not the process, would die (7.1, 11.2; TH10's M19). What the file tests is the bounded parser that is the reduction's seam (6.4) and the property one process makes critical: a bad file costs a refusal, never the process (TH10).

6.5 Browser workspace (P8)

Why

The filter epoch, concretely. Every filter change increments a counter, the filter epoch, and every query carries it; a response that arrives with an older number is dropped. In the example, selecting the destination is epoch 12, so the timeline's slower answer for epoch 11 is thrown away instead of briefly showing a number from the previous filter, and six linked views never mix two filters on screen.

Responsibility. Platform 6.5, the canvas island [built: the rendering], its library, linked filters, forms and the composer chat, with S01's keyboard path (N12). Reduction. Two apps on the platform's library, D5's nine kinds plus the CIDR lookup and the integer currency operators (C13), no kind added for the demo; the seam is the versioned registry and admission: a kind is a release, registered before the build digest is taken, so N9's zero deploys between acts 3 and 6 hold.

Example. Selecting 198.51.100.7 is epoch 12, six queries; the timeline's epoch-11 response, held late by the rehearsal script and labeled simulated, is dropped; clearing is epoch 13 and 1,140,000 returns (S02).

In a rehearsal. The 426 B left of the route's 28,100 B is Forma's own share (BUILD-819): a kind spends it only by importing a Forma module the four measured kinds did not, createResource or the HTML runtime (platform 6.5); its own code counts against the route's 365 KiB of JavaScript. Spend Review needs detail and status beyond the four (C13). The spike imports all nine (R11); over the budget, FORMA-232's application budget (K3) or a kind cut, D5 being two-way. Ceiling. That import. Cost: none beyond the platform's library.

6.6 The stores and the host's edge (DS1, DS2, DS3, P1)

Reduction. One deployment with small stores [reduced: the platform's Multi-AZ, CDN and WAF]: one PostgreSQL instance with the four roles and row-level security, one bucket with a prefix an organization under its own key in key management (platform D3), the host's load balancer ending TLS (P1), no cache, no rule set but M29's address allowlist. The seam is the store interfaces, the organization id leading every key from row one (D2): splitting the deployment moves bytes, not meaning. Acknowledged at the local commit; the recovery point is the pre-rehearsal snapshot (section 8). Ceiling. Kilobytes against gigabytes. Cost: money, metered (N10); one failure domain (6.9).

6.7 Demo-only components

Why

Two filters on the evidence. Chrome's sanitised export leaves out exactly three headers, Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization (Chrome DevTools), and keeps everything else. So the recorder files only what it needs, status codes, request ids and the named /v1/ bodies, drops every remaining header itself, and refuses a capture that still carries one of the three, the sign of an export made unsanitised. Two independent filters, Chrome's and the demo's, mean one mistake does not put a credential in front of every recipient (TH6).

Two conditions, not one, for the reset. The route registers at startup only when the rehearsal flag is set and role reset exists, and the role is created by the provisioning script, never by a migration. A deploy that copies the flag into the platform's task definition by mistake still finds no role there, so the route does not exist (TH1). A destructive operation behind one switch is one mistake away from a real organization; behind two switches set in different places it takes two.

Read "a memento" literally. A fixture state, both organizations' rows, objects and index file at the end of a clean act, is what the memento pattern names: saved state that the reset restores without the rest of the code knowing how it is laid out. Carrying the build digest and the audit sequence inside it means a state from another build, or another time, cannot pass for a fresh one.

The provisioning script (P9) runs from the operator's shell (EE2) before a rehearsal, idempotent, reading only the synthetic rows it captures (A10). Its fAuth steps are the viability check's: POST /platform/tenants for northstar and the canary, PATCH /manage/config for branding, redirect and invite-only signup, POST /manage/users for Maya, Sarah and Jordan, and the platform's oauth_clients row by hand, fAuth having no API for it (A13, D9), one redirect URI: a public PKCE client, the code verifier its proof, no client secret. Its keys (AS12), fAuth's database credential among them, used once for that row, live in the operator's keychain, read at run time, never in the repository, shell history or log. As an administrator of each organization in turn, through the administration group, it creates the Security and Finance spaces and aliases, the memberships of 4.1, Northstar's one independent-review policy (per organization, platform R9, so Finance shares it) and the operator role. It seeds no app, source or record; it captures the fixture states (s0 and s2 to s5, section 8): both organizations' rows and object listing with the build digest, under the operator prefix. Ceiling: two organizations, five people, five states; more is a manifest change. A wrong role flag over-grants (12.1); the pre-take assertion catches it, the canary suite (R8) behind. Cost: a manifest and the client row kept true by hand; the shell's keys as a surface (AR3); no money.

The evidence recorder (P10) assembles S07's packet after a take from only: the image digest and lockfiles; both admission reports; receipts and outcomes from the recording browser's captured responses, not a re-query; job and audit views as the operator (platform R16); and the rehearsal log: times per act, sample sizes, warm or cold, every seeded, simulated or manual step labeled. It reads Chrome's sanitised HAR export, which strips only Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization; it files only status codes, request ids and the named /v1/ bodies, drops every other header itself, and refuses a capture still carrying those three, an unsanitised export. It checks each shown number against its receipt's result digest, and the deploy log for silence between acts 3 and 6 (N9); a task start on the same image digest, act 4's restart drill, is not a deploy. After each take it writes the packet's manifest digest as an audit event, under the Object Lock anchor (M31). Ceiling: a few hundred receipts, megabytes. Cost: an hour of the operator's time a take; a filter in the trusted base (SI8); no money.

The reset (P11) is POST /v1/operator/reset with a state's name and digest, a job under the rehearsal flag with state visible within 1 s; its guard is section 9's. It runs as database role reset, created by the script, never by a migration; the route registers at startup only when both the flag and role reset exist, so the flag alone exposes nothing. Per organization, in one transaction, between takes only: it takes the membership row FOR UPDATE, serialising against in-flight commands as revocation does (platform C07); deletes the organization's rows whose commit sequence is past the state's and the objects absent from its manifest, outcomes and jobs included, keeping audit, which no role may delete, and sessions; inserts the state's rows; restores the object listing; bumps the membership epoch, so every open tab re-authorizes within 5 s and no session is lost; flushes P4's cache. Role reset is bound by row-level security like the four roles, with a policy admitting both organizations' rows under the flag's setting, neither BYPASSRLS nor a table owner; it is 409 while any job is claimed, and a worker's result and done mark commit together, so no claim outlives a reset. The state carries the build digest and the audit sequence at capture, so it is never mistaken for a fresh one: a memento, its cost a manifest format. Cost: a fifth role and a test on every build that the platform's deployment cannot reach it. Ceiling: seconds for kilobytes.

Try it

The reset keeps sessions and bumps the membership epoch. Predict what would change if it deleted every session row instead and left the epoch alone: for the take procedure, for fAuth, for role reset's grants, and for a tab still open from the previous take.

Answer

The procedure: every actor would have to sign in again through fAuth's page after every reset, instead of once within the idle hour (11.1, step 3, which relies on "the reset keeps sessions"). fAuth: more sign-ins per rehearsal push against its login limit, which the cold start already has to raise (11.1; 11.4's limiter row). The grants: role reset would need a grant on the session table, which SI7 forbids ("never deletes audit or sessions", enforced by reset's grants), so the most dangerous role in the demo would reach identity rows. The open tab: it would be denied at its next request because its session is gone, the same safety the epoch bump gives, bought with re-sign-ins. The epoch bump gets that safety without touching sessions: every open tab re-authorizes within 5 s against the restored membership rows and no session is lost (6.7, 8, TH9).

6.9 Dependencies

Why

Why act 4's restart drill runs with no job in flight. A worker claims a job for 120 s, its lease, and no other worker may take the job until the lease runs out. A restart in the middle of a job therefore leaves it stuck for up to two minutes, four times N2's 30 s, so the drill is staged while no import or generation is running; otherwise the stuck job would be the step that is not redone in time.

"Hard if changed". Forma 3.0.0 and DuckDB are linked into the binary, so they cannot be down, but an upgrade of either is a dependency change; under the one-digest rule (N9) an upgrade between acts would also be a deploy.

One host makes every runtime row hard (D1): the availability bound is the process, PostgreSQL and, cold, object storage and key management. N2 asks a 30 s recovery: saved work, records and sessions are in DS1, so a restart redoes only the step in flight (11.4); a job in flight waits out its 120 s lease or is redone with a new key, so the restart drill (act 4) runs with none. Soft: the parser sandbox (P6, imports fail visibly), the script and the reset (P9, P11, a rerun) and, in lockstep since one binary ships them, the AppDefinition, receipt and Parquet formats (N9). Linked in, hard if changed: Forma 3.0.0 2006423b and DuckDB at their pins (platform A14).

7. Data flows

Method

For. The reviewer asks: where does data go, who can touch it on the way, and what happens when a step fails? One data-flow diagram per key flow with trust boundaries drawn as dashed boxes, elements carrying identifiers (P for process, DS for store, EE for external entity, B for boundary) that the threat model cites, each flow as numbered phases ending in a terminal line, then the failure cases, and one sequence diagram for the trickiest flow.

Look for. Every arrow labelled with protocol, authentication and what data crosses. The boundary crossings: each one is where an attacker could stand, and section 10 will have a row for each. The failure cases under their own heading: a flow that only has a happy path is half a flow.

Pitfall. Treating the sequence diagram as decoration. It is the one place the exact order of checks is written down; read it line by line and ask at each step "what if this is forged?".

Why

Two F numberings, and one new boundary. This record numbers its own arrows, F1 to F13 on diagram 03 and F14 to F19 on diagram 04, and cites the platform's as "platform F22" and so on; 7.1 uses mostly the platform's, 7.2 and 7.3 the record's own. The diagrams keep the platform's element ids (P, DS, EE, B) with three changes, and the one to remember is B9, the operator's machine. The platform has no boundary there; the demo's operator runs two scripts on a laptop that also holds every key, every actor's session and the packet (AS13 in 10.2). A boundary is wherever trust changes, and the threat model gives this one its own row (TH15).

The demo's flows are the platform's three (platform section 7) on one process, each phase adding its evidence (D7). Elements keep the platform's ids with three changes: P1 is the host's load balancer, ending TLS [reduced: the platform's edge]; P2 to P5 and P7 share the one process under their own database roles, so B3 and B4 are roles, not hops (D1); P9 the provisioning script and P10 the evidence recorder run on the operator's machine, B9, the demo's own boundary, and P11 the reset in the process (6.7). B7, the organization boundary inside every store, rides every arrow. F1 to F13 are on diagram 03, F14 to F19 on 04 (7.3).

7.2 Act 6: the record command, the return to Security and the evidence

Why

What is the platform's and what the demo adds. F7, the one transaction, is the platform's command unchanged (its F46): the outcome lookup, the version check, the epoch check and the writes inside one PostgreSQL transaction the data service owns. What the demo adds is the circumstances around it: the lost response is the script's, labeled simulated; the canary's replay rides the same arrows; the recorder reads only what the browser received. B4 drawn inside B2 is the one-process change: the data service's boundary is a database role inside the host's network instead of a network hop, and the check it makes is the same.

Count what the conflicts add. The happy path ends with two transactions, two record revisions and two audit events. Notice what the retry and the stale edit add to that count: no revision and no audit event, only an attempt logged apart and a 409. A test can assert those counts directly, which is how "one mutation" becomes something the packet proves.

For Lesson 5's sequence diagram. This record draws none of its own, since "platform 7.3 holds its sequence", with the P2 to P4 hop a call in process here. Use the worked example's steps 3 to 5 instead, whose F numbers walk the same messages on diagram 03, and ask at each arrow what a forged or lost message would do: step 4 is that question answered for one lost response, and step 8, the canary's replay, for a forged identifier.

Diagram 03 (R7) follows Spend Review's decision through the one process into one PostgreSQL transaction and back, then the return to Security and the recorder's reads.

What matters is that F7 is the platform's F46 unchanged, outcome, version, epoch and writes in one transaction P4 owns; that B4 sits inside B2, the same check by database role rather than by hop (D1; platform D11); and that P3 is absent, P2 reading the record schema from the publication row (F5), so the control plane stays off the run path at migration (G7); platform 7.3 holds its sequence. The second app. By act 3's path, same build: a queue at amount_cents >= 20,000, EXP-002 alone at 45,000 cents, a detail view, a decision form with status in {needs_context, reviewed} and note, keyed by expense id in the saved work. That is the end: two transactions, two record revisions, two audit events, and the packet.

Things get more interesting when:

  • Revocation races a paused command. Revocation takes the membership row FOR UPDATE while the command holds it FOR SHARE, so they serialize (F7). Revocation first: epoch stale, denied, no mutation. Command first: it stays in history; P2 re-checks visibility before delivering, so a retry after revocation shows nothing (S06), both orders kept.
Try it

In act 6's lost response, ik-1 is posted twice, both times with expected version 0, though after the first post the record is at version 1. Suppose P4 compared the expected version before looking for the stored outcome: predict what the second post would return and what Maya and the packet would then show, and say what finding the outcome first protects. Then compare the two ways a client can recover from a lost response, retrieving the outcome by key first (section 9's rule) or re-submitting under the same key (the path the script forces): what would each leave in the packet, and which part of act 6's claim does only the second exercise?

Answer

Version first, the second post would fail: its expected version 0 no longer matches the record's version 1, so P4 would roll back and answer 409 with the recovery view, as it does for the stale edit under ik-3 (7.2, step 5). Maya would be told that her own decision conflicted with itself, and the packet would hold a 409 for a command that had in fact committed: the retry would look like a conflict, and G4's duplicate-safe retry could not be shown. Finding the stored outcome first is what makes a retry safe whatever the client believes: the first post stored its outcome under ik-1 in the same transaction as version 1 (F7), so the second finds it before any version check and returns version 1 (F7, F8; step 4), while authorization still runs again (F4), because a key names a command, not a permission. Retrieving first would leave one POST and one GET by key: it shows that an outcome is stored, but the server never sees the command twice. The forced re-submission leaves two POSTs under one key against one record revision, one audit event and "the attempt logged apart" (7.2, step 4): it exercises the duplicate path itself, the outcome found before the version check, which is G4's "an ik-1 retry yields one revision and one audit event". That is why the record calls it "the stronger proof" and labels it simulated (7.2, 9, G6).

Why

Why the operator's flows get their own diagram. A threat row names the element or crossing it attacks, and the platform's diagrams draw no operator's machine as a boundary, no reset and no recorder, so five of this record's threats, TH1, TH2, TH5, TH8 and TH15, would have no arrow to name. Diagram 04 gives each of them one. Read its arrows into B9 with TH15 beside you: what comes back to the operator's machine is a filtered export and the operator views, all of it synthetic, so the one machine that holds every key holds as little else as the demo can arrange.

Diagram 04 draws what diagram 03 leaves out: the operator's tools and the arrows the demo's threat rows cross (TH1, TH2, TH5, TH8, TH15).

What matters: F17 to F19 exist only under the flag with role reset (SI7); F15 is the platform's administration group under the operator's just-in-time session, no demo switch (D6); what returns to the operator's machine is F12's sanitised export and F13's operator views, synthetic data only (A10; platform R16). Simplified: P9's and P10's calls pass through P1 like every request; the unnumbered arrows are the operator starting the scripts; the manifest digest's write (M31) rides F13's session back.

8. Data model and storage

Method

For. The reviewer asks: what is stored where, why there, for how long, and what can be recomputed? Per store: the choice and its reason, whether it is the system of record or derived, how writes are acknowledged and what that means for data loss, and what guarantee a read has.

Look for. The record-or-derived column. Derived data can be rebuilt after a disaster; record data cannot, so that is where the backups and the strictest acknowledgement belong. The partition key: it decides which queries are cheap. Retention per class of data, and how deletion works in a store that never updates rows.

Pitfall. Pasting schemas. A column list goes stale in a week and tells the reader nothing about trade-offs; the entities and relationships that drive a decision are enough.

Why

Why the unique index, not the row lock, holds version 0. A command locks the record row FOR UPDATE before checking its version, but before the first decision there is no row to lock, so two first decisions on EXP-002 could both see "absent" and both try to write version 1. The unique index on (organization, work, record, version) settles it: the second insert of version 1 fails, so one commits and the other gets a conflict (unique indexes, row locks). Creation is the one case a lock cannot serialise, because there is nothing yet to hold.

An orphan, never a dangling row. Object storage acknowledges a write when the PUT returns, before the row that names the object commits. If the process dies between the two, an object exists that no row names, an orphan that wastes a few bytes; the reverse order could leave a row naming an object that was never written, a dangling reference that breaks every read of it. Choosing the order of two writes chooses which failure you get.

Why retaking an act retakes the acts after it. The recording joins one kept take per act, and each act's state is captured at the end of its kept take, so the next act starts from exactly what the camera saw: Sarah's approval in act 4 is of the digest act 3 formed on screen. Retake act 3 and its revision 5 may come out different, since the live model's arrangement need not repeat (13.3), so the s3 captured from it differs too, and an act 4 kept from the old s3 would approve a draft the recording no longer shows. The chain is the price of the stronger claim, every act continuing the one before, and it is what lets 13.3 answer "One take or many?" with one kept take per act.

What recovery is not. RPO, how much recent data a restore may lose, is one rehearsal, because the only snapshot is taken before each rehearsal; RTO, how long a restore takes, is unknown until S06's drill times one. "Reseeding fixtures is not recovery": loading the fixtures again proves nothing about restoring what a take committed.

The model is the platform's section 8 (D2, D3; platform D3, D4); only the differences follow.

Store The demo's shape Of record Acknowledged when Read guarantee
DS1 PostgreSQL, one RDS instance, no standby [reduced: the platform's Multi-AZ] every entity, sessions (DS4) included yes the primary's commit; snapshot before each rehearsal read-after-write, monotonic
DS2 one versioned S3 bucket, a prefix per organization originals, Parquet, previews, exports, the index file (DS6) originals; the rest rerun the PUT returns, before the naming row commits: a lost row orphans an object, never dangles written once; a reader holding the row finds it

DS3 is the platform's key management with one data key per organization: the canary's never unwraps Northstar's bytes (G5). The operator prefix (states, packet) sits under the platform's own key, so shredding both data keys after delivery leaves the packet readable.

Write paths are the platform's, READ COMMITTED with explicit locks for commands and adoption, SERIALIZABLE for publication (platform 6.2, 8) in D5's order. The record command locks EXP-002's current row FOR UPDATE and the membership row FOR SHARE; the key's unique index serializes the ik-1 retry; the unique index on (organization, work, record, version) makes two racing creates one commit and one conflict, since FOR UPDATE on an absent row locks nothing; publication and adoption move a pointer WHERE current = expected (C07, C09). Every table carries FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY under a NOLOGIN owner; no runtime role owns one or bypasses a policy.

Volumes. Thirteen fixture rows: originals under 10 KiB together, four Parquet revisions of one row group each. A rehearsal commits about twenty records at 2 KiB with audit and cites at most twenty receipts at 1 KiB, 60 KiB; ten rehearsals stay under 1 MiB a store. One unpartitioned primary; EXP-002 is one row lock, about 50 commits/s at an assumed 20 ms.

Caching. The result cache earns nothing here; the spike measures with it empty (N3). Sessions and the epoch are never cached; fAuth's key set (DS5) is refreshed hourly; /v1/ responses are no-store.

Retention and the reset. The platform's A6 values stand; none expires inside a rehearsal; S06's deletion row runs the platform's tombstone path, not the reset. Between takes, deletion is the reset (P11; 6.7, 9) to a fixture state: a manifest of both organizations' rows, objects and index file, captured by P9 at the end of each act's kept take, sealed with the build digest. s0 is provisioned, before act 1; s2 after act 2, nothing published; s3 after act 3, revision 5 admitted; s4 after act 4, publication 1 and Maya's case; s5 after act 5, Jordan's work and the revocation. The recording joins one kept take per act, each starting from the state the last ended in, so act 4 approves what act 3 formed; retaking act N retakes the acts after it. As role reset it deletes, in one READ COMMITTED transaction per organization, the rows whose commit sequence is past the state's and the objects absent from the manifest. It keeps the manifest's rows, sessions, the operator's account and every audit row (never reset, 90 days, G6), and bumps the membership epoch: every open tab re-authorizes within 5 s, no session lost.

Recovery. No standby, no daily backup [reduced: the platform's A7; Multi-AZ and the snapshot schedule the seam]: one snapshot before each rehearsal, with the bucket's object versions, both deleted after delivery (10.6). RPO is one rehearsal, about twenty records. RTO is unknown until S06 times the restore; reseeding fixtures is not recovery.

Try it

Section 8 lists s0 and then s2, and appendix A gives the reason: act 1 changes nothing a take restores. Test that claim instead of taking it: list what act 1 leaves behind (7.1) and say why, under the reset's rules (6.7, 8), none of it matters to a take of act 2; then name a change to act 1 that would force an s1 into existence. Finally, argue why a fixture state is captured from a clean take's act end rather than written by hand as the next act's starting rows, and name the two checks that stop a state altered after its capture from being restored unnoticed.

Answer

Act 1 leaves one session and one audit row and nothing else (7.1, act 1). The reset keeps every session and every audit row and deletes only rows committed after the state's point, so restoring s0 before act 2 removes nothing act 1 made, and act 2 starts from s0 too (8; 11.1, step 2). An s1 would be needed the moment act 1 committed a row a later act depends on, for example a space created on camera instead of by the provisioning script (6.7): a reset to s0 deletes every row past s0's point, so that row would be gone before act 2. A state captured from a clean take holds only rows the build's own code wrote, a revision 5 that admission accepted, a publication 1 the control plane wrote after Sarah's approval, under the build digest the state carries (8). Rows written by hand could hold something no mechanism produced, a publication with no approval behind it, and restoring them would put a state in front of the camera that no clean take reached. The reset itself is labeled, its audit event entering the rehearsal log as seeded state (9; appendix A's labeled step), but the act filmed after it is accepted as working, so it must start from rows a real take produced. The checks: the reset recomputes the state's digest, over manifest and build digest, against the pin file kept apart in the repository and refuses a mismatch with 412 (M3), and the recorder diffs each restored manifest, publication and approval digests included, against its capture (M4) (TH2, 8, 9).

All exercises

9. API surface

Method

For. The reviewer asks: what do callers see, including when things go wrong? The endpoints that matter, with authentication per endpoint, the error model, compatibility rules and how repeated requests behave.

Look for. The authentication column: an endpoint with none is either public on purpose or a hole. The error model: what a caller gets for a permission failure versus a missing object tells you whether the API leaks existence. Idempotency: what happens when the same request arrives twice, because on a network it will.

Pitfall. Listing every endpoint. The section is a sketch of the shape of the contract; the API's own reference is where the detail lives.

Why

Retrieve before you re-submit. After a timeout the browser cannot know whether its command committed. It asks first, by key, for the stored outcome, and re-submits under the same key only if there is none, so a command that did commit is not sent again; and if it is sent again anyway, as the rehearsal forces, the server returns the first outcome because the key is checked before anything else. Two layers: a careful client, and a server that does not depend on the client being careful.

Why 409 and not 422 for a reused key. The IETF draft on the Idempotency-Key header suggests 422 when a key comes back with a different payload (the draft); the platform answers 409, Conflict, and the demo serves the platform's API unchanged. The argument (platform 9) is about what is wrong: 422 says this request's content cannot be processed, but the request is well formed and only conflicts with an earlier request stored under the same key, part of the resource's current state, which is the conflict 409 names in HTTP (RFC 9110). One code for both conflicts, the stale version and the reused key, also gives the browser one way to recover: the authorized recovery view.

404 for an absent operation, 412 for a failed precondition. The reset's guard uses two different refusals on purpose. Where the flag is not set the route does not exist, so it is 404, like any unknown path. Where it exists but an organization lacks the synthetic label, the build digest differs from the state's or the manifest digest does not recompute, the operation is real and its precondition failed: 412. The two codes tell the operator which of two very different things went wrong.

Where the authentication column is. This section's table lists scenes and error codes rather than entry points, because the API is the platform's, unchanged; the demo's entry points and how each one authenticates are in 10.2's interface table, which is where to apply the method note's test.

The demo serves the platform's API unchanged (platform 9, D5, D13): server-rendered pages and the JSON API under /v1/, its groups, checks, error classes, compatibility rules and idempotency semantics, in one process (D1, D3). Sign-in is the platform's redirection through the identity adapter to fAuth's hosted page (D4, A12), same callback and session code. Every scene, the canary's replays included (R8), goes through these operations; the platform's schema-diff tests run on the demo build.

Beside the API, not in it. The provisioning script (D6) calls fAuth's management API for the tenants and users, adds the client row by hand (A13), then uses the platform's administration group as each organization's administrator: membership, spaces, aliases, policy (F14 to F16). Act 5's revocation is Maya's, from the share control (C11; platform 10.5): the epoch moves and Jordan's refresh within 5 s is denied by the platform's check, not a demo switch. The evidence capture (R9) reads only receipts and outcomes from responses, job states and the operator's views: synthetic data only (A10; platform R16).

The one added operation is the reset (P11, 6.7): POST /v1/operator/reset with a fixture state's name and digest (section 8: s0, s2 to s5), restoring both organizations' rows, objects and index file (sessions and audit survive, section 8) as a job, its state visible within 1 s. Its guard: the route exists only under the rehearsal flag, never set in the platform's deployment, so elsewhere it is 404; it needs the operator role, taken just in time; it refuses to register at startup without database role reset, which the platform's database lacks; it is 412 unless every organization carries the synthetic label, the organization row's synthetic flag that P9 sets and no member can (A10), the build digest matches the state's and the manifest digest recomputes; it carries an Idempotency-Key whose outcome lives in the operator's scope, outside the rows the reset clears, so a double click is one reset; its audit event survives the reset and enters the rehearsal log as seeded state, excluded from acceptance (G6, S07). Unversioned: it never ships.

Error classes the scenes exercise:

Code Scene, stimulus Platform rule
404 1, an unknown command; 5, Jordan's bare link; every canary replay denied, foreign and absent are one answer
403 4, Maya publishing her own draft names the rule; she may see the app
412 3, a stale patch; 4, an approval over a changed draft; the reset's guard names the current revision
409 6, the second expected-0 edit; ik-1 reused with another payload an authorized recovery view
422 2, the oversize XLSX (A6); a query past the grammar narrow_the_query
429, 503 S06 only: a full job slot; the provider down Retry-After; the published app unaffected (R13)

Idempotency (N5) is the platform's (platform D5): the island mints the key, ik-1 and ik-2 in scene 6; the data service enforces it inside the command's transaction, outcome before expected version, so the ik-1 retry returns version 1, one revision, one audit event (S05). After a timeout the island retrieves the outcome by key and re-submits under the same key only if none exists, the path the rehearsal forces (7.2); a key still in flight serialises on its row and returns the first outcome; a missing key is 400; the browser retries only a 503 with Retry-After. Outcomes live 24 hours, longer than any take; the reset deletes them, so a key reused after a reset is a new command.

10. Security and threat model

Method

For. The reviewer asks: did you find the threats a professional would find, did you decide what to do about each, and what still holds when part of the system is compromised? Scope and assumptions, then trust boundaries, invariants and assets, then actors and goals, then the STRIDE table built from the data-flow diagrams, then authentication and operator access, then secrets and data protection, then accepted risks and the continuous checks.

Look for. The invariants: a handful of properties, usually three to six, that must hold no matter what, each with the component that enforces it. That small set of components is the trusted computing base, and the rest of the section is about keeping it small and watched. The threat statements: each is a sentence with an actor, a prerequisite, an action and an impact, not a category name. The response column: mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept, and for accepted risks, who accepted them.

Pitfall. Padding. Twelve rows that each say "attacker does bad thing, we use TLS" is worse than four rows that each name a boundary crossing, an invariant at stake and a control with a test.

Why

When the data is fake, the asset is the claim. Every row is synthetic, so a leak harms no person; the impact scale is about the recording's claim instead: a leak to the canary, a seeded step passing as working or a lost audit row ends a goal (G5, G6). That is why the controls still run as for Confidential data, and why 10.4 adds "passes a seeded step as working" to what High impact means. Most of the section cites the platform; read what is written in full, which is what one process and one operator change.

The platform's section 10 run on one process with synthetic data: what holds is cited, what changes is written in full.

10.1 Scope and assumptions

Why

SA3 names the only hostile principal. In a rehearsal the one attacker who actually attacks is the canary, scripted by the operator; everyone else is trusted and audited. Real outsiders enter through the risk profile instead: a scan of a public host over weeks is rated moderately likely, which is why the load balancer admits only listed addresses during rehearsals (M29).

In scope: the demo build at one digest on one host (D1, D10), two synthetic organizations, section 7's elements and flows, the flag and the reset (P11), the operator's scripts (P9, P10), the recording browser and the packet (S07). Out: platform 10.1's exclusions; real data and a pilot (A10, 3.2); the release path (11.1).

  • SA1 The platform's SA1 to SA4 hold, SA1 sharper: one host is one compromise domain (D1); the five database roles separate modules, not credentials: one task role connects as any, so the walls hold against a logic bug alone (10.5; AR2).
  • SA2 fAuth at b750ca53 holds the platform as a registered client by one hand-added row (D9, A13), in scope; its internals are not.
  • SA3 The operator is trusted and audited, never a reader of organization data (A3; platform R16); the canary's suite is the only hostile principal.
  • SA4 The recording browser is the operator's Chrome, one profile an actor (A13); what it shows, the audience sees.

Risk profile. Likelihood is low for a targeted attack, moderate for a scan of a public host over weeks (M29); impact is to the claim: a leak to the canary, a seeded step passing as working or a lost audit row ends G5 or G6, so the controls run as for Confidential data (section 4); every row is synthetic (A10), no privacy regime applies (platform A12).

10.2 Trust boundaries, trust levels, and assets

Method

For. The trust levels, the invariants, the entry points and the assets are the vocabulary the STRIDE table speaks. Read them first or the rows will not parse.

Look for. A trust level for the system's own identities, not only for humans: the API's service account can reach things no user can, and a compromised API holds that level. The entry-point table's "where input is validated" column: every input is validated at a named place before anything trusts it.

Why

The platform's families this section extends. 10.2 adds to three lists it does not repeat, so here they are, from platform 10.2. The trust levels: TL0 anonymous, TL1 a member, TL2 a builder, TL3 a reviewer, TL4 an administrator, TL5 the operator just in time, TL6 an untrusted author (a dropped file until parsed, the model's proposal until admitted), TL7 the service identities, here one task role carrying five database roles, and TL8 the external systems and the release path. The invariants: SI1 scope, every read and write scoped by the verified session's organization, never a request value; SI2 authority, which no model output, file, link or stale job widens; SI3 governed writes, members seeing only publications control wrote over an approved digest and records changing only by declared commands; SI4 revocation within 5 s; SI5 an append-only audit; SI6 fair share between organizations. The assets: AS1 sessions and identity keys, AS2 publications and policy, AS3 records, work and the other Confidential rows, AS4 evidence, AS5 keys, AS6 index files, AS7 audit, AS8 the release path and logs. With them a row traces to the end, as Lesson 6 asks: TH4 puts SI1 at stake, and its "AS3, AS4" are the records and the evidence.

Why the whole binary is in the trusted computing base. The trusted computing base is the set of components that must work correctly for the invariants to hold (Building Secure and Reliable Systems, chapter 6). In the platform it is a list of enforcing components spread over separate deployments; here, because one task role can connect as every database role, a flaw anywhere in the binary can reach everything, so the base is the whole binary plus the reset's guard and grants and the recorder's filter. The record says so in one sentence rather than claiming a small base it does not have.

Two invariants about honesty. SI7 and SI8 protect no data; they protect the demo's truthfulness. The reset restores only a digest-matched state and never deletes audit or sessions, and the packet holds only what the browser received and the operator views returned. A threat model can carry invariants for the claim as well as for the data, and enforce them with the same tools: grants and a filter.

Added to the platform's TL0 to TL8 (TL7 now one task role carrying five database roles, D1): TL9 the canary's member, TL1 in the second organization, running the replay suite (R8); TL10 the operator's shell (EE2), running P9 and P10 with AS12's keys; TL11 the recording browser (SA4), the actors' sessions in turn; TL12 role reset, writing both organizations' rows, existing only where P9 created it.

The platform's SI1 to SI6 hold with the same enforcers, B3 and B4 now grants, not hops (D1), the sandbox a module in the one process (SI2), role reset without a grant on audit or sessions (SI5), SI6 moot with two organizations (N1). SI3 gains a clause: or a fixture state P9 captured from a clean take, restored whole by reset under the flag from a digest-matched manifest between takes (SI7); its enforcers gain P11, reset's grants and M3, M4 diffing digests. Two are the demo's:

  • SI7 (safety) Rehearsal: the reset exists only under the flag with role reset, restores only a digest-matched state, never deletes audit or sessions; enforced by reset's grants (none on audit or sessions), tested per build, and P11's guard.
  • SI8 (safety) Evidence: the packet holds only what the browser received and the operator views returned, every number matched to its receipt, no credential; enforced by P10's filter.

The trusted computing base is the one binary under one task role (AR2), P11's guard, reset's grants and P10's filter.

10.3 Threat actors and attack goals

Why

The platform's actors, cited bare. 10.3's opening line keeps the platform's TA1 to TA9 and drops TA10, so here they are, from platform 10.3: TA1 an outside attacker, TA2 a member of another organization, the canary's role here, TA3 a malicious or phished member, TA4 a builder steering the composer, TA5 an instruction injected into evidence, TA6 the model provider, TA7 a malicious dependency, TA8 a compromised CI, TA9 the insider operator, and TA10 future management, an acquirer or a court. The threat rows cite them the same way, so "(TA9, TA11)" in TH1 is the platform's insider operator beside this record's script bug.

The most likely attacker is your own script. TA11, a bug in the operator's scripts, is "the commonest cause": a wrong grant, a wrong policy kind, a wrong redirect URI, or the rehearsal script faulting the wrong step. Listing it as a threat actor puts the most probable failure through the same analysis as an attacker, so it gets a control, the pre-take assertion, rather than a hope. The platform's TA10 goes the other way, and is removed: future owners or a court have nothing to compel when every row is synthetic.

The platform's TA1 to TA9 hold, TA2 the canary, TA4 Maya steering the composer by script (S06), TA9 the operator; TA10 is removed, nothing synthetic being compellable:

10.4 STRIDE analysis

Method

For. One row per boundary crossing, with the STRIDE letter: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Likelihood and impact are High, Medium or Low with one line defining High, so the ranking stays comparable.

Look for. High rows carrying two mitigations, one that prevents and one that detects. The row about build and dependency tampering: every real system has a supply chain. The mitigation column: each mitigation is restated as an SR requirement in section 4, with its verification on the same line, so a row can be traced to the check that would catch it.

Why

The branch the platform lacks. Branch 4 of the attack tree, through the operator, is new: the shell's keys, the operator's machine, the packet and the recording, and a session surviving the reset are all surfaces the demo adds to the platform's. Read the four branches as a list of walls: the first three meet mostly the platform's controls (branch 3's fixture state, TH2, is the demo's own), the fourth meets controls this record writes in full (TH5, TH6, TH9, TH15).

Why the canary's row is the only High and High. TH4 is rated High on likelihood on purpose: the canary suite attempts that attack on every take, so it is certain to be tried. A scripted adversary turns likelihood into something you arrange, and the controls are measured against it every time instead of on the day a real one arrives.

Pitfall. The paragraph after the table re-rates three of the platform's rows, platform TH8, TH11 and TH14: the forwarded principal, the owner credential and the flood. This record's TH8, TH11 and TH14 are three different threats; the prefix is the only thing that tells them apart.

Rated on platform 10.4's scale: High likelihood needs only a seat or a file, Medium a mistake or a flaw in a built control, Low a compromised role or key; High impact crosses an organization, exposes a secret, breaks the publication or audit record or, added here, passes a seeded step as working (G6). The platform's mitigations this build implements are [proposed] here too, marked so in the existing-control cells, verified by the spike and the per-build tests. High rows carry a preventative and a detective mitigation; the body keeps the rows whose control is the demo's own, appendix C the rest, TH8 to TH15; the head owns every residual risk.

Why

The demo's signature risk. In TH1, the first row below, the reset is a destructive operation that ships inside the platform's own binary, and the threat is a deploy mistake that switches it on where real organizations live. The response has the two halves a High-impact row needs: a preventative control, two conditions the platform's deployment never meets, and a detective one, a test on every build that starts the image as the platform would and asserts that the route is 404 and the role absent. A control tested on every build is evidence; a control that is only designed is a hope.

Why

Keep the check away from the thing it checks. A fixture state lives in object storage under the operator prefix, so whoever can write there could alter it; if its digest lived beside it, they could alter both. So the digest lives in the pin file in the repository, at the build's tag, and the reset recomputes it before restoring: a tampered state is refused with 412. The detective half, the recorder diffing each restored manifest against its capture, catches what gets past the first.

Try it

The canary suite must get a 404 for every replay, each paired with the owner's 200 for the same identifier in that take (R8, SR2). Say in one sentence which property the suite proves. TH4's preventative half already puts row-level security on every table: argue why the row still needs this detective half, naming one thing the suite can catch that row-level security cannot. Then describe two different broken setups, one in the build and one in the suite's own script, that a suite of bare 404s would pass and the paired suite would fail.

Answer

It proves that nothing of Northstar's, data or metadata, reaches a session of another organization (G5, N7): it is TH4's detective half, M8, where SI1 is at stake, the platform's scope invariant that every read and write is scoped by the verified session's organization, never a request value (platform 10.2). Row-level security filters rows; it cannot see the rest of an answer. A handler that answers 403 where it should answer 404, or names the app in an error, tells the canary that Northstar's identifier exists without returning a single row, which is why R8 asks for denial "before data or metadata" and 5.1 for 404 rather than 403; and a policy missing from one table is a gap the preventative half cannot report about itself. The suite checks whole answers from outside, every take, so it sees both, which is why 10.4 gives every High row a preventative and a detective half. A broken build: a change that makes a route answer 404 to everyone, its owner included; the canary's 404 then proves only that the route is broken, and the owner's missing 200 fails the take. A broken script: replays built from the previous take's identifiers, which the reset deleted, so every replay is 404 because nothing exists; again no owner 200 in this take. In both a bare 404 cannot be told from a refusal, and the paired 200 is what proves the identifier was real and reachable by its owner at the time (R8, SR2, TH4; 11.1, steps 4 and 6).

10.5 Authentication and authorization

Method

For. One authentication mechanism, one place where access is decided, deny by default, never on the client. Operator access as design: who can reach production data, how a break-glass works, who reads its audit, and which actions need two people.

Look for. The break-glass path. If operators can read customer data without one, the company's own staff are the largest threat actor and the document has not said so.

Why

Why the service token is not minted. In the platform a call between roles crosses a network, so it carries a signed, short-lived token naming caller, callee and principal. Inside one process there is no network to cross, and a signing key would add a secret to protect without adding a wall that code in the process could not climb. A typed principal, a value only the authorizer's module can construct, gives the same protection against honest mistakes for nothing: a handler cannot fabricate one. When the roles split into services (G7), the signed token returns; until then it is "a seam, not a control".

Who reads the audit when there is no second person. With one founder there is no two-person rule and no breakglass reviewer (AR1). The record's answer is that the audience reads the audit, through the packet's anchored manifest (M31): the reader moves outside the company, the demo-scale substitute for a second operator.

Notice. "(F7; platform SA2)" in the record's second paragraph cites the platform's assumption that no internal caller is trusted, which is why the callees re-read membership (platform 10.1); this record's SA2 is a different assumption, fAuth's client row.

People authenticate at fAuth only (K4; platform 10.5), by the authorization-code flow with PKCE S256 as a registered client (platform M6; D9) on the platform's callback and session code, the token verified offline by kid (DS5), tenant_id the organization, sub the person, a token without tenant_id refused; the minimal login is the fallback behind the same adapter (D4). Authorization is the platform's one function, the epoch re-read on every request (F4).

What the one process changes. The forwarded principal is a typed value in process (F6), constructed only in the authorizer's module, so a handler's logic cannot forge one; the platform's service token (platform M16) is not minted; its return when roles split (G7) is a seam, not a control: module privacy stops a logic bug, not code in the process (platform TH8). P3 and P4 still re-read membership in their transactions (F7; platform SA2). No mTLS inside the host: one ECS task role allowed rds-db:connect as the five roles, reset included, each with its own pool opened at start, a 15-minute token and disjoint grants, so the write grants survive and the credential boundary does not (AR2); the parser module holds none and no path to the credentials endpoint (B6).

Operator access. The operator (TL10) holds AS12, takes the operator role just in time for one take (M9), and reaches only the reset, the administration calls and the operator views (F13; SA3); the audit's reader is the audience, through the packet's anchored manifest (M31). No two-person rule and no breakglass at demo scale (AR1).

10.6 Secrets and data protection

Why

One key per retention need. Each organization's data sits under its own key, and the operator prefix, which holds the fixture states and the packet, under the platform's own (section 8). After delivery both organizations' keys are scheduled for deletion, which makes everything encrypted under them unreadable at once (crypto-shredding), while the packet stays readable because it was never under those keys. KMS does not delete a key immediately: it waits at least 7 days, during which the key cannot be used and the deletion can still be cancelled (KMS key deletion); the platform's 24-hour hold comes before the schedule.

Read the fail-closed list as a choice of which failure to pay for. Every control in it can fail in one of two directions, and the record picks the one that costs a take: a failing canary suite could let the take run, or stop it; P10 could file a capture it cannot filter, or refuse it. Failing closed spends a retake, which a rehearsal can afford, to avoid what no retake undoes: a leak to the canary, a credential in the packet, a seeded step accepted as working once YC holds the packet (D7). A control that fails open turns its own outage into the breach it exists to prevent.

Per secret (lifetime; rotation trigger; emergency path). The two data keys (DS3) and the provider key, role worker: the rehearsal period; suspicion, the last take or a budget anomaly; a key disabled, reads failing within minutes, or a new provider key, workers reloading within 60 s. The actors' sessions: 12 hours, idle 1 hour; the last take; sign out everywhere and bump both epochs, every tab denied within 5 s.

The security-event table is the platform's plus three rows: the reset (operator, state and build digests, audit sequence at capture, rows deleted; to audit, surviving the reset); the canary suite's result and the pre-take assertion, kind rehearsal_check, inserted by workspace under the operator's session (build digest, take id, request-list digest, any non-404; to audit); the packet's manifest digest, by P10 before delivery (to audit, under the anchor; M31). No event holds a credential, token, body or row (platform M41).

Every control fails closed: the reset 404 without the flag, absent without the role, 412 on a mismatch (M1, M3); a failing canary suite or pre-take assertion means no take; a number without a receipt means no acceptance; an unreachable key set refuses act 1's sign-in (platform 10.6); P10 refusing a capture stops the packet.

Minimisation. The packet holds AS10's list and never a header, cookie, token or key; the recording shows the actors' screens only (M11), a cut replacing a blur. Shredding after delivery: both data keys scheduled for deletion after the platform's 24-hour hold (platform TH28), unusable at once, gone after the 7-day minimum; the pooled rows deleted by P9; the snapshots and the drill's environment deleted; the tenants soft-deleted at fAuth (a hard purge is a FORMA-247 item); sessions signed out; the packet stays readable under the platform's key.

Try it

Rank three leaks from least to most damaging, and for each say what it yields and what bounds it: (a) a copy of the oauth_clients row taken from fAuth's database; (b) fAuth's platform key, leaked a week after provisioning; (c) the operator's machine, taken during act 5. Then explain why the platform key is the first of the operator's keys to be deleted.

Answer

Least to most damaging: (b), (a), (c). (b) Nothing, if the rule was kept: the platform key creates tenants (appendix A, AS12) and "dies once the tenants exist" (10.6, M30), so a week after provisioning there is no key left to leak; it ranks first only because the rule held, and a key kept by mistake would be the power to create tenants at fAuth. (a) Next: the row holds no secret, only the client's registration and its one redirect URI (D9, 6.7). A code can be sent only to that URI, and redeeming one needs the code verifier the platform made for that one sign-in, which is never in the row (PKCE), so the copy signs nobody in; what remains is AR4, a wrong row added by hand, caught by the dry sign-in (M6). (c) Most: the machine holds every key still alive, the actors' sessions in their Chrome profiles, the raw export and the pin file at once (AS13, TH15), which is any principal in either organization and every operator power. It is bounded by M30 (fresh profiles destroyed after the last take, the raw file hashed, filtered and deleted in one step, full-disk encryption, the machine off the network except while a rehearsal runs), made visible afterwards by M31's anchored manifest, and the rest accepted (AR3). The platform key goes first because creating the tenants is the provisioning script's first fAuth step (6.7), so it is the first key whose job is over; the others still have work, the owner credential until its one run, fAuth's database credential until its one insert, the management keys until delivery (10.6). A key that will never be used again is only risk ("single use where possible", AR3).

10.7 Accepted risks and validation

Why

What "accepted" means. An accepted risk is a decision, not an omission: it has an owner, the head, a reason, and usually a bound, such as AR5's route proven dead on every build or AR1's every operator action listed against the script. Writing it down lets a reviewer disagree with a specific sentence, and lets the risk be revisited when its reason changes, for example when a second person joins. Pitfall. Reading "the platform's AR2 to AR11 hold" as these rows. The numbers collide again: this record's AR2 is one host and one process, the platform's AR2 is its pooled roles. The paragraph under the table does the same with SR: "platform SR1, SR2, SR4 to SR7 and SR10 to SR13 hold" names the platform's requirements, not this record's SR1 to SR6.

The head owns five accepted risks; the platform's AR2 to AR11 hold, AR7 moot for synthetic data, AR10 moot without an SLA (A8).

Why

The grants bound bugs; the suite only detects the rest. AR2's reason, in the second row below, splits the defence in two. The database grants stop an honest mistake from writing what its role may not write; the canary suite, run every take, detects what grants cannot see, such as a handler that forgets to scope a query to the session's organization. What neither stops, hostile code running inside the process, is the risk being accepted, with one rehearsal of data, the RPO, as the most that losing the one host can cost.

AR2 One host and one process: a compromise of the process is every role and both organizations; RPO one rehearsal D1, D10; the grants bound bugs; the canary suite only detects the rest
AR3 The operator's shell holds AS12's keys fAuth has no federation for a script and no client API at b750ca53 (platform AR4); the keychain, single use where possible and destruction after delivery bound it

Continuous checks: the canary suite per build and at both ends of every take (M8); the five roles' grants (SI7); the reset unreachability test (M2); the pre-take assertion (M6, M10, M16); P10's receipt and deploy-log checks (M28); the packet scan (M12); S06's restore drill (M14); the platform's policy tests.

The head re-runs this model on a change to the flag, the reset's grants or the fixture-state format, on any real row (A10), on a new element in diagrams 03 or 04, and before submission.

11. Operations

Method

For. The reviewer asks: can this be run, deployed and recovered by someone who is not you? The deployment view, rollout in gated waves with the one metric that triggers rollback, or why there are none, scaling with numbers including what changes at ten times the load, cost with its drivers, service level objectives and the indicators and alerts that measure them, or the reason for none, a failure-modes table with detection, mitigation and the operator's command, recovery, and how all of it would be tested.

Look for. The rollback metric: one named number, not "if problems occur". The failure table's detection column: a failure nobody can see is not mitigated. The cost line with its largest driver, because that is the number that decides what gets built next year. The alert on the age of the oldest message, not on queue depth: a deep queue draining fast is healthy; a shallow one not moving is not. Depth is for backpressure.

Pitfall. Operations as a list of tools. Naming a monitoring product is not an operations design; naming the dashboard an on-call engineer opens first, the alert that pages at 3 a.m. and why it is worth waking someone for, or why nobody is paged, is.

Why

Operations for takes, not for a service. Nobody runs this as a service and nothing promises uptime, so the unit of operations is the take, and the question each part of the section answers is what a failure costs a recording: a redone step, a retake or the rehearsal. Read it as the procedure that keeps a recording honest and repeatable.

One operator (A3) runs one process (D1) on one host for rehearsals, never a service; fAuth at b750ca53 signs every take in (K4, D4). Platform section 11 is the parent; here are the differences and the take.

11.1 Deployment view, rollout, and migration

Why

What the reset cannot restore. A fixture state holds only what the platform stores, rows, objects and the index file, so a reset cannot reach the browser or fAuth, and it leaves the platform's sessions alone on purpose (TH9). The one starting point act 1 needs, Maya signed out of the platform and of fAuth, whose live session would skip its page, is therefore something no reset can produce: step 3 of the take sets it by hand, and TH9's control counts on it (M17).

One digest, no waves. The platform rolls a release out in waves, so that a bad build reaches only part of its traffic first; the demo has one build for the whole recording, so there is nothing to stage. A new image means a new rehearsal and newly captured states, because each state carries the build digest it was captured on.

Platform diagram 08 is the deployment view, five reductions undrawn: its four ECS services are one Fargate task in one zone of the platform's region (D10, D2); no CloudFront or WAF, the load balancer ends TLS (P1) in two subnets of two zones, its listener behind M29's allowlist, the recording machine and the operator alone; no RDS standby; no NAT gateways, egress by the task's public address; the rest stays (section 8). fAuth is apart (A13, D9).

The rehearsal flag is one environment variable in the demo's task definition (6.7); every build starts the image under the platform's task definition against a database from the migrations alone: the reset is 404 and no reset role exists; the same build signs in through both adapters, so the fallback (D4) is a proven path, switched before a take, never during. No signed release [reduced: platform SR8; its release workflow the seam]: the image is built from pinned lockfiles and deployed by digest, the per-build test the gate.

Cold start, in order: DNS and certificates; keys, bucket, secrets; RDS, its four roles, then P9's fifth; the two alerts of 11.3; fAuth's four guards (FORMA-247), the redeploy at the pin, P9's invite-only tenants and users, the client row by hand (D9), the raised login limit; the task, alarming without fAuth's key set; P9's platform steps (6.7); a clean take writing s0 and s2 to s5; the assertion; the canary suite.

Rollout. One build digest for the recording (N9), no waves. A new image is a new rehearsal: the states carry the digest (section 8), so P9 recaptures them from a clean take before the snapshot; rollback is the previous task definition, triggered by a failing per-build test, assertion or canary suite; no upgrade or downgrade test, no state outliving a rehearsal.

Migration is platform 11.1's five steps, 1 to 3 true at birth (D2), the snapshot and the bucket's versions the way back. Step 4, one process to four services, needs what D1 keeps: the same request types in process as over HTTP, a typed principal, database roles (platform D11). Before any real organization: flag off, role reset dropped, states deleted, keys shredded (10.6).

A take, in order:

  1. Snapshot DS1 once, opening the rehearsal (section 8); a retake reuses it.
  2. Reset by P11 to the state before the act (section 8): s0 for acts 1 and 2, s2 for act 3, s3 for act 4, s4 for act 5, s5 for act 6; never during a take.
  3. Sign in Sarah and Jordan in their own profiles inside the idle hour (the reset keeps sessions); for act 1, Maya's profile is out of the platform and of fAuth, whose live session would skip its page. Only the actors' screens on camera (10.6), the address bar cut at the callback.
  4. P9's assertion: memberships and policies against the manifest, fAuth's user list per tenant, row counts against the restored state, a dry sign-in, the rate limit, the image digest; then the canary suite (R8). Any mismatch stops the take.
  5. Record, the rehearsal script (appendix A) pacing the actors and making 13.3's simulated faults. A provider failure, a lost scene or a miss of N2 ends the take, never continued on the labeled fixture (6.4); then step 2.
  6. The canary suite again, on the take's identifiers (R8). Capture and file: P10 reads the sanitised export and the operator views, checks each number against its receipt, files the packet and rehearsal log (R9) and anchors the manifest digest (M31). After the last take, 10.6's shredding.
Try it

Diagram 03 runs Spend Review's command with no control plane, P3, on it, yet the workspace server checks every decision against the pinned publication's record schema, read from the publication row (F5). Argue why reading the row is as safe as asking P3, from who writes a publication and what it names (6.2). Then predict what migration step 4, one process to four services, would have to add if P2 asked P3 for that schema on every command instead, and which failure would then stop a decision that the design as written survives.

Answer

Only role control writes a publication, inside the platform's SERIALIZABLE transaction, and a publication names one exact approved digest (6.2); a case stays pinned to its publication until an explicit adoption (R6). So the row cannot hold a schema P3 did not admit and publish, and it cannot change under a pinned case: asking P3 again would return the same answer, at the cost of a call, and the run path needs the database, not the control plane (7.2). If P2 asked P3 on every command, step 4 would turn that in-process call into a network hop on every decision, with its own request type and a principal carried across it, the things 11.1 says step 4 needs from D1, and the control plane's service would join the hard dependencies of every published app. Today the four roles share one process, so P3 cannot fail apart from P2; after step 4 it can, and a control-plane outage or deploy would then stop decision forms, where the design as written loses only what P3 itself does, admission and publication (6.2). That is what 7.2 means by "the control plane stays off the run path at migration (G7)" (7.2, 11.1).
