11.2 Scaling and cost

Why

The driver, and what "$17 a rehearsal" means. The largest line is Fargate, $85 of about $170, and its driver is the task's size, 2 vCPU and 8 GiB, not how much the task is used. "$17 a rehearsal" divides the month by ten rehearsals, so it is mostly fixed hosting spread over them; one more take costs only its tokens, as the paragraph under the table says.

Why N2 and M19 depend on the 8 GiB. A parser bomb that passes the byte cap meets A6's 50 MiB expanded cap next, which stops the parse and refuses the file (7.1); the module's 2 GiB memory cap is the backstop behind it, the point at which the runtime stops the module whatever the parse is doing. That backstop protects the process only if the module's 2 GiB fits beside everything else the process holds: the binary, two DuckDB operations, the result cache and some headroom. Sized to that sum, even a parse that got past the expanded cap would cost only the module; on a smaller task it could take memory the process needs, and the take would spend a restart, N2's 30 s, on what should have been a captured refusal.

The spend limit is a safety stop. The provider key sits in its own account unit with a spend limit just above the month's tokens, and hitting the limit is an error that is never retried: a runaway loop ends a take instead of running up a bill.

Nothing scales: N1 defers 10x to the platform (R10). Four numbers bind: a warm operation under 650 ms, a take's three waves of two inside N3's 2 s (6.3); 426 B of Forma's route share for a kind importing a new Forma module (6.5); a job in flight at a restart waits its 120 s lease, four times N2's 30 s, so act 4's drill runs with none (6.9); two 60 s generation attempts fit a five-minute act beside its other steps (6.4).

Overload cannot occur in a take: one actor at a time puts six operations at the data service, 2 running, 4 waiting, under the 20 that return 429 (5.2; platform 6.3); four simultaneous actors would queue 22 and see two 429s, so they are not a take. The task, 2 vCPU and 8 GiB: the binary about 1 GiB, two DuckDB operations at 1 GiB, the parser module's 2 GiB cap, the 2 GiB result cache, 1 GiB of headroom; N2's 30 s and M19's cap depend on it. The supervisor restarts in place, the task replacement unmeasured (5.2). The provider key sits in its own account unit with a spend limit just above the month's tokens (platform N10), the limit's error non-retryable, provider_unavailable.

Monthly cost, unit prices assumed: US East (N. Virginia) list at a 730-hour month, the platform's region (platform A9) until ruled, a European region about a tenth more; fAuth's hosting outside it:

Try it

Answer

1 GiB for the binary, 2 × 1 GiB for two DuckDB operations, the parser module's 2 GiB cap, the 2 GiB result cache and 1 GiB of headroom: 8 GiB. The month: $85 + $26 + $22 + $24 + $11 = $168, "about $170", and $16.80, about $17, a rehearsal at ten a month, $1.10 of it tokens. Tokens: 120 attempts are 2 attempts × 2 acts × 20 takes = 80, plus 40 for the spike and margin, at 8,000 tokens in and 3,000 out, $0.032 + $0.06 = $0.092 an attempt. At twenty rehearsals, 40 takes: 160 + 40 = 200 attempts, $18.40, so the month is about $175 and a rehearsal about $8.80. The driver is the Fargate line, and it does not move, because hosting runs whether or not anyone rehearses (11.2).

All exercises

11.3 Observability

Why

Alerts sized to the scene. The platform raises a ticket for a job queued over ten minutes (platform AL6), right for a service whose users can wait and wrong for a five-minute act; the demo pages on provider_unavailable within 1 s and ends the take. An alert's threshold follows the time scale of what it protects. The other page, any canary failure, is the platform's own: it means isolation may have broken, which is never something to leave until morning.

No SLO (3.2, A8): platform SLO1 has no meaning on one host; SLO2 to SLO5 become measurements with sample sizes; a miss is reported, only a platform-caused miss retaken (N2).

N3, at the client, from forma_rum_interaction_seconds{flow, device_class}: the six-view refresh from a whole-run take's 200 refreshes, the first cold after the reset (6.3); navigation and commits pooled over ten rehearsals, 400 and 200 samples; revocation once a take from forma_revocation_propagation_seconds. N2: the operator's restart to Maya's case reopening, one a whole-run take, the maximum over twenty. N6: P10's check of every shown number against its receipt, zero mismatches or the take fails.

Two alerts page the operator during a take: platform AL2, any increment of forma_canary_failures_total; and a provider failure: platform AL6 tickets it at ten minutes, too slow for a five-minute act, so provider_unavailable within 1 s (R13) pages and ends the take. Logs are the platform's, no intent text, rows or tokens, filed with the packet. Dashboard: the take id, the build digest, task CPU and memory against M19's headroom, the target's health, forma_job_oldest_age_seconds{kind}, p99 of forma_request_seconds by route, forma_canary_failures_total, forma_provider_spend_cents.

11.4 Failure modes and recovery

Why

Read the last column. Where the platform's table ends in diagnostics, this one ends in what happens to the take: it continues, waits, restarts the act or restarts the rehearsal. The decision is made in advance and in writing, so nobody improvises during a recording. The runbook rule under the table makes the procedure learn from the rehearsals, and its trigger is the second time: a one-off accident stays one blameless log line, and only what recurs earns a script step or a pre-take check that runs every take from then on.

Platform 11.4's rows for retry storms, silent numbers, approvals, placement and the browser hold; failover and rebalancing do not exist:

Failure Detection Mitigation The take
The process restarts, the host is lost, or the edge (P1) drops its target the island reloads; aws ecs describe-tasks, aws elbv2 describe-target-health in place or a new task, cache cold; state in DS1, one step redone; a job waits its 120 s lease; the target re-registers on the next check continues if the reopen lands inside 30 s; a lost host restarts the rehearsal
PostgreSQL down pool errors; aws rds describe-events nothing authorizes (6.9); wait, or restore the snapshot restarts; after a restore, the rehearsal
Bucket or KMS unreachable, cold path 503 on a cold refresh or import; forma admin key-status warm queries and commands continue; nothing fails open continues if warm; restarts if the cold refresh was the scene
fAuth down, limiter tripped, or a session lost the redirect's error or 429; forma admin keyset the raised burst (FORMA-247); sign-in inside the idle hour; sessions verify offline 12 h act 1 waits; later acts continue; a lost session restarts the act
The provider down, act 3 or 6 provider_unavailable within 1 s; forma admin jobs --stuck one jittered retry, then 503; queries and forms continue a retake from s2 or s5; the N4 drill is its own scene
The parser module dies at its 2 GiB backstop (P6) the job's failure reason; forma admin jobs --stuck the module dies, the process survives; the import fails visibly (S06) the take continues, the refusal captured

The reset racing a command, or a tampered state the reset's job state, or 412; forma admin epochs the membership row FOR UPDATE (6.7); never issued during a take; a state recaptured not reached; cannot start

Recovery is section 8's. S06's drill restores both in isolation and passes when Maya's case reopens at its pinned publication, audit intact, the canary passing; command to reopen is the RTO. Runbook rule: the take is the runbook; a remediation pasted twice becomes a P9 step or a forma admin command; a retake's cause is one blameless log line and, seen twice, a pre-take assertion.

Validation. Measurements: the ten rehearsals plus one open-loop replay at the envelope's burst of 24, then past where N3 breaks. Mitigations: drills, each a captured scene: the provider blocked in act 3, fAuth after act 1, the instance stopped, the process killed in act 4, a task replaced whole, the restore, the canary replaying throughout.

12. Alternatives considered

Method

For. The reviewer asks: did you choose, or did you build the first thing you thought of? First the drawbacks of the chosen design, on their own, then each major decision as a record: the drivers, the options, the one chosen and why, the good and bad consequences, and how the choice is confirmed. "Do nothing" and "reuse or buy" are always among the options.

Look for. What each rejected option optimises for. A rejected option that is simply "worse" was not a real option; a real one is better at something the design does not need, and the text says what. The confirmation line: a benchmark, a test suite or a drill that would show the choice was right, or wrong.

Pitfall. Straw men. If every alternative is obviously bad, the reader suspects the author never considered a good one. The honest version makes the best case for each option and then says why it loses here.

12.1 Drawbacks of the chosen design

Why

Drawbacks priced in takes and seconds. Each drawback names what it costs the recording and what catches it: one host makes a restart a scene, timed against N2; manual provisioning can over-grant an account, found by the assertion and the canary suite, and "nothing prevents it"; the demo-only route is dead without flag and role, proven every build. The phrase to copy is "nothing prevents it": a design that says which of its failures are only detected, not prevented, tells the reviewer where to look.

Why not a cheaper demo? One host (D1, D10): a fault in any role stops every role during a take, and a restart is a scene, not an incident, timed on camera against N2's 30 s, which limits the loss to one redone step. Manual provisioning (D6): a wrong flag in the script leaves an account over-granted; the pre-take assertion and the canary suite (R8) find it, nothing prevents it; the client row fAuth has no API for is inserted by hand (D9, AR4), so a wrong redirect URI is found by a dry sign-in, not a schema. The rehearsal flag puts a fifth database role and a demo-only route in the platform's binary (P11, AR5), dead without flag and role, proven every build. The operator's shell holds AS12's keys (AR3) because fAuth at b750ca53 federates no script and registers no client; the keychain bounds it. The integrity rule (D7) is a burden carried on camera: a slow spike delays the recording instead of hiding (A14). The platform's nine kinds (D5) express two apps; a kind asked for on the spot is a release, not a prompt (platform D1).

12.2 Alternatives

Why

"Reuse or buy", ranked by reuse risk. The parenthesis after each option says how much control the reuse would take from you: a library you call (a deck of mock-ups), a pattern you copy (design B v5 rebuilt), a framework that calls you and owns the control flow (a no-code tool). The more control it takes, the more of the claim rests on someone else's code; the no-code tool loses outright because it runs generated code as trusted, the thing the platform's typed definition exists to avoid.

Why

Option B is the trap this design is one setting away from. One process with one database credential is the simplest option, and it lets the code that handles model output insert a publication. The chosen design differs from B in one respect, each role connecting as its own database role with its own grants. The database itself is still shared, on purpose, so that a record, its outcome and its audit row commit in one transaction; what is not shared is the credential. (The shared database pattern lists the coupling costs of sharing a database; the record's objection to B is a different cost, authority.) The confirmation is a test that can fail, run on every build: workspace and worker try to write a publication through their own pools.

D1, one process. Drivers: A3, N9, G7, N7. Options: (A) the platform's roles as separate deployments, which optimises for the production shape but gives one founder eight things to restart during a take, losing against A3 and N2; (B) one process, one database credential, the shared-database antipattern, which optimises for simplicity but lets the role handling model output write a publication, losing against N7; (chosen) one process, each role its own database role, the parser a WebAssembly module in the worker (platform D11). Chosen because D11 allows it and the write grants survive the collapse (AR2). Good: one binary, one digest (N9). Bad: one fault stops all. Confirmed by the per-build test that workspace and worker cannot write a publication through their pools, which code holding the task role escapes (AR2).

Why

Why the keys are right from the first row. Of the rejected options, one organization per rehearsal leaves the canary nothing to replay, and adding the id later turns the seam into a migration of every stored row. Only the chosen option lets the canary suite test the platform's real keys on camera; isolation is the recording's claim, and keys cannot be retrofitted between takes.

D2, the organization id in every key. Drivers: N7, G5, G7. Options: one organization per rehearsal (nothing for the canary to replay, losing against G5); a demo schema with the id added later (the seam becomes a migration, losing against G7); (chosen) the platform's keys from row one. Chosen because isolation is the recording's claim and keys cannot be retrofitted on camera. Good: the canary suite runs unchanged. Bad: one instance, no standby. Confirmed by the suite each take (R8).

Why

"No fork" is what makes N9 structural. If the demo had its own definition format or its own admission, act 6 would prove the demo's code rather than the product's, and every contract would have to be proved twice. Using the platform's AppDefinition, admission, publication and command code means that N9's zero deploys between the two apps follow from the design instead of from discipline. Pitfall. Simplifying admission because it is only a demo: that is the fork this decision refuses, and full admission at demo scale is the price the record accepts for refusing it.

D3, the platform's code, no fork. Drivers: G2, N9, G7. Options: a demo-only definition format (act 6 becomes a second implementation, losing against G2); a demo-scale fork of admission (every contract reopens, losing against N9); (chosen) the platform's AppDefinition, admission, publication and command code. Chosen because two apps through one path (§18) proves nothing unless the path is the product's. Good: N9's zero deploys is structural. Bad: full admission at demo scale. Confirmed by S07's packet and the silent deploy log.

Why

What "two-way at the protocol" means. The adapter fixes the contract, a verified token carrying tenant_id and sub, and leaves the provider behind it free to change: fAuth now, the platform's minimal login as the fallback. Choosing fAuth also means that the organization the canary is refused by, and the person a revocation acts on, come from a real tenant boundary in a signed token that the demo did not have to build, rather than from a password store made for the recording. The dropdown, option C, loses not because it is short but because it is not a reduction: it removes authentication instead of shrinking it.

D4, the identity adapter. Drivers: A12, R1, N7, G7. Options: (C) an organization dropdown, which optimises for a short act 1 and is not a reduction, losing against G6; (D) fAuth's hosted sign-in, a real tenant boundary on camera for a second visual language and a client row; (E) the platform's minimal login, one fewer dependency; (chosen) the adapter with D behind it and E as the fallback (K4). Chosen because the token contract binds the demo and the provider does not (platform D6), and because the canary's denial (G5) and revocation then rest on a tenant boundary the demo did not build. Good: only act 1 changes; no password reaches the platform. Bad: a second deployment for one act, a client row by hand. Confirmed by the canary's token replay and the dry sign-in against both adapters on every build (M6; 11.1).

Why

The door that closes on someone else's desk. D7 is a working rule until submission, whose cost is retakes, and one-way after it, because the packet is then in YC's hands and a step cannot be relabeled. Most one-way doors are expensive because of stored data; this one is expensive because reversing it would need the recipient's action.

D7, the integrity rule. Drivers: G6, S07. Options: (F) a staged demo, fixtures wherever the path is slow, which optimises for a smooth take but makes the video the evidence, losing against G6 and R9; (chosen) every scene's mechanism named, its evidence captured, nothing simulated passes. Chosen because the partner's question is whether the second app is real. Good: a packet that outlives the video. Bad: retakes; one-way once submitted, a packet cannot be relabeled after YC has it. Confirmed by S07's packet checked against the build digest (M28).

Prior art is the platform's (platform 12.2); the demo adds none.

Try it

Make the strongest case, in three sentences and with this record's own numbers, for recording on the founder's machine or a single virtual machine instead of the ECS task (D10's alternative): what it would save a month and a rehearsal, and what the scenes would lose by it. Then argue the other side from G7 and from what the founder's machine could never measure, and, before reading 13.2, predict the one measurement that should settle the host, and which result would move the demo off the task.

Answer

For: on the founder's machine about $157 of the $168 month disappears, everything but the $11 of tokens, since a take's marginal cost is its tokens, "all the founder's machine (D10) costs" (11.2), so about $15.70 of each rehearsal's $16.80; a virtual machine needs no ECS account (12.2's table); one operator (A3) has one fewer system to provision and watch; and the restart the recording times is already a process restart under a supervisor (5.2), so the scenes lose nothing a task replacement would have shown. Against: the platform's own deployment is ECS on Fargate in one region, so a demo on the task is the platform's first deployment and its migration starts there, while a laptop or a virtual machine is a deployment to redo (G7). And the number the host question waits on, how long a full task replacement takes against N2's 30 s, can be measured only on the task: 5.2 leaves it unmeasured and times one apart, and the founder's machine "cannot time a task replacement" (12.2's table). So the deciding measurement is that one timed task replacement: if it meets N2's 30 s the task stays; if it misses, the host becomes one virtual machine, which is 13.2's current choice (5.2, 11.2, 12.2, 13.2).

12.3 Abandoned ideas

Why

Abandoned here, not forever. The MCP scene depended on a desktop assistant's handling of a local connector, outside the take's control, and the public page was reachable only on the machine that served it, so a partner could not test it; both, with the three surfaces, return as platform work (platform C14). Recording each idea's pitfall is what stops the next reader proposing it again without an answer.

Each with its pitfall. Three surfaces, design B v5's shape: three renderers in parity, isolation proved first on the surface with the most threats (platform 12.3). The MCP scene rested on Claude Desktop's handling of a local connector (v5 A6), outside our control during a take. The public page: public in shape, loopback in reach (v5 D28), so a partner cannot test it. All three return as platform work (§18; platform C14). Design B v5's insurance scenes and markup modules: a first scene waiting on two security-critical framework tickets (platform 12.3). The same-site refresh-cookie bridge: a session contract the platform would carry for one demo. The passkey button (K4): ten seconds narrating fAuth instead of Northstar. An organization dropdown: a login that is not a reduction, so G6 fails in act 1.

13. Risks, open questions, objections, and future work

Method

For. The reviewer asks: do you know what you don't know, and have you heard my objection already? Risks ranked on the same scale as the threat table, open questions with their candidate answers and the current choice, the three objections a reviewer will raise first with pointers to where the document answers them, and future work in a few lines.

Look for. Known unknowns listed as "what I would want a reviewer to look at". Open questions bucketed: before build, during build, later. The objections section: if your first question is not there, either the author missed it or the document answers it so well it was not an objection.

Pitfall. Using future work to excuse the design. "This will be addressed later" is not an answer to a risk; a mitigation with an owner is.

13.1 Risks

Why

A risk scale measured in takes. High ends a goal or the claim, Medium costs a take, Low moves a number: the same High as the threat table, with the lower grades translated into what a rehearsal loses. Why RK3 is looked at first, though Low on likelihood. A seeded step passing as working is unlikely, with the labels, the receipt check and a second viewer against it, but it cannot be undone once the packet is submitted (D7), and it voids the whole claim rather than one scene. Rank by what a failure would destroy, not only by how often it happens.

Platform 13.1 holds. The demo's, on 10.4's scale (likelihood/impact): High ends G5, G6 or the claim; Medium costs a take; Low moves a number.

ID Risk L/I Mitigation; if it happens

RK2 fAuth: the live service behind b750ca53, the client row by hand, keys on one shell (D9, AR3, AR4; FORMA-247, FORMA-248) M/H cold-start guards (11.1); dry sign-in (M6); keychain (M9). Act 1 stalls; the minimal login (D4)

13.2 Open questions

Why

Every question carries its current answer. Each open question names the choice the build proceeds with until it is answered, so nothing waits on it; a question without one either stops the build or is settled in passing by whoever meets it first, with no record. Notice also that the "Still unknown" line holds only what a measurement will settle, the spike's numbers, the timed task replacement, the RTO from S06's drill and a month's cost from the meter, never a decision someone has yet to make.

Before build. Host (D10): ECS task, virtual machine or the founder's machine; the task, kept if its timed replacement meets N2's 30 s, else one virtual machine. Region: the platform's, or European; the platform's until ruled. Spike provider (D8): the labeled fixture or a live call; the fixture, live from the first rehearsal.

During build. Rehearsals: ten, each filmed at most twice, or until three run clean; ten. The canary suite: on camera or in the packet; one replay on camera, the suite in the packet. A third app (§18): one labeled unscripted take a rehearsal, named by someone outside the team, filed admitted or refused naming the missing kind (platform R4). Restarts: one scene of ten, or one a take; one a take (11.3). Minimisation: blur or cut; cut (10.6). RTO: deferred to S06's drill.

Later. The packet to YC: a link or an appendix; a link, ruled at submission. POST /manage/oauth-clients (FORMA-247, optional): deferred to a second environment. Real-data terms (3.2, C15): deferred to a pilot.

Still unknown: the spike's four numbers, the task replacement, RTO, a month's cost. Future work: a pilot behind a data protection impact assessment (platform 13.2).

13.3 Objections

Why

Answered by evidence, not assurance. Each objection is answered with a pointer to sections, goals and fixtures rather than with a new argument, which is the test that the body already answers it. Notice the first, "Made on camera, or loaded?": its answer is one build digest and zero deploys, things the packet shows, rather than a promise. And notice the form of the third, "What is simulated?": an inventory of every labeled step under its label, which a skeptic can check against the packet item by item, where a general "nothing important is simulated" could only be believed.

  • "Made on camera, or loaded?" Made, through act 3's interface on one digest, zero deploys between (G2, N9; 7.2; S07).
  • "One take or many?" One kept take per act, each from where the last ended (8); the numbers repeat across takes, the model's arrangement may not, and the rehearsal log counts every discarded take (R9).
  • "What is simulated?" Captioned on screen as it happens, logged, and excluded from S07's acceptance measures (G6, D7). Seeded: each take's starting state and the spike's fixture proposal. Simulated by the rehearsal script at the client, server answers real: act 4's late answer, act 6's dropped response, stale and reused-key requests and late Finance answer. Manual: act 4's restart.
  • "So the second app skipped review?" No: policy is per organization (platform R9); Sarah approves Spend Review too (7.2).
  • "Does it survive the demo?" Every reduction names its seam (G7, 6.8); keys and request types are the platform's (platform 11.1).
Try it

The second-app objection is answered by one fact: policy is per organization. Make the founder's best case for letting Maya publish Spend Review herself under owner publication, to save ten seconds; then show what that change would break elsewhere in the recording and what it would prove instead. Finally, if the provisioning script set owner publication by mistake, say what a check must compare the policy row against to catch it before the camera rolls, and why checking once, right after provisioning, would not be enough.

Answer

For: Spend Review records internal decisions about synthetic expenses and pays nobody (7.2, step 6; 6.8's "no connector or external action"), so the founder can argue that a wrong decision costs little, that review adds only delay, and that ten seconds matter in a five-minute act. What it breaks: Security and Finance share Northstar's one policy row (6.2; 7.2, step 2), so owner publication for Spend Review is owner publication for the investigation app too; Maya's own publish in act 4 would succeed, and R4's refusal, the scene that proves independent review, would disappear (6.2's "act 4 loses its refusal"; RK4). What it would prove instead: that an administrator can set an owner-publication policy and the platform honours it, a claim about configurable policy rather than about a reviewer approving exactly what runs; and the partner would see an app nobody else approved, the very objection 13.3 answers. The check: the policy row against the provisioning script's manifest, the record of what the script meant to set, since the row alone cannot say it is wrong. Once is not enough, because the row can change after provisioning: the script is rerun when its output is wrong (11.4), and every reset restores rows from a captured state, so a wrong policy captured once comes back with each reset until the states are recaptured. That check is the pre-take assertion, reading each organization's one policy row against the manifest before every take (6.2; M10, as RK4 cites it), so a wrong kind stops the take before the camera rolls (R7, 13.3).

All exercises

Appendix

Method

For. Reference that nothing in the body depends on: the glossary, the references, the threat rows beyond the top ones where 10.4 keeps only those, the security tables 10.2 and 10.6 point to, the dependency table when section 6 names its hard rows and the bound they set (GUIDE 3.6), any full schemas, and for an as-built record the conformance table. Nothing here is required reading; everything here is where the body points when a reader wants proof.

Look for. Where there is a continued threat table, the same columns as 10.4, so any row there traces the same way, to its data-flow element, its invariant and the SR whose test would catch it. That trace, from threat to test, is the difference between a security section and a security design. In an as-built record, read the conformance table's counts first: met, partly met, unmet.

A. Glossary

Why

This edition's glossary has two sources. Appendix A repeats the record's own inline definitions, and its first sentence names the shared platform terms, from admission to space, that the platform's glossary defines. This layer defines those shared terms again for this edition, so you can read the demo without the platform's glossary open; both sets are merged on the Glossary tab.

The platform's glossary (its appendix A) defines the shared terms: admission, adoption, app definition, canvas, case, composer, control plane, data service, epoch, expected version, idempotency key, island, publication, receipt, record command, row-level security, space. The demo's own, repeating their inline definitions:

  • Act: one of the controlling definition's six scenes (§16); a take is one recording of an act or of the whole run, a rehearsal a timed whole run, filmed at most twice; the recording keeps one take of each act (8, 11.1).
  • Canary suite: the second organization's scripted replay of every call with Northstar's identifiers, run on every build and at both ends of every take, each reply 404 before data, paired with the owner's 200 (R8, SR2).
  • Client row: the oauth_clients row that makes the platform a registered client of fAuth, inserted by hand because fAuth has no registration endpoint; a public PKCE client, no secret (A13, D9).
  • Evidence recorder (P10): the operator's read-only script that assembles the packet from Chrome's sanitised export and the operator views, every remaining header dropped, the packet's manifest digest anchored (6.7).
  • Fixture state (s0, s2 to s5; no s1, act 1 changing nothing a take restores): both organizations' rows, objects and index file at the end of a clean act, written by the provisioning script under the operator prefix with a digest over manifest and build; a take of act N starts from the state before it (section 8).
  • Labeled step: a seeded, simulated or manual step named in the packet and excluded from acceptance (G6, D7); 13.3 lists them: seeded, simulated by the rehearsal script, manual.
  • Operator's machine (B9): the laptop holding the keychain, the actors' profiles, the raw export and the packet; the demo's own boundary (7.3, TH15).
  • Packet: the evidence delivered with the recording: pins, both definitions and digests, fixtures, receipts, record outcomes, admission reports and the rehearsal log (S07, R9).
  • Platform key, management key: fAuth's credentials for creating tenants and for configuring one tenant, held only by the operator's shell (AS12, AR3).
  • Pre-take assertion: the provisioning script's check of memberships, policies, fAuth's user list, row counts, a dry sign-in and the rate limit before every take (6.7, 11.1).
  • Provisioning script (P9): the operator's idempotent script that creates the tenants, users, spaces, memberships, policies, the client row and role reset, and writes the fixture states (6.7).
  • Rehearsal script: the take's driver on the operator's machine, over the Chrome DevTools Protocol: it brings one actor's profile forward at a time and makes 13.3's simulated faults at the client, a response held late, a response dropped after the server answered, the stale and reused-key requests; it adds no code to the product (D3; 11.1).
  • Rehearsal flag: the environment variable in the demo's task definition under which alone the reset route registers, with role reset present; never set in the platform's deployment (6.7, 11.1, SI7).
  • Reset (P11): the job that restores a named fixture state between takes under its own database role, keeping audit and sessions and bumping the membership epoch (6.7, 8, 9).
  • Spike: the measurement before any scene: the path from definition to reopen on the real library and route, the commit's latency, the restart maximum, the route's bytes and its server render rate (R11, D8).
  • Synthetic label: the organization row's synthetic flag the provisioning script sets and no member can, required on every organization before a reset (section 9).
  • Supervisor: the process inside the container that restarts the binary in place, so a restart is a process restart, not a task replacement (5.2, 11.2).

B. References

The platform record's appendix B lists the shared sources: the controlling definition, the contracts, the pins of Forma 3.0.0 (2006423b) and fAuth (b750ca53), the earlier records, the standards and the vendor documentation. The demo's own, each cited at its point of use:

  • PRODUCT-BRIEF.md (the demo's restatement of the controlling definition, whose sections are cited as §N: the six acts §16, the completeness test §18, the non-goals §19); SCENARIOS.md (S01 to S07, the fixtures and their arithmetic); BUILD-HANDOFF.md (the eight reductions and what is not a reduction); platform-contract-lock.json (edition prep-2026-10-22.1); input/brief.md; intake.md (A1 to A10, the K rulings); review/foundation-review.md.
  • The platform record, tasks/forma-generative-app-platform-v2/design.md, at the phase 7 commit this record cites, with its review/fauth-viability.md (fAuth at the pin, the handoff, the guards and the K4 ruling) and review/spike-native-composition/ (the four-kind canvas at 27,674 of 28,100 B).
  • Design B v5, the insurance demo this record revises in direction (tag task/forma-mvp/v5, folder tasks/forma-insurance-demo).
  • Tickets on the Forma work board: FORMA-232 and FORMA-246 (assumed done, K3); FORMA-247 (fAuth as the demo's login: the redeploy at the pin, tenant provisioning, the client row, the rehearsal rate limit); FORMA-248 (fAuth's signing key in KMS).
  • Vendor documentation, verified at the claims phase: AWS ECS on Fargate (task start and replacement, the public IPv4 charge per address), Application Load Balancer (the two-subnet minimum), RDS (single-instance snapshots inside the free allocation, IAM authentication's memory), S3 versioning, KMS key deletion (the 7-day minimum and the 24-hour hold the platform adds), Secrets Manager, the free 100 GB of egress; Chrome's sanitised HAR export and profiles; the Anthropic API's token pricing for the provider line.

C. Threat rows beyond section 10.4

Why

The numbers move between records. Appendix C's mapping sentence is a translation table: the platform's TH1, a member of another organization reading Northstar's data, is this record's TH4, and the platform's TH4, the parser bomb, is this record's TH10. Read "platform TH" with its prefix and use the mapping, or you will compare two different threats. Notice the three rows that are new, TH8 (the reset racing a command), TH14 (a deploy between acts) and TH15 (the operator's machine): each is a threat the platform cannot have, because it has no reset, no recording and no scripts run from a laptop.

The eight rows 10.4 does not keep, TH8 to TH15, on its scale and with its columns: the rows a platform control covers, re-rated for one process and one operator; every STRIDE category already has a row in 10.4. TH10 to TH12 are High on likelihood and Medium on impact because D1 and the platform's walls keep them inside one organization, TH10's escape half Low on likelihood and High on impact; TH14 is High on impact at Low likelihood; TH15 Medium and High; the rest Medium on both. The platform's rows map so: TH1 to the demo's TH4, TH3 to TH3, TH4 to TH10, TH7 to TH5, TH12 to TH9, TH13 to TH11, TH15 to TH12, TH16 to TH13; TH21 holds; the demo's TH8, TH14 and TH15 are new. Re-rated, with reasons: platform TH8, because platform M16's service token is not minted and a typed principal plus the callee's re-read of membership replace it, a control against a logic bug, not against code in the process, existing control none, Low/High, residual Medium (AR2); platform TH11, because the owner credential is a standing key in the operator's keychain with no breakglass and no outside reader, Medium/High, residual Medium (AR1, AR3), M31 making the audience the audit's reader; platform TH14, because the per-client edge limiter was a WAF rule and the WAF is reduced away while the host is public, so the in-process limits bound a signed-in member, not an outsider, High/Medium, residual Medium until M29's address allowlist at the load balancer is set (11.1), then Low; platform TH17 moot, synthetic rows and the snapshots deleted after delivery; platform TH27 removed with TA10. The head owns each residual risk.

Why

Why sessions surviving the reset is a threat row. Keeping sessions makes retakes quick, and it means a cookie from the previous take still works in the next. The control is the epoch: every request checks it with nothing cached in front of it, and the reset bumps it, so every tab re-authorizes within 5 s against the restored rows.

Why

One process changes the parser's worst case. In the platform an escaped parser reaches what the worker role can; here the module runs inside the one process, whose task role reaches every pool, both data keys and the provider key, so escape is rated High on impact. Exhaustion is the likelier half, High on likelihood because any file a builder drops can attempt it, and the design meets it in layers: the byte caps refuse an oversize file before parsing; A6's expanded cap stops a parse that inflates past 50 MiB; and behind both, the module's memory cap and its fuel, the runtime's budget of work, enforced below the task's memory, are the backstop, so that whatever gets past the first two kills only the module, never the process (M19; 7.1, 11.2).

Why

A threat the video cannot show. A deploy between acts 3 and 6 would change nothing on screen, because Spend Review looks the same on a different build, and its actor is the operator (TA9), so the operator's own word that nothing was deployed proves nothing. The control therefore reads what the operator does not write by hand, the task's image digest and the cloud's deploy log, and the row is High on impact at Low likelihood because what it would void is N9, the claim 4.2 ranks first.

Why

The laptop as one point of total compromise. Whoever controls the operator's machine gets every key, every actor's session, the unfiltered export and the pin file at once: everything the walls elsewhere protect. Nothing on one laptop can be walled off from whoever controls it, so M30 works on the two things a single machine still allows, how much is on it and for how long, and M31 adds a record made elsewhere, under the Object Lock anchor, so that tampering shows afterwards. What remains is accepted as the one machine (AR3).

Course

8 lessons that walk the record in its own order. Each names its sections, what you should be able to do afterwards, and how long a careful first read takes. Tick a lesson when you can do what it lists; the tick is kept in this browser.

Lesson 1: What a design document is for

45 minutes · sections 1. Summary, 2. Context and problem statement
  • Explain who reads a design document and what each reader is looking for.
  • Find the sentence that says what the design optimises for, and what it gives up.
  • Retell the problem as a mechanism: the component, the step and the number that fails.
  • Name the one-way doors and say why each is expensive to reverse.

Read the summary twice: once before the rest of the document and once after. The second time you will see how much of it is a promise the body keeps. Then read the context as if you had to solve the problem yourself tomorrow with a different design.

2 design notes in these sections · exercises: 1, 2

Lesson 2: Pinning the target

60 minutes · sections 3. Goals, non-goals, and assumptions, 4. Requirements
  • Tell a goal from a non-goal from an assumption, and say what each one is for.
  • Follow one quality requirement back to the arithmetic that produced its number.
  • Read a latency target written as percentiles and say what it allows.
  • Say which requirements the design deliberately lowers, and why that is honest rather than weak.

Pick one N requirement and rebuild its number on paper from the assumptions in section 3 and the load parameters in 4.2. A factor that appears from nowhere, a peak multiplier say, is a gap the document should have derived; note it. If you can rebuild the number, you now understand the scale the whole design is built for.

6 design notes in these sections · exercises: 3, 4

Lesson 3: The shape

60 minutes · sections 5. Architecture overview
  • Read a system context picture and a container picture, and say what each box and arrow means.
  • Tell the worked scenario back in your own words, end to end.
  • Use the key-decisions table as a map: for any box, find the decision that put it there.
  • Explain the fit check: which number lands on which component.

Cover the text and describe the system from the overview's pictures alone. Then read the scenario and check yourself. The things you got wrong are what the pictures do not say; a good document says them in the narration.

4 design notes in these sections · exercises: 5, 6

Lesson 4: Inside the boxes

75 minutes · sections 6. Component design
  • Read a component card and state the component's one job and what it refuses to do.
  • Find the ceiling of each component and the reason behind it.
  • Read a dependency table and say what happens when each dependency is down.
  • Explain an extension point in the form "to add Y you add Z without editing W".

For each card (a container without a hard choice gets a one-paragraph card with no headings), write the ceiling line in your own words before reading it. Then look at the worked example and change one value: does the mechanism still work? If the answer is not obvious, you have found a corner case the card should have covered.

9 design notes in these sections · exercises: 7, 8

Lesson 5: Following the data

75 minutes · sections 7. Data flows, 8. Data model and storage, 9. API surface
  • Read a data-flow diagram: processes, stores, external entities, and the trust boundaries between them.
  • Follow one flow through its phases to the terminal line, then through its failure cases.
  • Say for each store whether it is the system of record or derived, and what that decides.
  • Read an API sketch and say what a caller sees on permission failure, on a missing object, and on a repeated request.

Take the sequence diagram and, at each step, ask what would happen if the message were forged or lost. The flows are where the threat model comes from, so every answer you write here is a row you will recognise in section 10.

6 design notes in these sections · exercises: 9, 10

Lesson 6: Attacking the design

90 minutes · sections 10. Security and threat model
  • List the invariants and name the component that enforces each.
  • Read a STRIDE row and identify the actor, the prerequisite, the action, the impact and the asset.
  • Tell a preventative mitigation from a detective one, and say why High rows need both.
  • Explain the break-glass path and why operator access is a design question, not a policy.

Start with the trust levels and the assets, not the table. Then pick three rows with High impact, the ones the invariants exist for, and trace each to its data-flow element, its invariant and its security requirement in section 4. If a row does not trace, that is a finding.

8 design notes in these sections · exercises: 11, 12

Lesson 7: Running it

60 minutes · sections 11. Operations
  • Explain the rollout, staged or not, and name what triggers rollback.
  • Read an objective and the indicator that measures it, and say whether an alert measures it; an objective with neither an alert nor a stated reason for none is a finding.
  • Use the failure-modes table: for a given failure, say how it is detected, what mitigates it and what an operator types.
  • Say what changes at ten times the load, and which cost line grows first.

Imagine you are on call tonight. Which dashboard do you open, which alert, if any, would wake you, and what would you do when it did? The section should answer all three without you guessing.

5 design notes in these sections · exercises: 13, 14

Lesson 8: Being honest

60 minutes · sections 12. Alternatives considered, 13. Risks, open questions, objections, and future work, Appendix
  • Read a decision record: drivers, options, the choice, the consequences, the confirmation.
  • Say what each rejected alternative optimises for and why that is wrong here.
  • Rank a risk on the same scale as the threat table and say what failure would look like.
  • Read the objections section and check whether your own first question is there.

Write down the three questions you would ask the author before reading section 13.3. If they are there, the document works; if they are not, you have found either a gap or a question only you would ask, and both are worth knowing.

6 design notes in these sections · exercises: 15, 16

Glossary

237 terms. In the document the first use of each term in every section is a green link; hover to read the definition.

`__Host-` cookie
the platform's session cookie: opaque, carrying only a random id, and with a prefix that makes the browser accept it only over HTTPS from the host that set it (Set-Cookie) (10.6)
`BYPASSRLS`
a role attribute that skips every row policy; no runtime role carries it, and neither does reset (CREATE ROLE) (6.7, 8)
`createResource`
Forma's primitive for data that loads asynchronously, re-running a fetch whenever its source signal changes (Forma's core API); none of the four measured kinds imports it, so a kind that does would be the one to spend the 426 B (6.5)
`FOR UPDATE` (`FOR SHARE`)
row locks taken inside a transaction: an exclusive one on a row about to change, and a shared one that blocks any exclusive lock until the transaction ends (explicit locking) (6.7, 7.2, 8)
`FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`
the table setting that subjects even the table's owner to its row policies; without it the owner is exempt (row security policies) (8)
`no-store`
the cache directive that forbids any cache to keep the response; every /v1/ response carries it (RFC 9111) (8)
`NOLOGIN`
a role attribute that forbids connecting; a NOLOGIN owner of the tables means no connection ever acts as their owner (CREATE ROLE) (8)
`provider_unavailable`
the error the composer returns within 1 s when the model provider fails; during a take it pages and ends the take (6.4, 11.3)
`Retry-After`
the response header saying when to try again; the browser retries only a 503 that carries it (RFC 9110) (9)
`state`
a random value the client sends when sign-in starts and checks at the callback, so the callback is tied to the browser that began it (TH3, 10.2)
`tenant_id` (`sub`)
the claims in fAuth's token that name the tenant and the person; a session is minted from these two alone (6.1, 10.5)
28,100 B (route budget)
the most framework code one page, a route, may load, measured gzip-compressed (gzip); the composition fixture used 27,674 B, leaving 426 B (reading note, D5, 6.5)
403
Forbidden: the server understood the request and refuses it; here only where the caller may already see the thing, Maya's own publish (RFC 9110) (9)
404
Not Found, which HTTP also allows for a resource the server will not admit exists; here denied, foreign and absent are one answer (RFC 9110) (9, R8)
409
Conflict: the request conflicts with the current state of the resource, a newer record version or an earlier request under the same key (RFC 9110) (7.2, 9)
412
Precondition Failed: a condition the request depends on no longer holds, as with a stale patch, a changed draft or a state whose digest does not match (RFC 9110) (9)
422
Unprocessable Content: the request is well formed but cannot be processed, as with an oversize file or a query past the grammar (RFC 9110) (9)
429
Too Many Requests: the caller is being rate-limited, here by a full job slot or a queue past 20 (RFC 6585) (5.2, 9)
503
Service Unavailable: temporarily unable to answer, here because the model provider is down; sent with Retry-After (RFC 9110) (6.9, 9)
7-day minimum (waiting period)
the delay KMS imposes before deleting a key, 7 to 30 days, during which the key cannot be used and the deletion can still be cancelled (KMS key deletion) (10.6)
730-hour month
the pricing convention behind every monthly line: 365 days of 24 hours, divided by 12 (11.2)
Act
one of the controlling definition's six scenes (§16); a take is one recording of an act or of the whole run, a rehearsal a timed whole run, filmed at most twice; the recording keeps one take of each act (8, 11.1). from the record's glossary
actor
one of the fictional people as played on camera, Maya, Sarah or Jordan, each in their own Chrome profile; not a threat actor (A13, 11.1)
administration group
the platform API's operations for memberships, spaces, aliases and policy, called by an organization's administrator; the provisioning script uses it (6.7, 9)
admission (admission report)
the control plane's check of a proposed definition against the schema, the grammar, the complexity limits and the registered kinds and operators; the report says what it checked and refused, and a fixture proposal's report carries a fixture label (6.2, TH12)
adoption
explicitly moving a case to a newer publication of its app, by compare-and-set; until then it stays pinned (R6, 7.1)
alias
a short name such as /security that resolves to the same stable id as a click (R1, 6.4)
allowlist
a list of the only addresses allowed to connect, everything else refused; M29's admits the recording machine and the operator during rehearsals (10.4, 11.1)
anchor (anchored)
a copy of the audit chain's latest hash written where it cannot be changed, so the chain up to it cannot be rewritten unnoticed; here it goes to Object Lock every 15 minutes (TH7, SR4)
app definition (`AppDefinition`, typed app definition)
the typed description of an app, its views, queries, records and commands, that the model proposes and the platform validates and renders: data, never code (K1, 5, 7.1)
application budget
the size budget an application's routes get under FORMA-232, the Forma ticket for route size budgets that K3 assumes done; 6.5 names it as the way past the 28,100 B ceiling other than cutting a kind (6.5; platform appendix B)
attack tree
a goal broken into the ways of reaching it; OR means any one branch is enough (10.4)
audit (hash chain, chained)
the insert-only record of every governed action; its rows are chained by hash, each carrying the hash of the one before, so a deleted or altered row breaks the chain (10.6, TH7)
authorization-code flow (code flow)
the sign-in in which the browser returns from the identity service with a one-time code that the client exchanges for a token (RFC 6749, section 4.1) (A13, 10.5)
authorizer (authorization point)
the one function that decides whether a request may proceed, re-reading the membership epoch on every request; the workspace server holds it (5.2, 10.5)
availability zone (zone)
one of a region's separate data centres; the demo's task runs in one and its load balancer spans two (11.1)
binding (bindings)
the link from a case to the source revision or record collection it uses; Jordan's new work has its own (R6, 7.1)
blameless
a write-up of what went wrong that names causes and fixes, not people (postmortem culture) (11.4)
blast radius
what a compromise of one boundary can reach (10.2)
breakglass
an emergency path to powers beyond a person's normal role, logged and reviewed by someone else; the demo has none (AR1, 10.5)
build digest (image digest)
the digest of the exact container image that runs; one for the whole recording, read by the recorder at a take's start and end (OCI descriptors) (N9, 11.1, TH14)
BUILD-610 (BUILD-819)
the framework tickets behind the renderer's refusal of a computed kind and behind the 28,100 B route budget (TH12, reading note)
C01 to C16
the shared contracts between the platform and the demo, at lock edition prep-2026-10-22.1; this record cites them and restates what it relies on (reading note, 2)
canary (canary organization)
the second synthetic organization, whose member replays Northstar's calls with Northstar's identifiers and must be denied every time (reading note, 5.1, R8)
Canary suite
the second organization's scripted replay of every call with Northstar's identifiers, run on every build and at both ends of every take, each reply 404 before data, paired with the owner's 200 (R8, SR2). from the record's glossary
canvas
the surface on which an app's views are arranged, rendered by one browser island (reading note, 6.5)
capacity unit
the load balancer's usage measure, priced by the hour on top of its base rate (11.2)
case (saved work, work id)
a piece of saved work: one id pinned to the publication it was started on, with its bindings, records and notes (reading note, R5, R6)
CDN
a content delivery network that serves files from places near the user; the platform's edge has one and the demo's does not (5.2, 6.6)
Chrome profile (profile)
a separate set of Chrome data, history, passwords, settings and accounts, on one machine; one per actor keeps three sessions apart (Chrome profiles) (A13, 11.1)
CIDR (CIDR lookup)
the notation for an address range, an address and a prefix length such as /24 for 256 addresses (RFC 4632); the lookup matches a destination to the inventory, exact entry first (D5, 7.1)
Client row
the oauth_clients row that makes the platform a registered client of fAuth, inserted by hand because fAuth has no registration endpoint; a public PKCE client, no secret (A13, D9). from the record's glossary
CloudWatch
AWS's metrics and logs service; the cost table prices its logs and metric series (CloudWatch) (11.2)
cold (warm)
a cold query must first fetch and decrypt its source revision from object storage; a warm one finds it already in the process (5.2, 6.3)
cold start
bringing the whole environment up from nothing, in dependency order (11.1)
commit sequence
a counter that orders an organization's committed rows, so "everything after this point" is one comparison; the reset deletes past a state's point, and a receipt pins the record snapshot's to say which version it saw (6.7, 7.2, 8)
compare-and-set
change a value only if it still equals what you last read; publication and adoption move a pointer WHERE current = expected, so a stale attempt changes nothing (N5, 8)
completeness test (completeness clauses)
§18's checks that the product is a platform: two apps through one creation, publication, access and saved-work model, a second user working independently, saved work reopening with its context, revocation holding, a published app surviving a failing draft (2, G1)
component kind
one of the renderer library's view types, such as a summary, a table, a timeline or a form; the demo ships the platform's nine and adds none (D5, 6.5)
composer
the assistant that turns an intent into a proposed definition or patch, through a job the worker runs (5, 6.4)
compromise domain (failure domain)
everything one break-in, or one fault, takes down together; one host is one of each (SA1, D1)
connection pool (pool)
a set of open database connections a role reuses; here one per database role, each opened at start with its own 15-minute token (5.2, 10.5)
control plane
the role that admits definitions and alone writes publications and policy (6.2)
controlling definition (§16, §18, §19)
the App Platform definition the product is judged against, restated for the demo in PRODUCT-BRIEF.md: §16 is the six acts, §18 the completeness test, §19 the section the non-goals cite (reading note, 2)
credentials endpoint
the local address from which code in a task fetches the task role's credentials; the parser module has no path to it (6.4, 10.5)
data classes
the labels that decide protection and retention per kind of data: synthetic rows Confidential, credentials, sessions and keys Restricted, the recording Internal (4.2, 10.6)
data protection impact assessment
the risk assessment data protection law requires before high-risk processing of personal data; due before any pilot on real data (EDPB guidelines) (13.2)
data service
the role that runs typed queries and commits record commands, the only one that reads Parquet or writes records (6.3)
database role
a PostgreSQL identity with its own grants; here one for each platform role, workspace, control, data and worker, plus reset under the rehearsal flag (5.2, D1)
db.t4g.small
the database instance class in the cost table, whose 2 GiB of memory must also hold IAM authentication's overhead (instance classes) (11.2)
deploy log
the cloud's record of deployments; the recorder checks that it is silent between acts 3 and 6 (N9, 6.7)
design A (design B v5)
the earlier records: design A, the security-first platform on markup modules that the platform record revises, and design B v5, its insurance demo, which this record revises in direction and carries nothing from (cover, 12.3)
digest (SHA-256)
a short hash that names exact bytes, a definition, a fixture state or an image, so changing one byte changes it; SHA-256 is the function the record names for a state's (FIPS 180-4) (8, TH2)
drill
a failure or a restore staged on purpose to prove a mitigation; each is a captured scene here (11.4)
dry sign-in
a test sign-in before a take that checks the client row, its redirect URI and state; a failure stops the take (6.1, SR3, 11.1)
DuckDB
an analytical SQL engine that runs inside the process and reads Parquet directly; the data service's typed queries run on it (why DuckDB) (6.3, 6.9)
EdDSA
the signature scheme fAuth signs its tokens with; anyone holding the public key can verify a token, so the platform needs no secret of fAuth's (RFC 8032) (5.1)
egress
traffic leaving the host; only role worker may reach the provider (6.4, 11.1)
ends TLS
decrypts the HTTPS connection; past the load balancer, the hop to the process is plaintext HTTP (5.2, 10.6)
envelope
the assumed scale the design is sized for, an upper bound rather than a forecast (3.3, A4)
epoch (membership epoch, filter epoch)
a counter that a change advances so that a late answer can be told from a current one: the membership epoch moves on revocation or a reset and is checked on every request; the filter epoch moves with each canvas filter change, and the browser drops answers carrying an older one (reading note, 6.1, 6.5)
Evidence recorder
(P10): the operator's read-only script that assembles the packet from Chrome's sanitised export and the operator views, every remaining header dropped, the packet's manifest digest anchored (6.7). from the record's glossary
expected version
the record version an edit was based on; if the record has moved on, the edit is refused with 409 instead of silently overwriting (reading note, 7.2, 9)
explanation
in the platform, the job that sends one receipt, and only the fields the organization's policy names, to the model provider for an account of a number in words, refused if it cites a number the receipt lacks (platform 6.4); the demo's cost table budgets none (6.4, 11.2)
export
a labeled snapshot of selected findings with their source and app revisions and capture time; once downloaded it cannot be recalled (7.1, S04); in "the raw export" and "an unsanitised export", instead, the browser's HAR capture before the recorder filters it (6.7, 10.6)
Fargate task (ECS task, ECS)
the cloud's container service, and its mode in which the cloud runs the servers; the demo is one task, one running copy of the container (AWS Fargate) (D10, 11.1)
fAuth
Forma's own identity service, which the platform signs in through, run as its own deployment and pinned at b750ca53; it knows who signs in and never sees data (2, 5.1, 6.1)
fit check
the part of 5.2 that places the requirements' numbers on the components that carry them (5.2)
fixture (fixtures)
fixed synthetic inputs with known expected results, the scenarios S01 to S07 (2, 4.2)
Fixture state
(s0, s2 to s5; no s1, act 1 changing nothing a take restores): both organizations' rows, objects and index file at the end of a clean act, written by the provisioning script under the operator prefix with a digest over manifest and build; a take of act N starts from the state before it (section 8). from the record's glossary
Forma 3.0.0
the web framework the platform is built on, pinned at 2006423b; its compiler limits and its route budget bound the browser workspace (2, 6.5)
FORMA-247 (FORMA-248, FORMA-232, FORMA-246)
tickets on the Forma work board: FORMA-247 fAuth as the demo's login, FORMA-248 fAuth's signing key in KMS, FORMA-232 and FORMA-246 assumed done under K3 (appendix B, 11.1)
fuel
a WebAssembly runtime's budget of work, after which the module is stopped; with the memory cap it bounds a parse (TH10)
full-disk encryption
encrypting a machine's whole disk, so a stolen, powered-off laptop yields nothing readable (TH15)
gp3
the general-purpose SSD storage class the database's 20 GiB are priced at (RDS storage) (11.2)
grant (grants)
a permission a database role holds, such as inserting into one table; disjoint write grants mean no two roles share a write permission (5.2, 10.5)
half-open window
an interval that includes its start and excludes its end, written [10:00, 10:10), so an event at 10:10 belongs to the next window: S02's sixth event of build-worker-17, at 10:10:00 exactly, falls outside, which is why five of its six count (7.1; S02)
health check (grace)
the load balancer's periodic probe of its target; after a run of failures, three checks 10 s apart here, it takes the target out of service (target group health checks) (5.2, 11.4)
HTML runtime
the framework's code for mounting markup in the browser; the browser workspace stops fitting its route at the first component that imports it (6.5)
IAM token (`rds-db:connect`)
a 15-minute credential the database accepts from the task role instead of a stored password; rds-db:connect is the permission to get one for a named database role (IAM database authentication) (10.5, AS12)
idempotency key (`Idempotency-Key`)
a client-chosen id sent with a command so that a retry is recognised as the same command; ik-1 and ik-2 in act 6 (IETF draft) (9, 7.2)
independent review (owner publication, policy kind)
the two kinds of publication policy: under independent review an author's own approval is refused and someone else approves; under owner publication the owner may publish their own app (R4, 6.2)
integer currency
money kept as a whole number of the smallest unit, amount_cents here, never as floating-point dollars, with one declared currency; a sum across currencies is refused (D5, N6, 7.2)
invariant
a property that must hold however the environment misbehaves, with the components that enforce it named (10.2)
island
a piece of interactive browser code attached to a page the server already rendered; the canvas is one (6.5)
isolated environment
a separate environment a restore is rehearsed into and destroyed within the hour, so the drill touches nothing live (TH7, 11.4)
jitter (jittered)
a random delay added to a retry so that many clients do not retry at the same instant (timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter) (11.4)
job (job slot)
background work, an import or a generation, whose state a person can see within 1 s; a slot is one job's place in the worker, and a full slot answers 429 (6.4, 9)
just in time (just-in-time)
granting a role only for the task at hand and letting it lapse after, so nobody holds standing power; the operator role lasts one take (TH5, 10.5)
K1 to K5
the head's kickoff rulings of 2026-10-22, recorded in both tasks' intake: K1 the typed definition, K2 the mode, K3 the stack tickets assumed done, K4 fAuth first, K5 Parquet and DuckDB (reading note)
key management (data key)
the cloud's key service, KMS, holding one data key per organization and the platform's own key for the operator prefix; deleting an organization's key makes its objects unreadable (6.6, 8, 10.6)
key set (`kid`)
fAuth's published set of public signing keys, each named by a key id (kid) that a token's header carries, so a token is checked against the right key (RFC 7517, section 5) (5.1, 10.5)
keychain
the operating system's encrypted store for secrets, which asks before releasing one; the operator's keys (AS12) live in it (6.7, TH15)
L2
the factory's middle document level, for one service with its own stores, API and operations built by one team: it sets the record's length and asks for every section's full content, a fresh reviewer and a security reviewer; the head set it at kickoff (cover; the reading note's K2)
Labeled step
a seeded, simulated or manual step named in the packet and excluded from acceptance (G6, D7); 13.3 lists them: seeded, simulated by the rehearsal script, manual. from the record's glossary
lease
a time-limited claim on a job, 120 s here; until it runs out no other worker may take the job (6.9, 11.2)
linked views
views that share one filter, so a selection in one re-queries them all (R3, 6.5)
live work
saved work on a published app, as opposed to trial entries in a draft's preview (R5, 7.1)
load balancer
the host's edge, P1: it ends TLS and forwards requests to the one task over plaintext HTTP inside the host's network (6.6, 10.6)
lockfile (lockfiles)
the files pinning every dependency to an exact version, from which the image is built (6.7, 11.1)
logic bug
a mistake in honest code, such as a handler that forgets a check; the database roles' grants contain it, but nothing inside the host contains code an attacker runs in the process (5.2, SA1)
manifest
the list of what a fixture state or the packet holds; a state is sealed by a digest over its manifest and the build digest (8, TH2)
markup modules
apps written as generated markup rather than as a typed definition; the earlier designs' approach, reversed by the platform (12.3)
Maya (Sarah, Jordan)
Northstar's three fictional people: Maya builds both apps, Sarah reviews and approves, Jordan reopens shared work and starts his own (A2, 4.1)
MCP
the Model Context Protocol, by which an assistant application connects to outside tools and data (MCP); design B v5 had a scene on it (3.2, 12.3)
memento
the design pattern that saves an object's state so it can be restored later without exposing how the object stores it; the record calls a fixture state one (Memento) (6.7)
minimal login
the platform's own simple sign-in, kept behind the same adapter as the fallback if fAuth fails; proven on every build, switched before a take, never during (A12, D4, 11.1)
model provider
the hosted model that proposes app definitions from schemas and synthetic rows; only role worker calls it (5.1, 6.4)
module privacy
a language rule that only code inside one module can construct or call something; it stops an honest mistake elsewhere, not hostile code running in the process (10.5)
Multi-AZ (standby)
a synchronous copy of the database in a second availability zone that takes over if the primary fails; the demo has none (Multi-AZ) (5.2, 8)
NAT gateway
the managed path that lets private resources reach the Internet without being reachable from it; the demo has none and uses the task's public address instead (NAT gateways) (11.1, 11.2)
Northstar
the fictional company whose Security and Finance spaces the demo runs in (2, 5)
Object Lock
an S3 setting that stores objects write-once-read-many; in compliance mode no user, the root user included, can delete or overwrite them before their retention date (S3 Object Lock) (TH7, TH15)
object versions (versioned bucket)
S3 keeping earlier versions of each object, so an overwrite or a delete can be undone (S3 versioning) (8, TH2)
one-way door (two-way door)
a decision expensive to reverse, against one that can be changed later; 5.3 labels each (Amazon's 2015 letter) (1, 5.3)
open-loop replay (open-loop)
a load test that sends requests at a fixed rate whatever the system's speed, so a slowing system is not spared (11.4)
operator (operators)
the one person who provisions, resets, restores and files the packet, reading only synthetic data (4.1); in D5's "integer currency operators", instead, a registered calculation an app definition may call (D5)
operator prefix
the part of object storage, under the platform's own key, that holds the fixture states and the packet (6.7, 8)
operator role
the platform role that reaches only the reset, the administration calls and the operator views, never an organization's data; taken just in time for one take (9, 10.5)
operator views
the platform's pages and calls for jobs, audit and the build digest, which return audit events, job states and the build digest, synthetic data only in the demo (6.7, 7.3)
Operator's machine
(B9): the laptop holding the keychain, the actors' profiles, the raw export and the packet; the demo's own boundary (7.3, TH15). from the record's glossary
organization
a company on the platform, with its own members, spaces, policy, data key and rows; Northstar and the canary are the two (2, D2)
outcome (stored outcome)
the stored result of a record command under its idempotency key, returned unchanged to any retry for 24 hours (6.3, 9)
owner credential
the database's administrative credential, which creates the roles; used once by the provisioning script, then rotated into Secrets Manager (TH5, AS12)
p50 (median)
the value half the measurements fall below: the typical case (N3)
p99 (99th percentile)
the value 99 in 100 measurements fall below: the tail, meaningful only over hundreds of samples (SRE book) (N3, 11.3)
Packet
the evidence delivered with the recording: pins, both definitions and digests, fixtures, receipts, record outcomes, admission reports and the rehearsal log (S07, R9). from the record's glossary
Parquet
a columnar file format, values of one column stored together, in which each imported source revision is kept immutable (Parquet file format) (5, 6.4)
parser bomb
a small file that expands to a huge one when parsed, such as a compressed XLSX inflating past its expanded cap (OWASP file upload cheat sheet) (10.4, TH10)
passkey
a sign-in credential kept on the person's device instead of a password, built on the W3C's Web Authentication standard (WebAuthn); fAuth's server supports it and the demo leaves its button unwired (3.2)
patch (semantic diff)
a change to a draft expressed against a named earlier revision; the semantic diff shows what changed in meaning, a measure or a field, rather than which characters moved (R3, 7.1)
phase 7
the factory's finish phase, the seventh after intake in the Start here tab's account of how the record was made: the summary written last, the record built and sent through the gate, a script, fresh reviewers and the cross-checks; the platform record is cited at its phase 7 commit, the version that passed its gate (cover, 2, appendix B)
pilot
a first real customer's use of the platform on real data, under agreed terms; out of scope here (3.2, 13.2)
pin (pinned)
fixed to one exact version: a dependency at one commit, such as Forma at 2006423b, or a case to the publication it was started on until an explicit adoption (2, R6)
pin file
the file in the repository, at the build's tag, that holds the fixture states' digests apart from the store they protect (TH2, AS9)
PKCE (code verifier, S256)
proof key for code exchange: the client sends the hash (S256, SHA-256) of a random code verifier when sign-in starts and the verifier itself when it redeems the code, so a code stolen on its way back cannot be redeemed (RFC 7636) (D9, 6.7, 10.5)
Platform key, management key
fAuth's credentials for creating tenants and for configuring one tenant, held only by the operator's shell (AS12, AR3). from the record's glossary
pre-rehearsal snapshot
a stored copy of the whole database taken before each rehearsal, restorable into a new instance; the database's only backup (DB snapshots) (6.6, 8, 11.1)
Pre-take assertion
the provisioning script's check of memberships, policies, fAuth's user list, row counts, a dry sign-in and the rate limit before every take (6.7, 11.1). from the record's glossary
preview store
where trial form entries in a draft's preview are written, apart from live work, so publication carries none of them (7.1)
primitive (primitives)
a building block of the renderer library, a component kind or an operator; Spend Review uses some that Northstar's app never did (4.2, 6.5)
principal (typed principal)
the verified identity a request acts as; inside the one process it travels as a typed value that only the authorizer's module can construct (10.5)
provider tokens
the units a model provider bills by, in and out; the cost table's last line (11.2, N10)
Provisioning script
(P9): the operator's idempotent script that creates the tenants, users, spaces, memberships, policies, the client row and role reset, and writes the fixture states (6.7). from the record's glossary
public client (registered client)
an OAuth client the identity service knows by a registration but which holds no secret; PKCE ties each code to the client that started the sign-in (RFC 6749, section 2.1) (6.7, D9)
public IPv4 address
an Internet address charged by the hour; the cost table counts three, the load balancer's two and the task's (VPC pricing) (11.2)
publication
the record, written only by the control plane, that an exact definition digest was approved under the organization's policy and now runs (6.2, 7.1)
rate limit (login limit)
a cap on how many requests a caller may make in a period; fAuth's login limit is raised for rehearsals (11.1, 11.4)
READ COMMITTED (SERIALIZABLE)
two transaction isolation levels: under the first each statement sees what was committed when it began, so rules across rows need explicit locks; under the second transactions behave as if run one at a time (transaction isolation) (6.2, 6.3, 8)
real-data disclosure
the platform's option to let real rows reach the model provider, only in the fields an organization's policy names; off in the demo, where every row is synthetic (N8; platform N8)
receipt
the server's record of exactly which sources, revisions, parameters and policy produced a number, so the number can be reproduced and checked (reading note, 6.3)
record command
a declared command that changes an internal record in one transaction, with an expected version and an idempotency key; Spend Review's decision is one (R7, 6.3)
recovery view
the authorized current state returned with a 409, so the person can redo the edit on top of it (6.3, 9)
redirect URI
the one address the identity service may send the browser back to with a code; registering exactly one means a code cannot be delivered elsewhere (SR3, TH3)
reduction
a way the demo is smaller than the platform (fewer, smaller, by hand) that keeps the platform's interface for the thing reduced (6.8, R10)
region
a geographic area of the cloud with its own data centres; prices are US East's until the head names one (11.2, 13.2)
rehearsal
a timed whole run of the six acts, about 30 minutes, filmed at most twice, so one or two whole-run takes; ten are planned (appendix A, 4.2)
Rehearsal flag
the environment variable in the demo's task definition under which alone the reset route registers, with role reset present; never set in the platform's deployment (6.7, 11.1, SI7). from the record's glossary
rehearsal log
the packet's account of a take: times per act, sample sizes, warm or cold, and every labeled step (6.7, R9)
Rehearsal script
the take's driver on the operator's machine, over the Chrome DevTools Protocol: it brings one actor's profile forward at a time and makes 13.3's simulated faults at the client, a response held late, a response dropped after the server answered, the stale and reused-key requests; it adds no code to the product (D3; 11.1). from the record's glossary
Reset
(P11): the job that restores a named fixture state between takes under its own database role, keeping audit and sessions and bumping the membership epoch (6.7, 8, 9). from the record's glossary
residual risk
the risk left after the mitigations, rated on the same scale (10.4)
result cache
the data service's 2 GiB in-memory store of computed results; the reset flushes it so no take sees the last one's results, and the spike measures with it empty (6.3, 8, 11.2)
retake
running a take again from the fixture state before its act, after a failure ended it; retaking an act retakes the acts after it, since each starts from the state the last ended in (8, 11.1, 13.1)
retrieval
the search over an organization's index, the platform's catalog metadata and curated examples and later its published apps, that finds parts a new app can reuse; its index may lag a publication by 60 s (6.4, 7.1)
retrieved (adapted, generated)
the three labels on each part of a new app: found as it was, found and changed, or newly proposed by the model (R3, 7.1)
revocation
removing a grant or a membership; the epoch moves, so the next request within 5 s is denied, queued results included; a download already made cannot be recalled (R6, 7.1)
rollout (waves)
releasing a new build in stages, each to a share of traffic, so a bad one reaches few; the demo has one build for the whole recording and no waves (11.1)
row-level security
PostgreSQL policies that filter every row a role reads or writes, here by organization (row security policies) (3.1, 6.6, 8)
RPO (recovery point objective)
the most recent data a restore may lose, measured in time; here one rehearsal (AWS recovery objectives) (8, TH7)
RTO (recovery time objective)
the longest a restore may take; unknown until S06's drill times one (8, 11.4)
runbook
the written steps an operator follows when something happens; here the take's procedure is the runbook (11.4)
sandbox (parser sandbox)
the confined place the untrusted file parser runs: the WebAssembly module with no system interface, its memory cap and its fuel (5.2, 6.4)
sanitised HAR export (HAR)
HAR, the HTTP Archive, is a JSON file of a browser's captured requests; Chrome's sanitised export leaves out the Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers and nothing else (Chrome DevTools) (6.7, TH6)
scene
one of the six acts as the controlling definition calls them (§16; numbered 1 to 6 in section 9), or a filmed moment within an act that shows one mechanism, such as Maya's refused publish in act 4 (G6, D7)
seam
the interface a reduction keeps, through which the platform's full mechanism later replaces it without changing what is built on it (6.8, R10)
Secrets Manager
AWS's store for secrets; the owner credential and fAuth's database credential rotate into it after their one use, with no standing reader (Secrets Manager) (TH5, 10.6)
service token
the platform's signed, short-lived token between roles that run as separate services; not minted in the one process, and the seam for when the roles split (10.5)
session adapter (identity adapter)
the one component that turns a verified sign-in into a platform session, so the identity provider behind it can change without the rest noticing (6.1, D4)
shredding
deleting data by deleting the key it is encrypted under, instead of finding every copy; after delivery both organizations' keys are scheduled for deletion (10.6, 11.1)
sign-out everywhere (sign out everywhere)
ending every session of the actors at once; here it also bumps the membership epochs, so every open tab is denied within 5 s (10.6, TH15)
SLO (SLA)
an objective is a target for a measured value over a window; an agreement is a promise to users with consequences if it is missed; the demo has neither (SRE book) (3.2, A8, 11.3)
soft-deleted
marked deleted and hidden but kept, so it can be undone; fAuth's tenants are soft-deleted after delivery (10.6)
space
an area of apps inside an organization, Security and Finance here; grants, not the organization boundary, keep a Security-only member out of Finance (R7, 7.2)
spend limit
