a cap on what the provider's account unit may be billed, set just above the month's tokens; its error is never retried (11.2)
Spend Review
the demo's second app: a queue, a detail view and a decision form over a spending table in Finance (1, 7.2)
Spike
the measurement before any scene: the path from definition to reopen on the real library and route, the commit's latency, the restart maximum, the route's bytes and its server render rate (R11, D8). from the record's glossary
SSE-KMS
S3 encrypting each object on the server with a key held in the key management service; here one key per organization (SSE-KMS) (10.6)
status tag ([built], [proposed])
the bracketed mark saying how real a part is: [built] exists at a named pin, [proposed] is this design, still to be written, and [reduced: the platform's X] marks where the demo has something smaller than the platform's X, with a seam for X to return through; a tag may name the part it covers, as in [built: the rendering]; the platform's fourth, [deferred], designed for later, marks nothing in this record (reading note, 5; platform 5)
STRIDE
the six threat categories the table classifies by: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege (Microsoft) (10.4)
Supervisor
the process inside the container that restarts the binary in place, so a restart is a process restart, not a task replacement (5.2, 11.2). from the record's glossary
synthetic data (synthetic rows)
made-up data that describes no real person or company; every number in the demo is computed from it (A10, 4.2)
Synthetic label
the organization row's synthetic flag the provisioning script sets and no member can, required on every organization before a reset (section 9). from the record's glossary
system interface
the operating-system functions, files, sockets and clocks, that a host may give a WebAssembly module, standardised as WASI (WASI); the parser gets none, only an input and an output (5.2, 6.4)
take
one recording of an act or of the whole run; the recording keeps one take of each act, each starting from the state the last ended in, and the per-take counts of 4.2, 11.2 and 11.3, N2's restarts among them, are of whole-run takes, up to twenty over ten rehearsals (appendix A, 4.2, 8)
task definition
the description ECS starts a task from, with its image, CPU, memory and environment; the rehearsal flag is one environment variable in the demo's (task definitions) (11.1, TH1)
task replacement
ECS stopping a task and starting a new one from the image: pull, start, registration, health check; unmeasured against N2's 30 s, which is why a supervisor restarts in place (5.2, 11.2)
task role
the cloud identity a task runs as; here one task role may connect as all five database roles, which is why the walls stop mistakes and not code inside the process (task IAM roles) (5.2, 10.5, AR2)
tenant (tenants)
in fAuth, a separate group of users with its own sign-in settings; the demo has one per organization, northstar and the canary's (6.7)
the editions
the versions of this record the factory derives for particular readers, such as a reader's edition with presenter notes and this annotated edition; A1's "If wrong: the editions" means a different audience changes those, not the design (A1; Start here)
the head
the person who commissions this record, approves it and owns every residual risk (cover, 10.4, 10.7)
threat actor
who attacks, with their capability and motive, lettered TA; an operator script bug is one here (10.3)
tombstone
a small marker left where data was deleted, so readers know it is gone; S06's deletion takes the platform's tombstone path, not the reset (8)
trust boundary (trust boundaries)
a line on a data-flow diagram where trust changes, lettered B; each crossing gets a threat row (7, 10.2)
trust level
a class of caller with a given power, lettered TL; the demo adds the canary's member, the operator's shell, the recording browser and role reset (10.2)
trusted computing base (trusted base)
the components that must work for the invariants to hold; here the whole binary, the reset's guard and grants and the recorder's filter (Building Secure and Reliable Systems, chapter 6) (6.3, 6.7, 10.2)
two-person rule
a rule that a dangerous action needs a second person's approval; impossible with one founder, so accepted away (AR1)
typed props
the plain values, flags, lists and numbers, that the server computes for a renderer to draw (5.2)
unique index
an index that refuses a second row with the same key; on (organization, work, record, version) it turns two racing creates into one commit and one conflict (unique indexes) (7.2, 8)
vCPU (GiB, GB)
a unit of compute, and two sizes of gigabyte: a GiB is 1,024 cubed bytes and a GB 1,000 cubed; the cost table uses both (11.2)
verified offline
checking a token's signature against the cached key set without calling fAuth, so fAuth being down stops new sign-ins only (5.1, 6.9)
WAF
a web application firewall that filters requests by rules before they reach the application (AWS WAF); reduced away here, an address allowlist standing in during rehearsals (5.2, 10.4)
WCAG 2.2
the W3C's accessibility guidelines; N12 checks every state of the demo's components at level AA (WCAG 2.2) (N12)
WebAssembly module (WebAssembly)
a portable binary that runs inside a host program which decides exactly which functions it may call, so it reaches nothing the host does not hand it (WebAssembly security) (5.2, 6.4)
whole-window denominator
dividing the window's bytes by the whole ten minutes, 1,140,000 ÷ 10 = 114,000 bytes a minute, rather than by the five minutes the included events span, which gives 228,000; act 3's patch adds the transfer-rate measure with it, a change to a calculation rather than to a style (R3, 7.1; platform 2; S02)
work access (app access)
two separate grants, one to open a given case and one to run the app; a bare link carries neither (R6, 7.1)
YC (YC partner)
Y Combinator, the startup programme the recording is made for; a partner there is the viewer the demo is judged by (A1, 4)

Exercises

16 questions, each placed at the end of the section it follows. Answer in writing before opening the answer.

Exercise 1 after 1

The summary names three one-way doors: the organization id in every key (D2), the platform's definition and command code (D3), and the integrity rule once the packet is submitted (D7). Before reading 5.3, write for each what reversing it a month after the recording would require, and whose action it would need. Then say why the hand-added client row (D9), awkward as it is, is not on the list.

Answer

D2 needs our own action, but on everything stored: the organization id is in every key in every store from the first row, so reversing it means a migration of all stored data and every reference to it, and the isolation the recording showed would then describe keys the system no longer has ("keys cannot be retrofitted on camera", 12.2). D3 needs our own action too: a second implementation of the definition, admission and command code, after which every contract reopens and act 6 would have proved an implementation that no longer runs (12.2). D7 needs someone else's: the packet is with YC, so relabeling a step would take the recipient's action, not ours ("a packet cannot be relabeled after YC has it", 12.2). Two doors are one-way because of what a reversal would touch, the third because the reversal is out of our hands. D9 is one row and one redirect URI in fAuth's database: replacing it, with the refresh-cookie bridge or a future client API (13.2's POST /manage/oauth-clients), is our action on one adapter's input and touches nothing the platform stores, which is why 5.3 marks it two-way (1, 5.3, 12.2).

Exercise 2 after 2

Write a fourth shortcut in section 2's form, for act 5, share and reuse: the fastest way to make Jordan's reopening of Maya's case look right on screen, other than section 2's third, which already has one session play everyone. Then name what it leaves untested, by the goal or requirement it fails, and the observation in the packet that would expose it.

Answer

One version: give Jordan a copy of Maya's case under a new id; the screen shows the same findings. A copy is a different work id, so G3's "reopens Maya's case by its work id at its pinned publication with its records" fails, and so does R6's same id, records and pin. It also outlives revocation, because revoking Jordan's grant on Maya's case does not touch his copy, so R6's "revocation denies later results" cannot be shown, and a concurrent edit cannot conflict because the two cases share no record (G3's visible conflict). The packet would expose it twice. Act 5's "both work ids" must be Maya's own id, reopened under Jordan's session, and his new one for ops-runner-04; with the copy, the case Jordan opens carries an id Maya never had. And no denial follows the revocation (5 act 5's "Captured"; 7.1 act 5; S04). Any answer is right that names a mechanism replaced by its appearance and the identity or denial that the evidence would then lack (2).

Exercise 3 after 3.3

It is the morning of a rehearsal and sign-in is broken, in one of three ways: (a) fAuth's service is down; (b) the provisioning script inserted the client row with a typo in its redirect URI; (c) the head learns that fAuth at the pin cannot hold a registered client at all. From section 3 alone, name the assumption each case breaks, if any, and what you would do. Then derive what the assumptions only imply: for (a), what must already be true of the design for A12's "only act 1 changes" to hold; for (c), which goal A13's fallback strains, and why. Check (a) against 6.9 and 11.1, and (b) against SR3 and 11.4, when you reach them.

Answer

(a) breaks the first half of A12, fAuth opening act 1: wait for fAuth, or switch before the take to A12's fallback, the platform's minimal login behind the same adapter; either way only act 1's scene changes. For "only act 1 changes" to hold, a session must not need fAuth once it exists: the platform keeps its own sessions and checks fAuth's tokens without calling fAuth. It does: sessions are PostgreSQL rows that live 12 h, tokens are verified offline against the cached key set, and the fallback is switched before a take, never during it (5.1, 6.1, 6.9, 11.1; 11.4's fAuth row: act 1 waits, later acts continue). (b) breaks no assumption: A13 holds, since fAuth can hold the row, and the row is simply wrong, so nothing in the design moves. Correct the row by hand and prove sign-in before the camera rolls; the record's check is the dry sign-in, which stops a take until it passes (SR3, 6.1; 11.4's row for the provisioning script's output), and D9 being a two-way door is why a hand fix is enough. (c) breaks A13: its fallback is the same-site refresh-cookie bridge behind the same adapter, so act 1's mechanism changes and D9 would be revisited. The goal it strains is G7: the bridge is a session contract the platform never ships, so either the demo signs in in a way the platform does not, or the platform carries it for one demo, and 12.2 rejects it for that reason (12.2's table, 12.3). The three mornings look alike, "sign-in is broken", and the assumptions separate them: one has a fallback, one is an error to correct, one moves a decision (3.3, 5.3, 12.2).

Exercise 4 after 4.2

4.2's basis is ten rehearsals, each one whole-run take filmed at most twice, and a 30-minute rehearsal holds about 360 interactions: about 200 six-view refreshes (1,200 operations), 40 navigations, 20 commits, and edits and uploads for the rest. Rebuild the 360 and the 1,200, and work out how many edits and uploads remain. Then, before reading 11.3, decide over how many rehearsals you would pool navigations and commits to report a p99, and count the samples that would lie above the p99 in each case, compared with the 200 refreshes of one whole-run take.

Answer

30 minutes is 1,800 s; one action every 5 s is 360 interactions; 200 refreshes times six views is 1,200 query operations; 360 − 200 − 40 − 20 = 100 edits and uploads. A p99 leaves one sample in a hundred above it, so one whole-run take's 200 refreshes leave 2 above it, enough to say something, while its 40 navigations or 20 commits leave less than one, so their "p99" would just be the slowest sample. Pooling ten rehearsals, one whole run each, gives 400 navigations, 4 above the p99, and 200 commits, 2 above, which is what 11.3 does; the refresh needs no pooling because one take of the whole run already holds 200 (4.2, N3, 11.3). The counts are per whole run: a take of one act holds only that act's share of them.

Exercise 5 after 5.2

Rebuild a take's burst from 5.2's rules: how many query operations one filter change puts at the data service, how many run and how many wait, how many waves, and how long at 100 ms a warm operation. Then redo it for a version of Spend Review with eight linked views during a scene where two actors act at once: the operations, the waves, the time, any 429s, and the warm operation time at which N3's 2 s would stop holding.

Answer

One actor, six linked views: six operations; the data service admits two of an organization's at once, so 2 run and 4 wait, three waves, 0.3 s at 100 ms, inside N3's 2 s (5.2); the waves are why 6.3 puts the ceiling at a warm operation of about 650 ms, three waves inside 2 s. Two actors, eight views: 16 operations in one organization, 2 running and 14 waiting; 429s begin only past 20 waiting (5.2; platform 6.3), so none is refused; eight waves of two, 0.8 s at 100 ms, still inside 2 s; and N3's 2 s stops holding at a warm operation of about 2 s ÷ 8 = 250 ms. The envelope's burst of 24 is different in kind: 22 waiting is two past the 20, those two are the 429s, and that is why four simultaneous actors are not a take (5.2, 6.3, 11.2).

Exercise 6 after 5.2

5.2 has the supervisor restart the binary "inside the load balancer's grace of three failed checks 10 s apart". (a) From those two numbers, how soon after a crash can the third failed check come? (b) Predict what the take sees if the binary takes 40 s to come back. (c) Act 4's restart drill falls between acts 3 and 6, where N9 allows no deploy. From N9's own wording, decide what a change must alter to count as a deploy, and so whether the drill is one; then design the check that would tell a restart from a deploy in the evidence, and compare it with 6.7 and TH14 when you reach them.

Answer

(a) Checks come every 10 s, so the first failure lands up to 10 s after the crash and the third 20 s after the first: between about 20 and 30 s after the crash the target is taken out of service (5.2; the load balancer's failure threshold). (b) At 40 s the target has been taken out of service, so the load balancer stops sending it requests and Maya's reload fails until the binary is back and the checks pass again (11.4's first row: the target re-registers on the next check); the case reopens later than N2's 30 s, and a miss of N2 ends the take (11.1, step 5), so act 4 is retaken from s3, and the acts after it with it (8). One more consequence is an inference the record implies without stating it: 5.2 puts the restart inside the grace so that it triggers "no task replacement", so a restart past the grace may bring the task replacement as well, the sequence nobody has timed against 30 s (RK8). (c) N9 asks for one build digest for both apps and no deploy between acts 3 and 6, so what it forbids is a change of the image that runs. A restart, in place or even as a new task, runs the same image digest, so it is not a deploy, as 6.7 says outright: "a task start on the same image digest, act 4's restart drill, is not a deploy". The check follows from that definition: read the task's image digest at the take's start and end, and the deploy log between them. A restart leaves both unchanged; a deploy changes the digest or writes to the log, and either fails acceptance. That is TH14's M28, run by the evidence recorder (6.7, N9, TH14).

Exercise 7 after 6.4

Act 2 must capture one oversize refusal (S06). The platform record's example of a bomb is a 9 MiB XLSX that inflates past 100 MiB (platform 7.1). Explain why a 9 MiB file could never test the demo's expansion cap. Then, before reading 7.1's act 2, predict what a 4 MiB file that inflates past 50 MiB tests instead: which of A6's limits fires, and where; what stops and what survives; what the job and the recording show. Finally say what the module's 2 GiB memory cap is for, if a limit fires long before it.

Answer

A6 caps an XLSX at 5 MiB compressed and 50 MiB expanded, and a file's compressed size is known before anything opens it, so a 9 MiB file is turned away at the size check and never expands: it tests the byte cap, not the expansion cap (appendix C confirms it in TH10's M19: "the byte caps refuse before parsing"). In the platform, whose compressed cap is 10 MiB (platform A4), the same file does reach the parser, which is why it is the platform's example. The 4 MiB file passes the byte cap, so the parser starts inflating it inside its WebAssembly sandbox and meets the 50 MiB expanded cap: the parse stops there and the file is refused, the job carries the reason, the import fails visibly, the refusal is captured, and the process and the take carry on (7.1 act 2; 11.4's parser row). The 2 GiB memory cap never fires in this case: it is the backstop. If a parse ever got past the expanded cap, the runtime would still stop the module at 2 GiB, and the task's 8 GiB is sized so that 2 GiB fits beside everything else the process holds, so even then the module, not the process, would die (7.1, 11.2; TH10's M19). What the file tests is the bounded parser that is the reduction's seam (6.4) and the property one process makes critical: a bad file costs a refusal, never the process (TH10).

Exercise 8 after 6.7

The reset keeps sessions and bumps the membership epoch. Predict what would change if it deleted every session row instead and left the epoch alone: for the take procedure, for fAuth, for role reset's grants, and for a tab still open from the previous take.

Answer

The procedure: every actor would have to sign in again through fAuth's page after every reset, instead of once within the idle hour (11.1, step 3, which relies on "the reset keeps sessions"). fAuth: more sign-ins per rehearsal push against its login limit, which the cold start already has to raise (11.1; 11.4's limiter row). The grants: role reset would need a grant on the session table, which SI7 forbids ("never deletes audit or sessions", enforced by reset's grants), so the most dangerous role in the demo would reach identity rows. The open tab: it would be denied at its next request because its session is gone, the same safety the epoch bump gives, bought with re-sign-ins. The epoch bump gets that safety without touching sessions: every open tab re-authorizes within 5 s against the restored membership rows and no session is lost (6.7, 8, TH9).

Exercise 9 after 7.2

In act 6's lost response, ik-1 is posted twice, both times with expected version 0, though after the first post the record is at version 1. Suppose P4 compared the expected version before looking for the stored outcome: predict what the second post would return and what Maya and the packet would then show, and say what finding the outcome first protects. Then compare the two ways a client can recover from a lost response, retrieving the outcome by key first (section 9's rule) or re-submitting under the same key (the path the script forces): what would each leave in the packet, and which part of act 6's claim does only the second exercise?

Answer

Version first, the second post would fail: its expected version 0 no longer matches the record's version 1, so P4 would roll back and answer 409 with the recovery view, as it does for the stale edit under ik-3 (7.2, step 5). Maya would be told that her own decision conflicted with itself, and the packet would hold a 409 for a command that had in fact committed: the retry would look like a conflict, and G4's duplicate-safe retry could not be shown. Finding the stored outcome first is what makes a retry safe whatever the client believes: the first post stored its outcome under ik-1 in the same transaction as version 1 (F7), so the second finds it before any version check and returns version 1 (F7, F8; step 4), while authorization still runs again (F4), because a key names a command, not a permission. Retrieving first would leave one POST and one GET by key: it shows that an outcome is stored, but the server never sees the command twice. The forced re-submission leaves two POSTs under one key against one record revision, one audit event and "the attempt logged apart" (7.2, step 4): it exercises the duplicate path itself, the outcome found before the version check, which is G4's "an ik-1 retry yields one revision and one audit event". That is why the record calls it "the stronger proof" and labels it simulated (7.2, 9, G6).

Exercise 10 after 8

Section 8 lists s0 and then s2, and appendix A gives the reason: act 1 changes nothing a take restores. Test that claim instead of taking it: list what act 1 leaves behind (7.1) and say why, under the reset's rules (6.7, 8), none of it matters to a take of act 2; then name a change to act 1 that would force an s1 into existence. Finally, argue why a fixture state is captured from a clean take's act end rather than written by hand as the next act's starting rows, and name the two checks that stop a state altered after its capture from being restored unnoticed.

Answer

Act 1 leaves one session and one audit row and nothing else (7.1, act 1). The reset keeps every session and every audit row and deletes only rows committed after the state's point, so restoring s0 before act 2 removes nothing act 1 made, and act 2 starts from s0 too (8; 11.1, step 2). An s1 would be needed the moment act 1 committed a row a later act depends on, for example a space created on camera instead of by the provisioning script (6.7): a reset to s0 deletes every row past s0's point, so that row would be gone before act 2. A state captured from a clean take holds only rows the build's own code wrote, a revision 5 that admission accepted, a publication 1 the control plane wrote after Sarah's approval, under the build digest the state carries (8). Rows written by hand could hold something no mechanism produced, a publication with no approval behind it, and restoring them would put a state in front of the camera that no clean take reached. The reset itself is labeled, its audit event entering the rehearsal log as seeded state (9; appendix A's labeled step), but the act filmed after it is accepted as working, so it must start from rows a real take produced. The checks: the reset recomputes the state's digest, over manifest and build digest, against the pin file kept apart in the repository and refuses a mismatch with 412 (M3), and the recorder diffs each restored manifest, publication and approval digests included, against its capture (M4) (TH2, 8, 9).

Exercise 11 after 10.4

The canary suite must get a 404 for every replay, each paired with the owner's 200 for the same identifier in that take (R8, SR2). Say in one sentence which property the suite proves. TH4's preventative half already puts row-level security on every table: argue why the row still needs this detective half, naming one thing the suite can catch that row-level security cannot. Then describe two different broken setups, one in the build and one in the suite's own script, that a suite of bare 404s would pass and the paired suite would fail.

Answer

It proves that nothing of Northstar's, data or metadata, reaches a session of another organization (G5, N7): it is TH4's detective half, M8, where SI1 is at stake, the platform's scope invariant that every read and write is scoped by the verified session's organization, never a request value (platform 10.2). Row-level security filters rows; it cannot see the rest of an answer. A handler that answers 403 where it should answer 404, or names the app in an error, tells the canary that Northstar's identifier exists without returning a single row, which is why R8 asks for denial "before data or metadata" and 5.1 for 404 rather than 403; and a policy missing from one table is a gap the preventative half cannot report about itself. The suite checks whole answers from outside, every take, so it sees both, which is why 10.4 gives every High row a preventative and a detective half. A broken build: a change that makes a route answer 404 to everyone, its owner included; the canary's 404 then proves only that the route is broken, and the owner's missing 200 fails the take. A broken script: replays built from the previous take's identifiers, which the reset deleted, so every replay is 404 because nothing exists; again no owner 200 in this take. In both a bare 404 cannot be told from a refusal, and the paired 200 is what proves the identifier was real and reachable by its owner at the time (R8, SR2, TH4; 11.1, steps 4 and 6).

Exercise 12 after 10.6

Rank three leaks from least to most damaging, and for each say what it yields and what bounds it: (a) a copy of the oauth_clients row taken from fAuth's database; (b) fAuth's platform key, leaked a week after provisioning; (c) the operator's machine, taken during act 5. Then explain why the platform key is the first of the operator's keys to be deleted.

Answer

Least to most damaging: (b), (a), (c). (b) Nothing, if the rule was kept: the platform key creates tenants (appendix A, AS12) and "dies once the tenants exist" (10.6, M30), so a week after provisioning there is no key left to leak; it ranks first only because the rule held, and a key kept by mistake would be the power to create tenants at fAuth. (a) Next: the row holds no secret, only the client's registration and its one redirect URI (D9, 6.7). A code can be sent only to that URI, and redeeming one needs the code verifier the platform made for that one sign-in, which is never in the row (PKCE), so the copy signs nobody in; what remains is AR4, a wrong row added by hand, caught by the dry sign-in (M6). (c) Most: the machine holds every key still alive, the actors' sessions in their Chrome profiles, the raw export and the pin file at once (AS13, TH15), which is any principal in either organization and every operator power. It is bounded by M30 (fresh profiles destroyed after the last take, the raw file hashed, filtered and deleted in one step, full-disk encryption, the machine off the network except while a rehearsal runs), made visible afterwards by M31's anchored manifest, and the rest accepted (AR3). The platform key goes first because creating the tenants is the provisioning script's first fAuth step (6.7), so it is the first key whose job is over; the others still have work, the owner credential until its one run, fAuth's database credential until its one insert, the management keys until delivery (10.6). A key that will never be used again is only risk ("single use where possible", AR3).

Exercise 13 after 11.1

Diagram 03 runs Spend Review's command with no control plane, P3, on it, yet the workspace server checks every decision against the pinned publication's record schema, read from the publication row (F5). Argue why reading the row is as safe as asking P3, from who writes a publication and what it names (6.2). Then predict what migration step 4, one process to four services, would have to add if P2 asked P3 for that schema on every command instead, and which failure would then stop a decision that the design as written survives.

Answer

Only role control writes a publication, inside the platform's SERIALIZABLE transaction, and a publication names one exact approved digest (6.2); a case stays pinned to its publication until an explicit adoption (R6). So the row cannot hold a schema P3 did not admit and publish, and it cannot change under a pinned case: asking P3 again would return the same answer, at the cost of a call, and the run path needs the database, not the control plane (7.2). If P2 asked P3 on every command, step 4 would turn that in-process call into a network hop on every decision, with its own request type and a principal carried across it, the things 11.1 says step 4 needs from D1, and the control plane's service would join the hard dependencies of every published app. Today the four roles share one process, so P3 cannot fail apart from P2; after step 4 it can, and a control-plane outage or deploy would then stop decision forms, where the design as written loses only what P3 itself does, admission and publication (6.2). That is what 7.2 means by "the control plane stays off the run path at migration (G7)" (7.2, 11.1).

Exercise 14 after 11.2

Rebuild the task's 8 GiB from its five parts, and the $85 Fargate line from the task's size and unit prices. Then rebuild the month of about $170 from its five lines and its $17 a rehearsal. Finally predict both numbers if the head asks for twenty rehearsals a month instead of ten, assuming the spike and margin stay at 40 generation attempts. Which line is the driver, and does it move?

Answer

1 GiB for the binary, 2 × 1 GiB for two DuckDB operations, the parser module's 2 GiB cap, the 2 GiB result cache and 1 GiB of headroom: 8 GiB. Fargate: 2 vCPU × 730 h × $0.04048 = $59.10, plus 8 GiB × 730 h × $0.004445 = $25.96, so $85.06. The month: $85 + $26 + $22 + $24 + $11 = $168, "about $170", and $16.80, about $17, a rehearsal at ten a month, $1.10 of it tokens. Tokens: 120 attempts are 2 attempts × 2 acts × 20 takes = 80, plus 40 for the spike and margin, at 8,000 tokens in and 3,000 out, $0.032 + $0.06 = $0.092 an attempt. At twenty rehearsals, 40 takes: 160 + 40 = 200 attempts, $18.40, so the month is about $175 and a rehearsal about $8.80. The driver is the Fargate line, and it does not move, because hosting runs whether or not anyone rehearses (11.2).

Exercise 15 after 12.2

Make the strongest case, in three sentences and with this record's own numbers, for recording on the founder's machine or a single virtual machine instead of the ECS task (D10's alternative): what it would save a month and a rehearsal, and what the scenes would lose by it. Then argue the other side from G7 and from what the founder's machine could never measure, and, before reading 13.2, predict the one measurement that should settle the host, and which result would move the demo off the task.

Answer

For: on the founder's machine about $157 of the $168 month disappears, everything but the $11 of tokens, since a take's marginal cost is its tokens, "all the founder's machine (D10) costs" (11.2), so about $15.70 of each rehearsal's $16.80; a virtual machine needs no ECS account (12.2's table); one operator (A3) has one fewer system to provision and watch; and the restart the recording times is already a process restart under a supervisor (5.2), so the scenes lose nothing a task replacement would have shown. Against: the platform's own deployment is ECS on Fargate in one region, so a demo on the task is the platform's first deployment and its migration starts there, while a laptop or a virtual machine is a deployment to redo (G7). And the number the host question waits on, how long a full task replacement takes against N2's 30 s, can be measured only on the task: 5.2 leaves it unmeasured and times one apart, and the founder's machine "cannot time a task replacement" (12.2's table). So the deciding measurement is that one timed task replacement: if it meets N2's 30 s the task stays; if it misses, the host becomes one virtual machine, which is 13.2's current choice (5.2, 11.2, 12.2, 13.2).

Exercise 16 after 13.3

The second-app objection is answered by one fact: policy is per organization. Make the founder's best case for letting Maya publish Spend Review herself under owner publication, to save ten seconds; then show what that change would break elsewhere in the recording and what it would prove instead. Finally, if the provisioning script set owner publication by mistake, say what a check must compare the policy row against to catch it before the camera rolls, and why checking once, right after provisioning, would not be enough.

Answer

For: Spend Review records internal decisions about synthetic expenses and pays nobody (7.2, step 6; 6.8's "no connector or external action"), so the founder can argue that a wrong decision costs little, that review adds only delay, and that ten seconds matter in a five-minute act. What it breaks: Security and Finance share Northstar's one policy row (6.2; 7.2, step 2), so owner publication for Spend Review is owner publication for the investigation app too; Maya's own publish in act 4 would succeed, and R4's refusal, the scene that proves independent review, would disappear (6.2's "act 4 loses its refusal"; RK4). What it would prove instead: that an administrator can set an owner-publication policy and the platform honours it, a claim about configurable policy rather than about a reviewer approving exactly what runs; and the partner would see an app nobody else approved, the very objection 13.3 answers. The check: the policy row against the provisioning script's manifest, the record of what the script meant to set, since the row alone cannot say it is wrong. Once is not enough, because the row can change after provisioning: the script is rerun when its output is wrong (11.4), and every reset restores rows from a captured state, so a wrong policy captured once comes back with each reset until the states are recaptured. That check is the pre-take assertion, reading each organization's one policy row against the manifest before every take (6.2; M10, as RK4 cites it), so a wrong kind stops the take before the camera rolls (R7, 13.3).

Flashcards

Click a card to flip it. "Got it" retires a card until you reset the deck; "Again" puts it back a few cards later. Progress is kept in this browser. The same cards are in flashcards.tsv for Anki (File, Import, fields front, back, deck).

Reading

The topics this design touches first, then the rest. Primary sources where they exist: the standard, the vendor's own documentation, the free chapters.

For this design

Writing and reading design documents

  • Design Docs at Google (Malte Ubl) what a design document is for, the sections most carry and why, and the case for writing down the alternatives.
  • Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals the public index of a large project's design proposals, by area, stage and release; the KEP template in the kubernetes/enhancements repository carries the production-readiness questionnaire.
  • Rust RFC book a language's accepted design proposals, one page each; new ones start from the template linked below.
  • Rust RFC template a "guide-level" explanation that teaches the change, then a "reference-level" one that specifies it.
  • Fuchsia RFC best practices include a detail only if it has material impact, asked there as whether anyone would change their vote because of it.
  • Google technical writing courses courses for engineers who write; Technical Writing One, on its own page, teaches clear, short sentences, lists and focused paragraphs.

Decisions and trade-offs

  • Documenting architecture decisions (Michael Nygard) the decision record in five parts: title, context, decision, status, consequences; adr.github.io credits it with popularising the form.
  • Markdown Architectural Decision Records (MADR) a decision-record template with the considered options, the outcome, the consequences and a confirmation, the form the alternatives section follows.
  • Amazon's 2015 shareholder letter the one-way door and two-way door distinction, in its original words.
  • Fundamentals of Software Architecture the book's companion site, with its architecture katas; the book's first chapter (not on the site) states the first law, that everything in software architecture is a trade-off, which the decision records practise.

Threat modeling and secure design

  • Threat modeling cheat sheet (OWASP) the four questions, the process and the output a threat model should have.
  • STRIDE threats (Microsoft) the six categories, each defined, most with an example.
  • Threat Modeling Manifesto the values and the anti-patterns, in one page.
  • Building Secure and Reliable Systems (Google) readable online; invariants, least privilege and recovery, and in chapter 6 the trusted computing base.
  • Application Security Verification Standard (OWASP) the verification standard: requirement lists, downloadable as CSV and JSON, for designing, building and testing web applications.
  • Secure design principles (NCSC) establish the context, make compromise difficult, make disruption difficult, make compromise detection easier, and reduce its impact.

Authentication, sessions and OAuth

  • OpenID Connect Core the ID token, its claims and how a relying party validates it.
  • OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) the authorization code flow, refresh tokens and scopes.
  • OAuth 2.0 threat model (RFC 6819) what goes wrong with tokens, and the countermeasures.
  • OAuth 2.0 security best current practice (RFC 9700) the current security advice, which updates RFC 6749 and RFC 6819.
  • Session management cheat sheet (OWASP) cookie flags, lifetimes, rotation and revocation.
  • CSRF prevention cheat sheet (OWASP) why a cookie alone is not enough for a mutation.
  • Identity-Aware Proxy overview a central authorization layer for applications reached over HTTPS, checking identity before the request reaches the app.
  • Service account impersonation (Google Cloud IAM) how one principal acts as a service account through short-lived credentials instead of a key.

Multi-tenant systems

  • Tenancy models for a multitenant solution (Microsoft) tenancy models, isolation, noisy neighbours and the cost of each choice.
  • Silo, pool and bridge models (AWS SaaS Lens) dedicating or sharing resources per tenant, and the bridge between them, where some layers are siloed and others pooled.
  • Google Identity Platform multi-tenancy identity tenants, each with its own users and sign-in providers, inside one project.

Data stores, isolation and pagination

  • Row security policies (PostgreSQL) policies the database applies to every row a role reads or writes, once row security is enabled on the table; table owners are exempt unless the table forces them, and superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS always are.
  • Transaction isolation (PostgreSQL) what read committed, repeatable read and serializable promise.
  • Use The Index, Luke: fetching the next page why offsets get slower with every page, and the seek method, keyset pagination, that does not.
  • Partitioned tables (BigQuery) how a time partition bounds what a query scans.
  • Clustered tables (BigQuery) sorting within a partition so filters on a few columns read less.
  • BI Engine (BigQuery) BigQuery's in-memory analysis service: what it caches, and how a reservation sizes it.
  • Transactional outbox writing an event in the same transaction as the row, so it is never lost; the relay may send it twice, so consumers must be idempotent.
  • Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (Stripe) the idempotency key, and what to do when the same request arrives twice.
  • Designing Data-Intensive Applications the book's site; the book is the source of the consistency, partitioning and fault-model vocabulary used here.

Operating, deploying and observing

  • Monitoring distributed systems (SRE book) the four golden signals and what to page on.
  • Automating safe, hands-off deployments (Amazon Builders' Library) waves, bake time and automatic rollback.
  • Using load shedding to avoid overload (Amazon Builders' Library) goodput, and what to drop first.
  • Postmortem culture (SRE book) blameless postmortems, and the follow-up actions that keep an incident from recurring.
  • Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework recommendations by pillar for systems on Google Cloud.
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework the same idea by pillar for systems on AWS.

Requirements, numbers and service levels

  • Latency numbers every programmer should know the ladder of costs, from an L1 cache reference past a round trip across an ocean, now with rows for model calls, that estimates start from.
  • Service Level Objectives (Google SRE book) why percentiles, what an objective is for, and why 100 percent is the wrong target.
  • Implementing SLOs (SRE workbook) a step-by-step recipe for choosing indicators and setting objectives, and a pointer to the workbook's example SLO document.
  • arc42 quality requirements the scenario form, with a source, a stimulus and a measurable response.

Queues, jobs and background work

  • Cloud Run request timeout one platform's ceiling on a request's life, up to an hour, and its advice to make long requests idempotent and resumable.
  • Pub/Sub push subscriptions push delivery to an HTTPS endpoint, its acknowledgement deadline, redelivery and authenticated push.
  • Understand Cloud Tasks scheduled and rate-limited delivery of work to a service.
  • Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs (Amazon Builders' Library) the age of messages in the queue as the backlog signal, and fairness between tenants.
  • Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (Amazon Builders' Library) the retry rules behind every "with backoff" in the failure table.

Builds, packages and the release path

  • SLSA build track (v1.2) the build levels, each a stronger guarantee about how an artefact was built and how hard its provenance is to forge.
  • Secure use reference (GitHub Actions) one CI platform's hardening: script injection, locking or pinning third-party actions, OpenID Connect instead of stored cloud keys.
  • Generating provenance statements (npm) one registry's signed link from a package to the source and the build that produced it, and how consumers verify it.

Diagrams that say something

  • The C4 model context, containers, components, code: the four hierarchical levels this document's pictures follow.
  • C4 diagram notation what every box and arrow must carry to be readable without its author.
  • C4 review checklist the questions to ask of any architecture diagram before it ships.
  • Mermaid sequence diagrams the syntax behind the sequence diagram in the data flows section.

Front ends in the browser

  • TanStack Table the headless grid that leaves the markup to the design system.
  • TanStack Query server state in the browser: caching, and refetching in the background.
  • Progress indicators (Nielsen Norman Group) a looped spinner for waits of 2 to 10 seconds, a percent-done bar for longer ones, and why the bar makes a long wait tolerable.
  • Render and Commit (React) trigger, render, commit: the steps from a change of state to the screen, in one framework's words.
  • Intro to reactivity (Solid) signals and their subscribers, so that a change updates only what reads it.
  • Islands architecture (Astro) interactive components on an otherwise static, server-rendered page, each hydrated on its own.
  • Web Vitals (web.dev) loading, interactivity and visual stability, measured on real page loads and assessed at the 75th percentile.
  • Strict Content Security Policy (web.dev) a nonce- or hash-based policy with 'strict-dynamic' against cross-site scripting, and its limits.
  • require-trusted-types-for (MDN) the directive that controls what may reach the DOM's script-injection sinks.
